rustamid-imamate.t: An Ibadi imamate ruled from Tahert in Algeria, known for learning, trade and religious tolerance in the early Islamic Maghreb.
rustamid-imamate.o: Abd al-Rahman ibn Rustam, of Persian descent, had governed Kairouan for the Ibadi Imamate of Tripolitania. After its defeat in 761 he fled west and founded the city of Tahert (near modern Tiaret), where around 777 the Ibadi community elected him imam.
rustamid-imamate.r: In theory the imamate was elective, but in practice the Rustamids ruled hereditarily, advised by religious scholars. Tahert attracted merchants from Kairouan, Basra and Persia, and its scholars debated theology freely. The state relied on Berber tribes and Ibadi communities as far as the Jebel Nafusa and Ouargla, and profited from caravan trade to the Sahara. Aflah ibn Abd al-Wahhab ruled for about fifty years.
rustamid-imamate.e: In 909 Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i, leading the Kutama armies of the Fatimid movement, captured Tahert. The surviving Ibadis fled to Ouargla and Sedrata, and later to the Mzab, where the Mzab confederation preserved their tradition.

republic-of-colombia.t: The centralised Colombian republic founded by the constitution of 1886, which lost Panama, endured decades of internal conflict and made peace with the FARC in 2016.
republic-of-colombia.o: After the Liberal federation of the United States of Colombia failed, Rafael Núñez and the Conservatives imposed the constitution of 1886, which created a centralised Republic of Colombia, gave the president strong powers and restored the Catholic Church's role in education.
republic-of-colombia.r: The Thousand Days' War of 1899 to 1902 devastated the country, and in 1903 Panama seceded with United States support. Coffee became the main export. The assassination of Jorge Eliécer Gaitán in 1948 unleashed La Violencia, a civil conflict ended by the power-sharing National Front from 1958 to 1974. Guerrilla groups such as the FARC, founded in 1964, and drug cartels such as Pablo Escobar's in Medellín fuelled violence for decades.
republic-of-colombia.e: A new constitution in 1991 replaced that of 1886. President Juan Manuel Santos signed a peace agreement with the FARC in 2016, winning the Nobel Peace Prize. Gustavo Petro became the first left-wing president in 2022.

ramadanids.t: A Turkmen dynasty that ruled Adana and the Cilician plain for over 250 years, first under the Mamluks and then under the Ottomans.
ramadanids.o: After the Mamluks broke the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, Turkmen of the Uc Ok group settled the Cilician plain. Around 1352 their leader Ramadan Bey was recognised by the Mamluks as emir of the region, with Adana as his seat.
ramadanids.r: The Ramadanids ruled as hereditary Mamluk vassals over Turkmen tribes and the cotton and grain lands of the Cilician plain, guarding the frontier with the Karamanids and the Ottomans. In 1516-1517 they went over to Selim I and were kept as hereditary governors of the Ottoman sanjak of Adana. Piri Mehmed Pasha, a 16th-century ruler, built the Great Mosque complex of Adana.
ramadanids.e: The family lost its hereditary governorship in 1608, when Adana became an ordinary Ottoman province. The Ramazanoglu mansion and mosque in Adana survive.

republic-of-venice.t: The 'Most Serene Republic', a merchant state on the lagoon that ruled a maritime empire across the Adriatic and Aegean for a thousand years until Napoleon ended it in 1797.
republic-of-venice.o: Refugees from mainland cities settled the lagoon islands during the barbarian invasions. Venetian tradition places the election of the first doge, Paolo Lucio Anafesto, in 697, under Byzantine overlordship. After resisting Pepin of Italy in 810 the government moved to the Rialto islands, and in 828 merchants brought the relics of Saint Mark, the city's patron.
republic-of-venice.r: Venice was an aristocratic republic headed by an elected doge for life, whose power was increasingly checked by councils. The 1297 'Serrata' closed the Great Council to a hereditary nobility, and the Council of Ten guarded security. Trade privileges in Byzantium from 1082 and the Fourth Crusade of 1204, led by Doge Enrico Dandolo, built a Stato da Mar of Dalmatia, Crete, Corfu and later Cyprus. The Arsenal, glass-making and printing made it an industrial and cultural centre.
republic-of-venice.e: Wars with the Ottomans cost Venice Cyprus (1571), Crete (1669) and the Morea (1718). In 1797 Napoleon forced the last doge, Ludovico Manin, to abdicate, and the Treaty of Campo Formio handed Venice to Austria. It joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1866.

republic-of-the-seven-tenths.t: Alpine peasant republic of the upper Rhône valley, an ally of the Swiss Confederacy that ruled itself through seven communal districts.
republic-of-the-seven-tenths.o: The communities (Zenden) of the Upper Valais had long contested power with the prince-bishop of Sion. After decades of struggle, the Zenden forced Bishop Hildebrand Jost to abandon most of his temporal rights in 1628 and finally in 1634, and the Valais became a republic of seven tenths: Goms, Brig, Visp, Raron, Leuk, Sierre and Sion.
republic-of-the-seven-tenths.r: Sovereignty lay with the Diet (Landrat), in which each tenth sent delegates, while the bishop kept a largely honorary role. The republic was a Zugewandter Ort, an associate of the Old Swiss Confederacy, and governed the French-speaking Lower Valais as a subject territory. Its economy rested on Alpine farming and trade over the Simplon pass, dominated by families such as the Stockalper of Brig.
republic-of-the-seven-tenths.e: The Lower Valais rebelled in 1798 and French troops entered the country. Valais was incorporated into the Helvetic Republic in 1798, later becoming the Rhodanic Republic, a French department, and in 1815 a Swiss canton.

republic-of-pirates.t: The pirate stronghold at Nassau that, for a decade after the War of the Spanish Succession, sheltered Blackbeard and the leading pirates of the golden age.
republic-of-pirates.o: French and Spanish raids in 1703 and 1706 wrecked Nassau on New Providence and drove off the governor, leaving the Bahamas without effective authority. Privateers left idle by the end of the War of the Spanish Succession, and sailors who had plundered the wrecks of the 1715 Spanish treasure fleet, gathered in its harbour.
republic-of-pirates.r: It was not a formal state but a loose community of pirate crews, often called the Flying Gang, who elected captains and shared plunder under ship articles. Benjamin Hornigold and Henry Jennings were leading figures, alongside Edward Teach, Charles Vane, Sam Bellamy and Calico Jack Rackham. Merchants from New England and the islands traded supplies for loot, and the shallow harbour protected pirate sloops from warships.
republic-of-pirates.e: In 1718 Woodes Rogers arrived as royal governor with a royal pardon. Many pirates accepted it, and Hornigold even hunted former comrades; Vane escaped and fought on, while Teach was killed off North Carolina that year. Eight pirates were hanged at Nassau in December 1718, and the base was closed.

russian-sfsr.t: Soviet Russia, the first socialist state, created by the October Revolution and later the largest republic of the Soviet Union.
russian-sfsr.o: In the October Revolution of 1917 the Bolsheviks under Vladimir Lenin overthrew the Russian Republic's Provisional Government in Petrograd and proclaimed Soviet power. In January 1918 the state was declared a Soviet republic, the capital moved to Moscow in March, and the first constitution of July 1918 named it the Russian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic.
russian-sfsr.r: Power lay with the Communist Party, which ruled through soviets and the secret police, the Cheka. The Bolsheviks nationalised land and industry, made peace with Germany at Brest-Litovsk and won the Civil War against the Whites. In 1922 the republic co-founded the Soviet Union, after which it was governed largely through Union institutions, without its own Communist Party until 1990.
russian-sfsr.e: In 1990 the republic declared sovereignty, and Boris Yeltsin was elected its president in 1991. After the failed August coup, the Soviet Union was dissolved in December 1991, and the republic became the Russian Federation, continuing as the Soviet Union's successor state.

republic-of-el-salvador.t: The smallest and most densely populated country of Central America, independent since 1841, shaped by coffee oligarchy, military rule and civil war.
republic-of-el-salvador.o: After the Federal Republic of Central America broke apart, El Salvador adopted a constitution in February 1841 declaring itself a sovereign and independent state. For decades it remained entangled in the wars of its neighbours, often allied or opposed to Guatemala's Rafael Carrera, while some leaders still hoped to restore the union.
republic-of-el-salvador.r: From the 1860s coffee replaced indigo, and laws of 1881 to 1882 abolished communal lands, concentrating property among a small elite. In 1932 the regime of Maximiliano Hernández Martínez crushed a peasant uprising in La Matanza, killing thousands, many of them indigenous. Military governments ruled for half a century. The Football War with Honduras came in 1969, and from 1980 to 1992 civil war between the army and the FMLN guerrillas killed about 75,000 people.
republic-of-el-salvador.e: The Chapultepec Peace Accords of 1992 ended the war. El Salvador adopted the US dollar in 2001. President Nayib Bukele, elected in 2019, adopted bitcoin as legal tender and imposed a long state of exception against gangs, reshaping the country's politics.

republic-of-mahabad.t: The short-lived Kurdish republic of 1946, the first modern Kurdish state, whose leaders' fate shaped Kurdish nationalism for generations.
republic-of-mahabad.o: During the Soviet occupation of northern Iran, Kurdish nationalists in Mahabad formed the Komala society and then the Kurdistan Democratic Party under Qazi Muhammad, a respected judge and religious leader. With Soviet backing, the Kurdish Republic was proclaimed in Mahabad on 22 January 1946.
republic-of-mahabad.r: The republic controlled a small area around Mahabad. It made Kurdish the language of schools and government, published newspapers and journals, and created a small army whose most important commander was Mustafa Barzani, leader of Iraqi Kurdish fighters who had taken refuge in Iran. It cooperated with the Azerbaijan People's Government in Tabriz while disputing border districts with it.
republic-of-mahabad.e: After the Soviet withdrawal, Iranian troops entered Mahabad in December 1946. Qazi Muhammad was hanged in March 1947; Barzani led his men on a march to the Soviet Union, later returning to lead the Kurdish movement in the Republic of Iraq.

rajahnate-of-cebu.t: The Visayan port kingdom of Sugbu, where Magellan baptised Rajah Humabon in 1521 and Spain founded its first Philippine settlement in 1565.
rajahnate-of-cebu.o: Cebu grew as a trading port on the east coast of Cebu Island, linked to Chinese, Siamese and other Asian traders by the 15th century; Chinese ceramics are common in its burials. A later tradition, the Aginid, attributes its founding to a prince called Sri Lumay, but this is not supported by contemporary sources.
rajahnate-of-cebu.r: Cebu was ruled by a rajah over datus, freemen and dependants, and taxed visiting ships. Antonio Pigafetta, who arrived with Ferdinand Magellan in April 1521, described its trade and court. Rajah Humabon and hundreds of his people were baptised, but the alliance broke down after Lapulapu of Mactan killed Magellan in battle on 27 April 1521.
rajahnate-of-cebu.e: Miguel Lopez de Legazpi arrived in 1565 and Humabon's successor Rajah Tupas submitted to Spain. Cebu became the first Spanish city in the islands and the seat of the Captaincy General of the Philippines until 1571. Magellan's Cross and the Santo Nino image recall the first encounter.
rajahnate-of-cebu.re: Indigenous Philippine religion, later Roman Catholicism

republic-of-south-africa.t: South Africa as a republic since 1961, from the height of apartheid to the democratic transition led by Nelson Mandela in 1994.
republic-of-south-africa.o: After a whites-only referendum in 1960, the Union of South Africa became a republic on 31 May 1961 and left the Commonwealth. Prime Minister Hendrik Verwoerd was the leading architect of grand apartheid, while the African National Congress, banned after Sharpeville in 1960, turned to armed struggle.
republic-of-south-africa.r: The apartheid state classified people by race, created Bantustans such as Transkei and Bophuthatswana, and imprisoned leaders including Nelson Mandela after the Rivonia Trial of 1964. The Soweto uprising of 1976, township revolts and international sanctions weakened the regime. Mining, especially of gold, and manufacturing made it Africa's largest economy. Pretoria, Cape Town and Bloemfontein shared capital functions.
republic-of-south-africa.e: F. W. de Klerk unbanned the ANC and released Mandela in 1990. The first democratic elections, on 27 April 1994, made Mandela president, and the 1996 constitution set up a multiracial democracy with eleven official languages.
republic-of-south-africa.la: isiZulu, isiXhosa, Afrikaans, English, Sesotho, Setswana

republic-of-yucatan.t: Breakaway republic on the Yucatán Peninsula that twice left Mexico in the 1840s and returned in 1848 as the Caste War threatened its existence.
republic-of-yucatan.o: Yucatán's elites resented the Centralist Republic of Mexico and its taxes and levies. A federalist revolt led by Santiago Imán in 1839 to 1840 restored local autonomy, and in 1841 the peninsula declared itself independent, with Mérida as capital. A brief reunion in 1843 broke down, and Yucatán separated again in 1845 to 1846.
republic-of-yucatan.r: Its 1841 constitution, drafted largely by Manuel Crescencio Rejón, introduced the amparo, a citizen's legal protection against unconstitutional acts that later entered Mexican law. Politics was dominated by the rivalry of Santiago Méndez of Campeche and Miguel Barbachano of Mérida. The economy relied on henequen, sugar and maize, and Maya peasants bore heavy taxes, debt and loss of land, while being armed for the factions' wars.
republic-of-yucatan.e: In 1847 Maya communities rose in the Caste War and nearly drove the whites from the peninsula. Desperate, the government offered sovereignty to the United States, Britain and Spain. Mexico sent troops and money, and Yucatán formally rejoined Mexico in August 1848. Rebel Maya later founded Chan Santa Cruz.

rambrai-state.t: A small Khasi chiefdom of the West Khasi Hills, one of the 25 Khasi states that acceded to India in 1948.
rambrai-state.o: Hima Rambrai was one of the Khasi chiefdoms of the Meghalaya plateau; its origins are known only from oral tradition, and the register's start date is approximate.
rambrai-state.r: Rambrai was headed by a Syiem chosen from a royal clan, with succession through the female line and decisions taken with clan elders in a dorbar. Little written record of its history exists.
rambrai-state.e: Rambrai came under British supervision in the 19th century and acceded to India in 1948, joining Assam. It is now part of West Khasi Hills district, Meghalaya.

ryuzoji-clan-domain.t: The domain of the Ryuzoji of Hizen, whose ruthless lord Ryuzoji Takanobu briefly dominated northwestern Kyushu.
ryuzoji-clan-domain.o: The Ryuzoji were vassals of the Shoni family in Hizen province. Ryuzoji Takanobu, once a monk, succeeded to the headship and around 1550 secured control of Saga; he then broke the power of his former masters, the Shoni, and subdued rival local lords.
ryuzoji-clan-domain.r: After the Otomo were crushed by the Shimazu at Mimikawa in 1578, Takanobu expanded quickly across Hizen, Chikugo and parts of Chikuzen, becoming one of three great powers of Kyushu alongside the Otomo and Shimazu. He was known as the bear of Hizen and governed through force, with his retainer Nabeshima Naoshige as his chief commander and adviser.
ryuzoji-clan-domain.e: In 1584 Takanobu attacked the Arima family, who were supported by the Shimazu, and was killed at the battle of Okitanawate. Power passed in practice to Nabeshima Naoshige, whose family founded the Saga Domain.

ruperts-land.t: The vast Hudson Bay watershed granted to the Hudson's Bay Company in 1670 and run as a fur-trading empire for 200 years before passing to Canada.
ruperts-land.o: In 1670 Charles II chartered the Hudson's Bay Company, giving it trading rights and ownership of all lands draining into Hudson Bay, named Rupert's Land after its first governor, Prince Rupert. The grant covered much of what is now northern Quebec and Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and parts of the northern United States, though the company knew little of the interior.
ruperts-land.r: For a century the company kept to coastal forts such as York Factory, where Cree and Assiniboine traders brought beaver pelts in exchange for guns, kettles and cloth. French raids under Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville captured several posts until the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713. Competition from the North West Company pushed the company inland after 1774, ending in merger in 1821. Under governor George Simpson it ruled the West, and the Red River Colony and Métis society grew.
ruperts-land.e: Under the Deed of Surrender of 1869 the company sold Rupert's Land to the new Dominion of Canada for 300,000 pounds, and the transfer in 1870 followed the Red River Resistance led by Louis Riel.

remi.t: Belgic people of Champagne who sided with Caesar from the start, making Reims the chief Roman city of northern Gaul.
remi.o: The Remi held the chalk plains of Champagne around Durocortorum (Reims). In 57 BCE, while the other Belgae formed a league against Rome, they sent the envoys Iccius and Andecomborius to offer Caesar their submission and support.
remi.r: They shared laws and magistrates with their kinsmen the Suessiones and controlled a network of oppida. Their loyalty brought them supremacy over neighbouring peoples, and Caesar used their land as a base throughout his campaigns.
remi.e: Under Rome Durocortorum became capital of the province of Gallia Belgica, with monuments such as the Porte de Mars. As Reims it became an archbishopric, where Bishop Remigius baptised Clovis of the Kingdom of the Franks and French kings were later crowned.

republic-of-geneva.t: The Calvinist city-republic on Lake Geneva, the 'Protestant Rome', which threw off its bishop and Savoy in 1535.
republic-of-geneva.o: Geneva was ruled by the Prince-Bishopric of Geneva, with the Duchy of Savoy exerting growing influence. The townspeople allied with the Canton of Fribourg and the Canton of Bern in 1526, and in 1535, with Bernese support, they drove out the bishop and adopted the Reformation, making the city an independent republic.
republic-of-geneva.r: John Calvin, who settled there in 1536 and again from 1541, shaped its church ordinances; the Consistory enforced strict morals, and the Academy, founded in 1559, trained Reformed pastors for France, Scotland and the Netherlands. Councils dominated by leading families governed, and the city prospered from printing, banking and watchmaking, much of it brought by Huguenot refugees. In 1602 Genevans repelled Savoy's night attack, the Escalade.
republic-of-geneva.e: France annexed Geneva in 1798, making it the capital of the department of Léman. Freed in 1813, it joined the Swiss Confederation as a canton in 1815.

ramnad-kingdom.t: The kingdom of the Sethupathi chiefs of Ramanathapuram, guardians of the pilgrimage route to Rameswaram.
ramnad-kingdom.o: The Maravar chief Sadaikka Thevar was recognised as Sethupathi, protector of the causeway to Rameswaram, by the Madurai Nayak dynasty around 1605. His successors ruled the dry coastal region of Ramnad as vassals of Madurai until Kizhavan Sethupathi asserted independence in the late 17th century.
ramnad-kingdom.r: The Sethupathis led a warrior society of Maravar clans and controlled the pilgrim route and pearl fisheries of the Palk Strait. They endowed the Ramanathaswamy temple at Rameswaram, building its long corridors. Kizhavan Sethupathi persecuted Jesuit converts and executed the missionary John de Britto in 1693.
ramnad-kingdom.e: Ramnad lost territory to Thanjavur and the Sivaganga chiefdom in the 18th century. After the Nawabs of Arcot and then the British took control, the British East India Company deposed the Sethupathi in the 1790s and turned Ramnad into a zamindari estate in 1803.

republic-of-spanish-haiti.t: The first, nine-week independence of the Dominican east of Hispaniola, declared in 1821 and ended by Haitian occupation in 1822.
republic-of-spanish-haiti.o: Frustrated by Spain's neglect during España Boba, the lawyer and official José Núñez de Cáceres led a bloodless coup in Santo Domingo on 1 December 1821. He proclaimed the Independent State of Spanish Haiti and sought union with Simón Bolívar's Gran Colombia.
republic-of-spanish-haiti.r: Núñez de Cáceres headed a provisional government and issued a constitutive act modelled on the Spanish American republics. The new state kept slavery and the existing social hierarchy, which alienated many black and mulatto Dominicans, and some frontier towns declared for Haiti instead. Bolívar's government never replied to the request for union.
republic-of-spanish-haiti.e: Jean-Pierre Boyer, president of the Republic of Haiti, marched east with an army, and Santo Domingo surrendered without resistance on 9 February 1822. The whole island was united under Haiti until 1844, and the period is remembered in the Dominican Republic as the 'Ephemeral Independence'.

ruteni.t: Gallic people of the Rouergue whose land later produced the red samian pottery of La Graufesenque, sold across the Roman world.
ruteni.o: The Ruteni lived in the modern Aveyron, around Segodunum (Rodez). After 121 BCE part of their territory was annexed to the Roman Province, so that Caesar distinguishes the Ruteni provinciales from the independent Ruteni.
ruteni.r: They were clients of the Arverni. Their land held silver mines, and they struck their own coins.
ruteni.e: The independent Ruteni joined Vercingetorix in 52 BCE. Under Rome Segodunum became Rodez, and the workshops of La Graufesenque near Millau made millions of red-gloss pots exported as far as India. The medieval Rouergue kept their name.

republic-of-counani.t: A self-proclaimed republic in the jungle territory disputed by France and Brazil, created by French adventurers and never recognised.
republic-of-counani.o: The land between the Oyapock and Araguari rivers, now the Brazilian state of Amapá, was claimed by both France and Brazil. In 1886 a group of settlers at Counani, encouraged by French adventurers, proclaimed an independent republic, and the geographer Jules Gros, who never visited it, was named president for life in Paris.
republic-of-counani.r: The republic existed mainly in Paris, where Gros issued decrees, created an order of chivalry and sold titles and stamps. On the ground Counani was a small settlement of a few hundred people, mostly of African and indigenous descent, living from gathering and gold prospecting. Neither France nor Brazil recognised it, and the French government disavowed it in 1887.
republic-of-counani.e: The republic faded by 1891. A gold rush in the territory in the 1890s raised tensions, and in 1900 Swiss arbitration awarded the disputed region to Brazil. Later attempts to revive the republic came to nothing.

rueda-de-jalon-hudid.t: The last refuge of the Hudid kings of Zaragoza, a castle state on the Jalón kept alive through alliance with the Christian kings.
rueda-de-jalon-hudid.o: When the Almoravids took Zaragoza in 1110, the Hudid heir Abd al-Malik Imad al-Dawla withdrew to the strong castle of Rueda de Jalón, west of the city, and continued to rule a small territory from there, relying on Alfonso I of Aragon against the Almoravids.
rueda-de-jalon-hudid.r: The Hudid remnant was a client principality, surviving between Almoravid Zaragoza and the advancing Kingdom of Aragon. After Abd al-Malik's death in 1130 his son Ahmad Sayf al-Dawla, known to Christians as Zafadola, negotiated with Alfonso VII of Castile.
rueda-de-jalon-hudid.e: Zafadola handed Rueda to Alfonso VII in exchange for lands near Toledo and became a Castilian vassal. He later led Andalusi revolts against the Almoravids and was killed in 1146. The castle passed to Aragon.

radimichs.t: An East Slavic tribe on the Sozh river, tributaries first of the Khazars and then of Kiev, best known from a chronicle taunt.
radimichs.o: The Primary Chronicle says the Radimichs descended from Radim, who came with his brother Vyatko from the west and settled on the Sozh, a tributary of the Dnieper in modern Belarus and western Russia. Archaeology dates their settlement to the 8th century.
radimichs.r: They lived from farming and forest crafts in small fortified settlements, and their women wore distinctive seven-rayed temple rings. Like their neighbours they paid tribute to the Khazars, reportedly a silver coin per plough. In 885 Prince Oleg ordered them to pay that tribute to him instead.
radimichs.e: In 984 the general of Vladimir I, nicknamed Wolf's Tail, routed them on the river Pishchana, and the chronicle mocks them with the saying that Radimichs run from a wolf's tail. They disappear as a separate tribe in the 12th century, their lands divided between the principalities of Chernigov and Smolensk.

republic-of-maryland.t: A colony of free Black Americans at Cape Palmas, founded by Maryland colonisationists, which became an independent republic before joining Liberia in 1857.
republic-of-maryland.o: The Maryland State Colonization Society, founded to remove free Black people from Maryland, sent settlers in 1834 under its agent James Hall. They bought land at Cape Palmas from Grebo rulers and founded the town of Harper. The colony, known as Maryland in Africa, stayed separate from the Colony of Liberia.
republic-of-maryland.r: In 1836 John Brown Russwurm, a Jamaican-born graduate of Bowdoin College and co-founder of the first African American newspaper, became governor, the first Black governor of the colony, serving until 1851. The economy rested on farming and coastal trade. Relations with the numerous Grebo communities were tense over land and trade.
republic-of-maryland.e: Maryland declared independence in 1854 with William Prout as governor. War with the Grebo in 1856-1857 nearly destroyed it, and after Liberian troops came to its aid it was annexed to Liberia in 1857 as Maryland County.

regency-of-algiers.t: The Ottoman corsair state of Algiers, governed by pashas, aghas and finally deys, a major Mediterranean naval power for three centuries.
regency-of-algiers.o: In 1516 the corsair Oruç Barbarossa seized Algiers. After his death, his brother Hayreddin placed the city under the Ottoman Empire in 1519, receiving troops and the title of beylerbey. In 1529 he took the Spanish fortress on the Peñon, giving Algiers a secure harbour.
regency-of-algiers.r: Power passed from beylerbeys to pashas, then to aghas of the Janissary corps and, from 1671, to elected deys. Beys ruled the provinces of Constantine, Titteri and the West. The state lived from corsairing, ransoming captives such as Cervantes, tribute paid by European states, and grain exports. Uluj Ali was among its famous commanders.
regency-of-algiers.e: Attacks by the United States in 1815 and an Anglo-Dutch bombardment in 1816 weakened Algiers. After Hussein Dey struck the French consul with a fly-whisk in 1827, France invaded in 1830, and the Dey capitulated, beginning French Algeria.

republic-of-lithuania.t: The modern Lithuanian state, proclaimed in 1918, annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940 and the first Soviet republic to restore its independence, in 1990.
republic-of-lithuania.o: The Council of Lithuania, the Taryba, declared independence in Vilnius on 16 February 1918 during the German occupation run by Ober Ost. After Germany's defeat, Lithuania fought the Bolsheviks, the Bermontians and Poland. Poland seized Vilnius in 1920, so Kaunas became the temporary capital, and in 1923 Lithuania took the Klaipėda Region.
republic-of-lithuania.r: Interwar Lithuania carried out land reform and built national institutions; Antanas Smetona, its first president, returned to power in a 1926 coup and ruled as an authoritarian leader. The Soviet Union occupied and annexed the country in 1940, creating the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic, followed by Nazi occupation and the Holocaust, which destroyed Lithuanian Jewry.
republic-of-lithuania.e: The Sąjūdis movement led to the declaration of restored independence on 11 March 1990 under Vytautas Landsbergis. Soviet troops killed fourteen civilians in Vilnius on 13 January 1991, but independence was recognised later that year. Lithuania joined the EU and NATO in 2004 and the eurozone in 2015.

republic-of-bolivia.t: The landlocked Andean republic named after Simón Bolívar, born from Upper Peru in 1825 and refounded as a plurinational state in 2009.
republic-of-bolivia.o: After Antonio José de Sucre's victory at Ayacucho in 1824, an assembly in Chuquisaca declared the independence of Upper Peru, the former Royal Audiencia of Charcas, on 6 August 1825. The new state was named after Bolívar, and Sucre became its first elected president.
republic-of-bolivia.r: Andrés de Santa Cruz formed the Peru-Bolivian Confederation from 1836 to 1839. Bolivia lost its coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific, Acre to Brazil in 1903, and much of the Chaco to Paraguay in the Chaco War. Silver and then tin mining dominated the economy. The 1952 revolution under Víctor Paz Estenssoro brought universal suffrage, land reform and nationalisation of the mines, followed by military regimes from 1964 to 1982.
republic-of-bolivia.e: Democracy returned in 1982. In 2006 Evo Morales became the first indigenous president, and a 2009 constitution renamed the country the Plurinational State of Bolivia. Sucre remains the constitutional capital, while La Paz is the seat of government.

republic-of-mainz.t: The first democratic republic on German soil, a short experiment under French protection in revolutionary Mainz.
republic-of-mainz.o: French troops under General Custine took Mainz in October 1792, and the elector fled. A Jacobin club formed, and in early 1793 elections were held under French supervision. On 18 March 1793 the Rhenish-German National Convention proclaimed a free state covering the left bank of the Rhine from Landau to Bingen.
republic-of-mainz.r: The convention, led by the professor Andreas Joseph Hofmann and the naturalist Georg Forster, abolished feudal rule. Many inhabitants refused to vote or swear oaths, and the republic had no real authority beyond the French army's reach. On 21 March the convention asked to be annexed to France, and Forster went to Paris to present the request.
republic-of-mainz.e: Prussian and Austrian forces besieged Mainz, which surrendered in July 1793, and the Jacobins were persecuted. Forster died in exile in Paris in 1794. The left bank later passed to France, and the republic is remembered as an early German democracy.

reformed-government-of-the-republic-of-c.t: A Japanese-sponsored puppet government for occupied central China, set up at Nanjing in 1938 in the aftermath of the Nanjing Massacre.
reformed-government-of-the-republic-of-c.o: After capturing Shanghai and Nanjing in late 1937, the Japanese Central China Area Army sought Chinese collaborators to administer the lower Yangtze. On 28 March 1938 it inaugurated the Reformed Government of the Republic of China at Nanjing, under Liang Hongzhi, a former official of the Beiyang government.
reformed-government-of-the-republic-of-c.r: The regime nominally governed occupied parts of Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Anhui and the Chinese districts of Shanghai, but its ministers had little authority and its revenues depended on Japanese approval. Its members were mostly older politicians from the warlord era, and it had little public support in a region devastated by war.
reformed-government-of-the-republic-of-c.e: In March 1940 it was dissolved into the Wang Jingwei regime, which took over its offices at Nanjing. Liang Hongzhi held posts in the new government and was executed for treason in 1946.

raumarike.t: Petty kingdom of the Romerike plain north-east of Oslo, site of the Eidsivating assembly and an early conquest of Halfdan the Black.
raumarike.o: Raumarike covered the broad farming lowland of Romerike, north-east of the Oslofjord. It is known only from the sagas, which describe it as a small kingdom taken by Halfdan the Black of Vestfold in the 9th century.
raumarike.r: The district was among the most fertile in eastern Norway, with dense settlement along the Glomma and Vorma rivers. The Eidsivating, the law assembly of the Upplands, met at Eidsvoll in the region, giving it a role in the legal life of inland Norway.
raumarike.e: Halfdan the Black and his son Harald Fairhair incorporated Raumarike into their growing realm, and it became part of the Kingdom of Norway. Eidsvoll later gained national fame as the place where Norway's constitution was adopted in 1814.

republic-of-texas.t: The Lone Star Republic, which broke away from Mexico in 1836 and stayed independent for nearly ten years before joining the United States.
republic-of-texas.o: From the 1820s Mexico invited American settlers, led by empresarios such as Stephen F. Austin, into Coahuila y Tejas. Tension over centralist rule and slavery led to revolt in 1835. Independence was declared at Washington-on-the-Brazos on 2 March 1836; after the fall of the Alamo, Sam Houston defeated Santa Anna at San Jacinto in April.
republic-of-texas.r: The republic had a president, congress and constitution modelled on the United States, and it protected slavery. Cotton farming expanded and settlers poured in with offers of free land. Mexico never recognised independence and raided San Antonio in 1842. Debts mounted, Mirabeau Lamar's ill-fated Santa Fe Expedition failed, and policy towards the Comanche swung between war and Houston's attempts at peace. Austin became the capital in 1839.
republic-of-texas.e: Most Texans wanted annexation, delayed in Washington by the slavery question. Congress approved it in 1845, and Texas became the 28th state in December. The annexation was a cause of the Mexican-American War of 1846 to 1848.

rhegion.t: Greek city on the toe of Italy guarding the Strait of Messina, which under the tyrant Anaxilas controlled both shores of the strait.
rhegion.o: Chalcidians from Euboea, joined by exiles from Messenia, founded Rhegion around 720 BCE at the southern tip of Calabria, on the Delphic oracle's advice according to tradition. Facing Zancle across the Strait, it controlled shipping between the Tyrrhenian and Ionian Seas.
rhegion.r: Rhegion adopted the laws of Charondas and was ruled by an aristocracy of Messenian descent until Anaxilas made himself tyrant around 494 BCE. He seized Zancle, renamed it Messana, and allied with Carthage. The city was later a democracy and an ally of Athens. The lyric poet Ibycus and the sculptor Pythagoras came from Rhegion. Its coins showing a lion's head and a hare are well known.
rhegion.e: Dionysius I captured and destroyed Rhegion in 387 BCE, but it revived. In 280 BCE, during the war with Pyrrhus, a Roman garrison of Campanian troops seized the city; Rome retook it in 270 BCE and executed the mutineers. It remained a Greek-speaking ally, later Rhegium Iulium, and is today Reggio Calabria.

republic-of-tarnobrzeg.t: A short-lived peasant republic in south-eastern Poland, led by a radical priest who demanded land reform after the First World War.
republic-of-tarnobrzeg.o: In November 1918, as Austrian authority in Galicia collapsed, a radical priest, Eugeniusz Okon, and the peasant activist Tomasz Dabal called on peasants and returning soldiers around Tarnobrzeg to take power. At a rally on 6 November they proclaimed a republic in the district.
republic-of-tarnobrzeg.r: The movement demanded the division of large estates among peasants and the removal of landlords and officials. Its leaders formed a local council and militia, and peasants seized estate grain and forests. It never had a settled administration or defined borders and was more a social revolt than a state.
republic-of-tarnobrzeg.e: The new Polish government sent troops to restore order, and by spring 1919 the movement had been suppressed and its leaders arrested. Both Okon and Dabal were later elected to the Sejm of the Second Polish Republic, and Dabal became a communist.

republic-of-ancona.t: Self-governing Adriatic port and maritime republic that traded with Dalmatia and the Levant until the papacy took full control in 1532.
republic-of-ancona.o: Ancona, a port founded by Greeks from Syracuse in about 387 BCE, kept trading links across the Adriatic through the early Middle Ages. Around the start of the 11th century it began governing itself as a commune within the March of Ancona, under loose papal and imperial overlordship.
republic-of-ancona.r: Ancona was ruled by elected consuls, later by a council of elders, and was a merchant republic with trading houses in Constantinople, Alexandria and the Dalmatian ports, often allied with Ragusa against Venice. It famously resisted Frederick Barbarossa's siege in 1173 with Byzantine support; the widow Stamura became a local heroine. Its maritime statutes regulated Adriatic trade.
republic-of-ancona.e: In 1532 Pope Clement VII brought Ancona under direct papal rule, installing a garrison and building a fortress. The city remained the main port of the Papal States until it joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1860.

rasulid-dynasty.t: The most brilliant medieval dynasty of Yemen, whose scholar-sultans ruled from Ta'izz, grew rich on Aden's trade and built famous madrasas.
rasulid-dynasty.o: Nur al-Din Umar ibn Rasul, a commander of Turkmen origin, was left as deputy when the last ruler of Ayyubid Yemen departed in 1229. He soon declared himself sultan and obtained recognition from the Abbasid caliph in 1235, founding a dynasty based in Ta'izz and Zabid.
rasulid-dynasty.r: Under al-Muzaffar Yusuf, who reigned for 45 years and took Dhofar in 1279, the state reached from Mecca's borders to Dhofar. The Rasulids taxed the spice and textile trade of Aden, exchanged embassies with Egypt, India and China, and received Ming fleets in the 15th century. Several sultans were scholars: al-Ashraf Umar wrote on astronomy, medicine and farming. Ta'izz and Zabid gained mosques and Sunni Shafi'i madrasas.
rasulid-dynasty.e: From the late 14th century revolts by slave troops, tribes and family rivals weakened the dynasty. After disputed successions in the 1440s, the Tahirid Sultanate took power in 1454. The Rasulid period is remembered as Yemen's medieval golden age.

russian-republic.t: Russia's brief democratic republic between the fall of the tsar and the Bolshevik seizure of power in 1917.
russian-republic.o: The February Revolution of 1917 forced Nicholas II to abdicate, ending the Russian Empire. A Provisional Government formed from the Duma, first under Prince Georgy Lvov, shared power with the Petrograd Soviet. On 1 September 1917 Alexander Kerensky, by then its head, formally proclaimed Russia a republic.
russian-republic.r: The government granted civil liberties, abolished the death penalty and promised a Constituent Assembly, but it kept fighting the First World War and postponed land reform. A failed offensive in June, the July Days and General Lavr Kornilov's attempted march on Petrograd in August weakened it, while the Bolsheviks gained support in the soviets.
russian-republic.e: The Bolsheviks overthrew the Provisional Government in the October Revolution and created the Russian SFSR. The Constituent Assembly, elected in November, met in January 1918 under Viktor Chernov and proclaimed a Russian Democratic Federative Republic, but the Bolsheviks dispersed it the next day.

ratlam-state.t: A Rathore Rajput state of Malwa founded under Shah Jahan, later known for its trade in opium and gold.
ratlam-state.o: Ratlam was granted in 1652 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan to Ratan Singh, a Rathore descended from Raja Udai Singh of Marwar, in reward for service. Sailana and Sitamau later branched off from the same family.
ratlam-state.r: The Maharajas ruled a fertile plateau of wheat and opium. Ratlam became a trading town known for its markets, gold and the savoury sev that still carries its name. Under British paramountcy it was a salute state of the Malwa Agency; Sajjan Singh reigned from 1893 to 1947.
ratlam-state.e: Ratlam joined Madhya Bharat in 1948 and Madhya Pradesh in 1956. It is now a district headquarters and a railway junction.

republic-of-alsace-lorraine.t: A short-lived republic declared in Strasbourg as German rule collapsed in November 1918, swept away when French troops arrived days later.
republic-of-alsace-lorraine.o: As the German Empire collapsed in November 1918, soldiers' and workers' councils formed in Strasbourg and other towns of the Imperial Territory of Alsace-Lorraine. On 11 November the regional parliament constituted itself as a national council, and a republic was declared amid competing plans for autonomy.
republic-of-alsace-lorraine.r: Power was divided between the soldiers' councils, some influenced by revolutionary socialism, and the national council and Strasbourg's socialist mayor, Jacques Peirotes. The new authorities tried to keep order as German troops withdrew, but the republic had no recognition or real administration.
republic-of-alsace-lorraine.e: French troops entered Strasbourg on 22 November 1918 and the councils dissolved. The Treaty of Versailles confirmed the return of Alsace-Lorraine to France.

republic-of-vietnam.t: South Vietnam, the US-backed anti-communist state of 1955 to 1975, whose fall to North Vietnamese forces ended the Vietnam War.
republic-of-vietnam.o: In October 1955 Ngo Dinh Diem, prime minister of the State of Vietnam, deposed Bao Dai through a referendum and proclaimed the Republic of Vietnam with himself as president. It controlled the territory south of the 17th parallel, with nearly a million northern refugees, many Catholic, among its people.
republic-of-vietnam.r: Diem's government, dominated by his family, was authoritarian and repressed communists, sects and, in 1963, Buddhist protesters. It fought a growing insurgency led by the National Liberation Front. After Diem's overthrow and murder in November 1963, a series of generals ruled until Nguyen Van Thieu became president in 1967. More than half a million US troops fought in the country by 1968.
republic-of-vietnam.e: After the Paris Peace Accords of 1973 US forces withdrew, and North Vietnam's spring offensive of 1975 overran the south. Saigon fell on 30 April 1975. Authority passed to the Republic of South Vietnam, and many South Vietnamese fled abroad as boat people.

rusellae.t: Etruscan hill city near modern Grosseto, ringed by massive walls, which overlooked the Lake Prile lagoon until Rome captured it in 294 BCE.
rusellae.o: Rusellae, modern Roselle, occupied two hills above the coastal plain of the Ombrone, then bordering the lagoon of Lake Prile. Settled from the Villanovan period, it grew into a city in the 7th century BCE, when houses of unbaked brick were built, and in the 6th century it was enclosed by walls of huge polygonal blocks some 3 km long.
rusellae.r: Its prosperity came from farming the Ombrone plain, fishing and salt in the lagoon, and links with the mining districts of Vetulonia, which it overtook in importance during the 6th century BCE. Excavation has revealed a forum area, houses and craft quarters, but little is known of its government beyond the general Etruscan pattern of aristocratic magistrates.
rusellae.e: Livy records that Lucius Postumius Megellus stormed Rusellae in 294 BCE, taking 2,000 prisoners. As a Roman ally it sent grain and timber for Scipio's fleet in 205 BCE, and later became a Roman colony with a forum, baths and amphitheatre. It remained a bishopric until the see moved to Grosseto in 1138.

republic-of-ezo.t: A short-lived breakaway regime in Hokkaido set up by shogunate loyalists, whose leaders were chosen by an election of officers.
republic-of-ezo.o: When the shogunate surrendered Edo in 1868, Admiral Enomoto Takeaki sailed north with much of the shogunal navy, picking up defeated soldiers and French military advisers including Jules Brunet. In late 1868 his forces landed in Ezo, took the star fort of Goryokaku at Hakodate and captured Matsumae.
republic-of-ezo.r: In January 1869 officers voted to elect Enomoto as president, with other posts filled by election, an unprecedented step in Japan. The regime sought recognition from foreign powers as a de facto authority and asked to develop Ezo under a Tokugawa lord, but received only cautious neutrality.
republic-of-ezo.e: Imperial forces landed in spring 1869. The warship Kaiyo Maru had already been lost, and after the battle of Hakodate, where Hijikata Toshizo was killed, Enomoto surrendered Goryokaku in June 1869. He was later pardoned and served the Meiji government.

red-river-colony.t: A settlement founded by Lord Selkirk at the forks of the Red and Assiniboine rivers, cradle of the Métis nation and of the province of Manitoba.
red-river-colony.o: In 1811 the Hudson's Bay Company granted Thomas Douglas, Earl of Selkirk, about 300,000 square kilometres of Rupert's Land for a farming colony. Scottish settlers, many displaced by the Highland Clearances, arrived in 1812 under Governor Miles Macdonell. The rival North West Company and its Métis allies saw the colony as a threat to the pemmican supply of the fur trade.
red-river-colony.r: Conflict culminated in the Battle of Seven Oaks in 1816, in which Governor Robert Semple and about twenty colonists were killed. After Selkirk's heirs sold it back to the Company in 1836, the district was governed by the Council of Assiniboia. Its population was mostly Métis and English-speaking country-born families living by farming, freighting and the buffalo hunt.
red-river-colony.e: When the Company sold Rupert's Land to Canada without consulting residents, the Métis under Louis Riel formed the Provisional Government of Assiniboia in 1869. Negotiations led to the creation of Manitoba as a province of Canada in 1870.

republic-of-marseille.t: A brief maritime commune in which the merchants of Marseille governed their port independently before Charles of Anjou crushed it.
republic-of-marseille.o: In the early 13th century the citizens of the lower town of Marseille bought out the rights of their viscounts and formed a commune, organised around the Confraternity of the Holy Spirit. The register dates the republic from 1214, while the upper town remained under the bishop.
republic-of-marseille.r: The commune elected a podestà on the Italian model and a council of citizens, issued statutes and ran its own trade with the Levant, Sicily and North Africa, rivalling Genoa and Pisa. It joined the opposition to the counts of Provence and backed Raymond VII of Toulouse.
republic-of-marseille.e: Charles of Anjou, the new count of Provence, forced the city to submit in 1252 and, after further revolts, imposed the Chapters of Peace in 1257, ending its independence. Marseille kept municipal privileges within the County of Provence.

republic-of-costa-rica.t: Central America's most stable democracy, independent since 1848, known for coffee, abolishing its army in 1948 and its long peaceful elections.
republic-of-costa-rica.o: Having left the Central American federation in 1838, Costa Rica formally declared itself a republic on 31 August 1848 under President José María Castro Madriz. Coffee exports through the port of Puntarenas had already created a prosperous Central Valley elite and a large class of smallholders.
republic-of-costa-rica.r: Juan Rafael Mora Porras led the Central American war that defeated William Walker in 1856 to 1857, in which the drummer Juan Santamaría became a national hero. Tomás Guardia's rule from 1870 began the railway to Limón, built by Minor Keith, which spawned the banana industry. The death penalty was abolished in 1882, and the 1889 election is often regarded as the first truly free one. The Tinoco dictatorship of 1917 to 1919 was a rare break.
republic-of-costa-rica.e: After a short civil war in 1948, José Figueres abolished the army, and the 1949 constitution confirmed it. Costa Rica has since held regular peaceful elections, became a leader in ecotourism and conservation, and Óscar Arias won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1987 for Central American peace efforts.

russian-state.t: The White government of Admiral Kolchak, based in Omsk, which claimed to rule all of Russia against the Bolsheviks in 1918 to 1920.
russian-state.o: In September 1918 anti-Bolshevik groups meeting at Ufa created an All-Russian Provisional Government, a five-member Directory led by Nikolai Avksentiev. Based in Omsk, it called its territory the Russian State. On 18 November 1918 officers overthrew the Directory and made Admiral Alexander Kolchak Supreme Ruler.
russian-state.r: Kolchak ruled as a military dictator, and other White leaders, including Denikin, formally recognised his authority. His government controlled Siberia and the Urals and held most of the Russian gold reserve. Its armies advanced towards the Volga in spring 1919, but reprisals, corruption and failure to win over peasants undermined it.
russian-state.e: The Red Army counter-attacked, and Omsk fell in November 1919. Kolchak was handed over by the Czechoslovak Legion in Irkutsk and shot in February 1920. Remnants of his forces retreated to the Far East.

republic-of-florence.t: The city-republic of bankers and wool merchants that minted the florin and nurtured Dante, Giotto, Brunelleschi and the Medici-led Renaissance.
republic-of-florence.o: After Matilda of Canossa died in 1115, Florence's citizens took control of the city, and consuls are recorded by the 1130s. The commune conquered its rural territory, destroyed nearby Fiesole in 1125 and became the strongest power in Tuscany during the 13th century.
republic-of-florence.r: Florence was ruled by priors elected from the guilds, under the Ordinances of Justice of 1293 that excluded magnates. The gold florin, first minted in 1252, became Europe's standard coin, and banks such as the Bardi, Peruzzi and Medici lent across Europe. Guelph-Ghibelline and Black-White feuds exiled Dante. From 1434 Cosimo de' Medici and his grandson Lorenzo steered the republic informally while patronising Renaissance art and learning.
republic-of-florence.e: The Medici were expelled in 1494; Savonarola and then Piero Soderini led the restored republic until the Medici returned in 1512. A last republic fell after the siege of 1529–1530, and in 1532 Alessandro de' Medici became duke, creating the Duchy of Florence.

rajpipla-state.t: A Gohil Rajput state in the Narmada valley of Gujarat, the largest in the Rewa Kantha Agency, whose last Maharaja won the English Derby in 1934.
rajpipla-state.o: Tradition holds that a Gohil Rajput prince inherited the hill country south of the Narmada from his maternal grandfather, a Parmar chief, in the mid-14th century, founding the dynasty that ruled until 1948.
rajpipla-state.r: Rajpipla was hilly and forested, with a large Bhil and Vasava population. It faced pressure from the Gujarat Sultanate, the Mughals and later the Gaekwads of Baroda State, to whom it paid tribute. Under the British it was the leading state of the Rewa Kantha Agency. Maharaja Vijaysinhji built a new palace and railway, and his horse Windsor Lad won the Derby in 1934.
rajpipla-state.e: Rajpipla merged into Bombay State in 1948 and is now in Narmada district, Gujarat.

rhenish-republic.t: Separatist state proclaimed in the occupied Rhineland in 1923 with French backing, which collapsed amid popular hostility.
rhenish-republic.o: During the hyperinflation and the Franco-Belgian occupation of the Ruhr in 1923, Rhenish separatists sought a state independent of Prussia and Berlin. In October 1923 armed groups seized town halls in Aachen, Koblenz, Trier and other towns, and a Rhenish Republic was proclaimed, with a provisional government in Koblenz led by Josef Friedrich Matthes and Hans Adam Dorten.
rhenish-republic.r: The republic controlled little beyond public buildings occupied with the tolerance of French and Belgian troops. It had no administration, money or popular support, and its armed bands requisitioned food and goods. In November 1923 local residents fought separatists in the Siebengebirge near Aegidienberg, and a related separatist government in the Palatinate was ended by the assassination of its leader in January 1924.
rhenish-republic.e: Faced with hostility and British opposition, France withdrew support, and the movement collapsed by early 1924. The Rhineland remained part of Prussia within the Weimar Republic.

republic-of-peru.t: The Andean republic that grew from the heart of the Inca Empire and Spain's richest viceroyalty, declared independent in 1821.
republic-of-peru.o: José de San Martín proclaimed Peru's independence in Lima on 28 July 1821, establishing the Protectorate of Peru. A constituent congress met in 1822, and Bolívar took command in 1823. The victory of Antonio José de Sucre at Ayacucho in December 1824 ended Spanish power, and the last royalists at Callao surrendered in 1826.
republic-of-peru.r: Early decades were marked by rivalry between military caudillos and the Peru-Bolivian Confederation. The guano boom of the 1840s to 1870s funded railways, and Ramón Castilla abolished slavery and the Indian tribute in 1854. In the War of the Pacific Chile occupied Lima in 1881 and took Tarapacá. Twentieth-century politics swung between oligarchic, military and populist governments, including Juan Velasco Alvarado's reformist regime from 1968.
republic-of-peru.e: Peru returned to civilian rule in 1980 but suffered the Shining Path insurgency. Alberto Fujimori ruled from 1990 to 2000. Since then it has seen strong growth based on mining and frequent clashes between presidents and Congress.

redones.t: Gallic people of eastern Brittany whose chief town Condate became the city of Rennes.
redones.o: The Redones lived in the basin of the Vilaine, in the modern Ille-et-Vilaine. Caesar lists them among the Armorican peoples who submitted to Publius Crassus in 57 BCE.
redones.r: Their oppidum of Condate stood at the confluence of the Ille and the Vilaine, as its Gaulish name, meaning confluence, indicates. They struck gold coins of Armorican type.
redones.e: They sent troops to relieve Alesia in 52 BCE. Under Rome Condate became a walled civitas capital, called Redones in late antiquity, the origin of Rennes, later the capital of the Duchy of Brittany.

republic-of-turkey.t: The nation state founded by Mustafa Kemal Ataturk on the ruins of the Ottoman Empire, spanning Anatolia and eastern Thrace.
republic-of-turkey.o: The Government of the Grand National Assembly won the War of Independence, abolished the Ottoman sultanate and secured recognition at Lausanne in July 1923. On 29 October 1923 the assembly proclaimed the republic, with Ankara as capital and Mustafa Kemal as president.
republic-of-turkey.r: Ataturk's reforms abolished the caliphate (1924), replaced Islamic law with European-based codes, introduced the Latin alphabet (1928), gave women the vote (1934) and made secularism a constitutional principle. Ismet Inonu continued one-party rule until multi-party elections brought Adnan Menderes to power in 1950. Turkey joined NATO in 1952. The army intervened in 1960, 1971 and 1980, and Kurdish insurgency began in 1984.
republic-of-turkey.e: Turkey became an EU candidate in 1999. Recep Tayyip Erdogan, prime minister from 2003, became president in 2014, survived a coup attempt in 2016 and introduced a presidential system in 2018. In 2022 the country adopted Turkiye as its international name.

rajgarh-state.t: An Umat Parmar Rajput state of Malwa, sister state of Narsinghgarh, ruled from Rajgarh on the Newaj river.
rajgarh-state.o: Rajgarh was ruled by the Umat clan of Parmar Rajputs, settled in the region of Malwa known after them as Umatwara. The capital was established at Rajgarh around 1640. In 1681 the estate was divided and Narsinghgarh State formed from part of it.
rajgarh-state.r: The rulers, styled Rawat and later Raja, governed a rolling plateau of wheat and opium farming. In the 18th century they paid tribute to the Marathas, especially Sindhia, before British paramountcy in 1818. Rajgarh was an eleven-gun salute state of the Bhopal Agency.
rajgarh-state.e: Rajgarh joined Madhya Bharat in 1948 and Madhya Pradesh in 1956. It is now a district headquarters.

republic-of-entre-rios.t: A short-lived federal republic of the Argentine Littoral, created by the caudillo Francisco Ramírez in 1820.
republic-of-entre-rios.o: After defeating Buenos Aires at Cepeda in 1820 and signing the Treaty of Pilar, Francisco Ramírez broke with his former leader José Artigas of the Federal League and defeated him. In September 1820 he proclaimed the Republic of Entre Ríos, uniting Entre Ríos, Corrientes and Misiones, with himself as Supreme Chief.
republic-of-entre-rios.r: Ramírez organised the republic with its seat at Concepción del Uruguay. He issued regulations on administration, justice and the army, promoted schools and set up a printing press. The republic was largely a military creation built around his personal authority and his gaucho cavalry.
republic-of-entre-rios.e: In 1821 Ramírez launched a campaign against Buenos Aires and Santa Fe. He was defeated and killed in July 1821, and Estanislao López displayed his head in Santa Fe. The republic broke up, and Entre Ríos, Corrientes and Misiones became separate provinces.

republic-of-prekmurje.t: Week-long republic proclaimed in 1919 in the Slovene-speaking Prekmurje region, caught between Hungary and the new Yugoslav state.
republic-of-prekmurje.o: Prekmurje, between the Mura river and the Hungarian border, had a Slovene-speaking majority but had long belonged to Hungary. In the chaos of 1919, with Hungary under the Hungarian Soviet Republic, the local politician Vilmos Tkálecz proclaimed an independent Mura Republic at Murska Sobota on 29 May 1919, hoping for foreign recognition.
republic-of-prekmurje.r: Tkálecz formed a small government and tried to raise a militia, but the republic had no real army, money or international support. Most of the population was rural, Slovene and Hungarian-speaking, Catholic and Lutheran, and was more concerned with food and order than with independence.
republic-of-prekmurje.e: Troops of the Hungarian Red Army retook Murska Sobota on 6 June 1919, ending the republic after about a week; Tkálecz fled. In August 1919 the Yugoslav army occupied Prekmurje, and the Treaty of Trianon in 1920 assigned it to the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. It is now part of Slovenia.

republic-of-latvia.t: The Latvian nation-state, proclaimed in Riga in 1918, annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940 and restored to independence in 1990-1991.
republic-of-latvia.o: The People's Council proclaimed the Republic of Latvia on 18 November 1918, with Kārlis Ulmanis as prime minister. It had to fight the Latvian Socialist Soviet Republic, the German Freikorps and the Bermontians in the War of Independence, which ended with the peace treaty with Soviet Russia in August 1920.
republic-of-latvia.r: The Satversme, adopted in 1922, created a parliamentary democracy, with Jānis Čakste as first president, and a land reform redistributed Baltic German estates. Ulmanis seized power in 1934 and ruled as an authoritarian leader. In 1940 the Soviet Union occupied and annexed Latvia as the Latvian Soviet Socialist Republic, followed by Nazi occupation and further Soviet rule.
republic-of-latvia.e: The Popular Front and events such as the Baltic Way of 1989 led to a declaration restoring independence on 4 May 1990, completed on 21 August 1991. The Satversme was restored, and Latvia joined the EU and NATO in 2004 and the eurozone in 2014.

republic-of-mirdita.t: Short-lived breakaway state of the Catholic Mirdita highlands in northern Albania, backed by Yugoslavia in 1921.
republic-of-mirdita.o: The Catholic Mirdita clan region in northern Albania had long enjoyed autonomy under its hereditary captains. Opposing the new government in Tirana, the clan leader Gjon Marka Gjoni, with backing from the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, proclaimed the Republic of Mirdita in July 1921, the declaration being made in Prizren on Yugoslav territory.
republic-of-mirdita.r: The republic existed mainly as an armed revolt of Mirdita tribesmen, supplied and armed from Yugoslavia, which hoped to weaken Albania and claim border areas. It appealed to the League of Nations for recognition, but had no institutions beyond the clan leadership.
republic-of-mirdita.e: Albanian government forces, with commanders including Ahmet Zogu, crushed the revolt in November 1921, while the Conference of Ambassadors confirmed Albania's 1913 borders, ending Yugoslav claims. Gjon Marka Gjoni fled to Yugoslavia and later reconciled with the government.

republic-of-guatemala.t: Guatemala as an independent republic since 1847, marked by coffee dictatorships, a CIA-backed coup in 1954 and a long civil war with genocide against the Maya.
republic-of-guatemala.o: After the collapse of the Federal Republic of Central America, the conservative caudillo Rafael Carrera formally proclaimed the Republic of Guatemala on 21 March 1847. Carrera ruled, with short interruptions, until his death in 1865, from 1854 as president for life, in close alliance with the Catholic Church and the Guatemala City merchants.
republic-of-guatemala.r: The Liberal Revolution of 1871 brought Justo Rufino Barrios, who expropriated church lands and drove coffee expansion using forced Maya labour. Dictators Manuel Estrada Cabrera and Jorge Ubico favoured the United Fruit Company. After the 1944 revolution, Juan José Arévalo and Jacobo Árbenz pursued reform, but Árbenz's land reform provoked a CIA-backed coup in 1954. Civil war from 1960 to 1996 killed about 200,000 people, most of them Maya.
republic-of-guatemala.e: Peace accords in 1996 ended the war, and a UN-backed truth commission found that acts of genocide had been committed against Maya communities. Guatemala remains a presidential republic; Bernardo Arévalo, son of the reformist president, took office in 2024.

raurici.t: Celtic people of the Rhine bend around Basel who joined the Helvetii's failed migration and later saw Rome found Augusta Raurica.
raurici.o: The Raurici lived along the upper Rhine around the Basel region and in the southern Alsace and Jura. Caesar records them as neighbours and allies of the Helvetii.
raurici.r: Their oppidum on the Münsterhügel in Basel and the earlier open settlement at Basel-Gasfabrik show a wealthy community trading on the Rhine.
raurici.e: In 58 BCE they burned their homes and joined the migration of the Helvetii, but after the defeat at Bibracte they were sent back. Around 44 BCE Lucius Munatius Plancus founded the colony of Augusta Raurica (Augst) in their land.

rhode.t: A small Greek colony at Roses on the Catalan coast, linked to Emporion and Massalia, whose silver coins bore a rose.
rhode.o: Ancient writers credited Rhode to settlers from Rhodes, but archaeology shows a Greek settlement founded in the 5th to 4th century BCE, probably by Massalia or nearby Emporion, on the Gulf of Roses in north-east Catalonia.
rhode.r: Rhode was a small Greek trading town with its own pottery workshops. In the 3rd century BCE it minted silver drachms showing a rose, a pun on its name, widely copied in southern Gaul. Excavations in the Ciutadella of Roses have uncovered its houses and streets.
rhode.e: During the north-eastern revolt of 195 BCE Rhode was held against Rome and was captured by Cato. It continued as a small town under Roman rule, later giving its name to Roses.

realm-of-the-gyulas.t: Semi-independent realm of the gyulas in Transylvania, whose Orthodox-leaning rulers were subdued by Stephen I of Hungary in 1003.
realm-of-the-gyulas.o: After the Hungarian conquest, Transylvania was held by a branch of chiefs bearing the title gyula. Byzantine sources record that a gyula was baptised in Constantinople around 952 and brought back the monk Hierotheos as bishop. Their seat was probably at Gyulafehérvár (Alba Iulia), on a Roman fort.
realm-of-the-gyulas.r: The gyulas ruled largely independently of the Árpád grand princes, controlling Transylvanian salt and the routes to Byzantium. Their daughter Sarolt married Grand Prince Géza and was the mother of Stephen I. Their Christianity was oriented to Byzantium, unlike the Western church favoured at Esztergom.
realm-of-the-gyulas.e: In 1003 Stephen I attacked his maternal uncle, Gyula the Younger, captured him and annexed Transylvania to the Kingdom of Hungary (1000-1301). The region later became the Voivodeship of Transylvania.

ravala.t: Coastal Estonian county around Lindanise, the site of modern Tallinn, conquered by King Valdemar II of Denmark in 1219.
ravala.o: Rävala occupied the northern coast of Estonia around the bay where Tallinn now stands. A harbour and stronghold at Lindanise served Baltic shipping, and the Arab geographer al-Idrisi's 1154 map may record it as a town called Qlwry. The county appears in Henry of Livonia's chronicle in the early 13th century.
ravala.r: Its elders controlled the harbour and the trade passing between Scandinavia, Finland and Novgorod. The county farmed the coastal plain and kept close ties with Harjumaa inland. Little else is known of its institutions.
ravala.e: In 1219 Valdemar II of Denmark landed with a crusading army, defeated the Estonians at the Battle of Lindanise and built a castle on Toompea; legend places the falling of the Danish flag, the Dannebrog, from the sky at this battle. Rävala became the core of the Duchy of Estonia (1219-1346), and Lindanise grew into Reval.

republic-of-burundi.t: The republic that replaced Burundi's monarchy in 1966, marked by military rule, mass killings and civil war before a fragile peace from 2000.
republic-of-burundi.o: In November 1966 Captain Michel Micombero deposed the young king Ntare V, ending the Kingdom of Burundi and proclaiming a republic. Power rested with a Tutsi-dominated army and the single party UPRONA, founded by the independence hero Prince Louis Rwagasore, who had been assassinated in 1961.
republic-of-burundi.r: After a Hutu rebellion in 1972 the army killed perhaps 100,000 to 200,000 Hutu, mainly the educated, in the killings known as the Ikiza. Further coups brought Jean-Baptiste Bagaza in 1976 and Pierre Buyoya in 1987. In 1993 Melchior Ndadaye became the first elected Hutu president, but his assassination months later started a civil war that killed some 300,000 people.
republic-of-burundi.e: The Arusha Accords of 2000 and a 2005 constitution introduced ethnic power-sharing, and Pierre Nkurunziza ruled from 2005 to 2020, his disputed third term sparking a crisis in 2015. Under Evariste Ndayishimiye the political capital moved to Gitega in 2019.

royal-audiencia-of-quito.t: The Spanish colonial province of the northern Andes, governed from Quito, famed for its textile workshops and baroque art, and the forerunner of Ecuador.
royal-audiencia-of-quito.o: After the Spanish conquest of Quito in 1534, the region was governed from Lima. In 1563 Philip II created the Royal Audiencia of Quito, a high court with governing powers, covering the territory of modern Ecuador and parts of southern Colombia and northern Peru, within the Viceroyalty of Peru.
royal-audiencia-of-quito.r: The Audiencia was headed by a president. Its economy rested on textile workshops called obrajes, which used indigenous labour to produce woollen cloth sold across the Andes, and on haciendas. Guayaquil was the main port and shipbuilding centre. Quito became renowned for the Quito School of painting and sculpture and for churches such as La Compañía. The Rebellion of the Barrios in 1765 protested new taxes.
royal-audiencia-of-quito.e: Quito was attached to the Viceroyalty of New Granada in 1739. A junta in Quito on 10 August 1809 was one of the first in Spanish America, followed by the State of Quito. Sucre's victory at Pichincha in 1822 brought Quito into Gran Colombia.

republic-of-iraq.t: The Iraqi state since the 1958 revolution: military regimes, Ba'athist dictatorship under Saddam Hussein, war and occupation, and a federal democracy since 2005.
republic-of-iraq.o: On 14 July 1958 the Free Officers under Abd al-Karim Qasim overthrew the Kingdom of Iraq and proclaimed a republic. Qasim left the Baghdad Pact, began land reform and claimed Kuwait, but was killed in a Ba'athist coup in 1963. The Arif brothers then ruled until the Ba'ath Party took power again in 1968.
republic-of-iraq.r: Under Ahmad Hasan al-Bakr and, from 1979, Saddam Hussein, oil wealth funded development alongside a pervasive police state. Iraq fought Iran from 1980 to 1988, conducted the Anfal campaign against the Kurds, including the gas attack on Halabja, and invaded Kuwait in 1990, leading to the Gulf War and sanctions. A US-led invasion in 2003 overthrew Saddam, and a 2005 constitution created a federal parliamentary system with a Kurdistan Region.
republic-of-iraq.e: Sectarian war followed in 2006 to 2008, and the Islamic State seized Mosul in 2014 before its defeat in 2017. Iraq remains a federal parliamentary republic, governed through power-sharing between Shia, Sunni and Kurdish parties.

rouran-khaganate.t: The steppe empire that dominated Mongolia between the Xianbei and the Turks, and the first whose rulers bore the title khagan.
rouran-khaganate.o: The Rouran traced their origin to Mugulü, a slave of the Tuoba Xianbei in the 4th century, whose followers formed a band in the Mongolian steppe. Shelun united the tribes in 402, defeated the Gaoche and took the title khagan, establishing a confederation that stretched from Manchuria to the Tarim Basin.
rouran-khaganate.r: The Rouran khagans ruled a mobile court over many subject peoples, including the Turks, whom they used as ironsmiths in the Altai. Their main rival was the Northern Wei, which mounted repeated campaigns against them; the Chinese called them Ruanruan, 'wriggling insects', as an insult. They also exercised influence over the Tarim oasis states and the Yueban.
rouran-khaganate.e: In 552 their Turkic vassals under Bumin, angered when the khagan Anagui refused him a bride, revolted and destroyed the khaganate, founding the Turkic Khaganate. The last Rouran remnants were wiped out in 555. Some historians link them to the Pannonian Avars, though this is disputed.

republic-of-baden.t: Democratic successor of the Grand Duchy of Baden, a stable Weimar-era state on the French border, divided after 1945.
republic-of-baden.o: In November 1918 a provisional government was formed in Karlsruhe and Grand Duke Frederick II abdicated. In January 1919 Baden elected a constituent assembly, the first German election in which women could vote, and its constitution, approved by referendum in 1919, made Baden a democratic republic.
republic-of-baden.r: Baden was governed by a stable Weimar coalition of the Catholic Centre, Social Democrats and liberals. As a border state facing France, it suffered from the demilitarised zone along the Rhine and economic isolation. The Nazis took control in March 1933 under Reich governor Robert Wagner, who in 1940 deported Baden's Jews to the Gurs camp in France.
republic-of-baden.e: In 1945 Baden was divided between the American zone in the north, joined to Württemberg-Baden, and the French zone in the south, which became the state of Baden. All were merged into Baden-Württemberg in 1952.

republic-of-finland.t: Nordic republic that won independence from Russia in 1917, survived a civil war and two wars with the Soviet Union, and became a prosperous democracy.
republic-of-finland.o: Finland's parliament declared independence from Russia on 6 December 1917, under the Senate led by Pehr Evind Svinhufvud. A brutal civil war in 1918 between Reds and Whites ended in a White victory, and after a failed attempt at monarchy in the Kingdom of Finland (1918), the 1919 constitution made Finland a republic with K. J. Ståhlberg as first president.
republic-of-finland.r: Finland built a parliamentary democracy with a strong presidency, bilingual in Finnish and Swedish. The Soviet Union attacked in the Winter War of 1939-1940, and Finland fought again alongside Germany in the Continuation War of 1941-1944, losing Karelia but keeping its independence. During the Cold War President Urho Kekkonen pursued neutrality and close relations with Moscow.
republic-of-finland.e: Post-war Finland industrialised quickly, developing forestry, engineering and later electronics, and created a Nordic welfare state with a celebrated school system. It joined the European Union in 1995, adopted the euro in 2002 and joined NATO in 2023 after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

republic-of-uhtua.t: Finnish-backed provisional government of East Karelia in 1919-1920, based in the village of Uhtua, which sought union with Finland.
republic-of-uhtua.o: After the Russian Revolution, Finnish nationalists hoped to join East Karelia, homeland of much Kalevala folk poetry, to Finland. Finnish volunteer expeditions entered the region in 1918-1919, and in 1919 local Karelians and Finnish activists set up a Provisional Government of East Karelia at Uhtua (now Kalevala).
republic-of-uhtua.r: The government controlled only the area around Uhtua in the White Sea Karelia region. It held a meeting of Karelian representatives that voted for separation from Russia, issued its own stamps and relied on Finnish volunteers and supplies.
republic-of-uhtua.e: The Red Army retook the area in 1920, and the government fled to Finland. The Treaty of Tartu of 1920 left East Karelia in Soviet Russia, which created a Karelian Labour Commune. A further uprising in 1921-1922 also failed, and the area later formed the Karelo-Finnish Soviet Socialist Republic.

royal-niger-company-territories.t: The lands along the Niger and Benue ruled by George Goldie's chartered company, which secured the region for Britain against French and German rivals.
royal-niger-company-territories.o: George Taubman Goldie merged rival British trading firms on the Niger into the United African Company in 1879, renamed the National African Company in 1882. He bought out French competitors, and his agents signed hundreds of treaties with local rulers. In 1886 Britain granted the firm a royal charter as the Royal Niger Company, with power to govern the lower Niger and the Benue.
royal-niger-company-territories.r: The company used its charter to enforce a trade monopoly, charging heavy duties that ruined African middlemen such as the Nembe traders of Brass, who attacked its depot at Akassa in 1895. It kept its own constabulary, administrative centre at Asaba and trading posts up the rivers. In 1897 its forces defeated the Bida Emirate and the Ilorin Emirate.
royal-niger-company-territories.e: Criticism of the monopoly and the need for state forces against French expansion led Britain to revoke the charter on 1 January 1900. The territories passed to the Protectorates of Northern and Southern Nigeria, and the company continued as a trading business.

republic-of-noli.t: A tiny Ligurian seaside republic that kept its independence, under Genoese protection, from 1192 until 1797.
republic-of-noli.o: Noli, a small port on the western Riviera, freed itself from the Del Carretto marquises and became a self-governing commune in 1192. It soon placed itself under the protection of the Republic of Genoa while keeping its own institutions.
republic-of-noli.r: Noli was governed by consuls and later by a council and podestà, and lived from fishing, shipbuilding and sea trade. Its ships joined Genoese expeditions, including crusading voyages. In 1239 Pope Gregory IX made it a bishopric, a sign of its standing. The town kept its medieval walls, towers and the Romanesque church of San Paragorio.
republic-of-noli.e: Noli survived as a nominal republic allied to Genoa for six centuries. It was absorbed into the French-backed Ligurian Republic in 1797.

republic-of-lydenburg.t: A breakaway Boer republic in the eastern Transvaal that resisted union with Pretoria for four years.
republic-of-lydenburg.o: Voortrekkers abandoned malaria-ridden Andries-Ohrigstad and founded Lydenburg in 1849. Its leaders distrusted Marthinus Wessel Pretorius and the western Transvaal, and in 1856 the Lydenburg community declared itself a separate republic, De Republiek Lydenburg in Zuid-Afrika.
republic-of-lydenburg.r: The small republic had its own Volksraad and a church tradition closer to the Dutch Reformed establishment of the Cape. Its farmers lived from cattle, hunting and trade towards Delagoa Bay, and lived alongside the Pedi Kingdom to the west, with whom relations were uneasy.
republic-of-lydenburg.e: Lydenburg absorbed the Republic of Utrecht in 1858, and in 1860 the combined state rejoined the South African Republic. The town remained a district centre and later a base in wars against the Pedi.

revolutionary-serbia.t: Insurgent Serbian state of the First Serbian Uprising, which drove out Ottoman janissaries and laid the foundations of modern Serbia.
revolutionary-serbia.o: In 1801 renegade janissaries, the dahije, seized power in the Pashalik of Belgrade and terrorised the Serbian population. After they murdered dozens of Serbian notables, an assembly at Orašac in February 1804 chose Karađorđe Petrović to lead a revolt. The uprising soon turned against Ottoman rule itself, winning battles at Ivankovac in 1805 and Mišar in 1806.
revolutionary-serbia.r: The insurgents took Belgrade in 1806 and created a Governing Council in 1805, alongside assemblies of local leaders and Karađorđe's growing personal power as supreme leader. Russia supported them during its war with the Ottomans. The scholar Dositej Obradović became the first minister of education, and a Great School opened in Belgrade in 1808.
revolutionary-serbia.e: When Russia made peace at Bucharest in 1812 to face Napoleon, the Ottomans reconquered Serbia in 1813 and Karađorđe fled to Austria. The Second Serbian Uprising of 1815 under Miloš Obrenović led to the autonomous Principality of Serbia.
