republic-of-zamboanga.t: Short-lived revolutionary republic in western Mindanao, formed as Spanish rule collapsed in 1899.
republic-of-zamboanga.o: Zamboanga was the main Spanish stronghold in Mindanao. In 1899, as Spain prepared to withdraw after ceding the islands, local revolutionaries under General Vicente Alvarez fought the garrison, and after the Spanish departure in May they proclaimed a republic with Alvarez as president.
republic-of-zamboanga.r: The republic governed the Christian, Chavacano-speaking town and its surroundings, but it was divided by rivalries between revolutionary factions and with neighbouring Muslim datus, who distrusted a Christian-led government. Alvarez was ousted, and Isidoro Midel led the government that negotiated with the Americans.
republic-of-zamboanga.e: Midel surrendered Zamboanga to American forces in November 1899. A local government using the republic's name survived under American supervision until 1903, when Zamboanga became the capital of the new Moro Province.

rauracian-republic.t: Short-lived revolutionary republic in the Jura, the first sister republic created by the French Revolution.
rauracian-republic.o: The French army occupied the northern part of the Prince-Bishopric of Basel in 1792, driving out the prince-bishop. Local revolutionaries proclaimed the Rauracian Republic on 27 November 1792 at Porrentruy, naming it after the Rauraci, a Celtic people of the area recorded by Caesar.
rauracian-republic.r: The republic had a national assembly and adopted French revolutionary institutions, but it was deeply divided between those who wanted independence and those who sought union with France. It depended entirely on the French army and had no real independent existence; most of its history consists of debates over annexation.
rauracian-republic.e: On 23 March 1793 the French National Convention annexed the territory as the department of Mont-Terrible. It later merged into Haut-Rhin, and in 1815 the area was given to the Swiss canton of Bern, much of it now forming the canton of Jura.

recuay.t: A highland culture of Peru's Callejón de Huaylas known for fine kaolin pottery, stone sculpture of warriors and elite residences built around fortified compounds.
recuay.o: The Recuay culture arose around the start of the Common Era in the Callejón de Huaylas and the upper valleys of Ancash, in the same region where Chavín had flourished. Communities built hilltop settlements and stone compounds above the Santa river valley.
recuay.r: Recuay society was led by local chiefs and warrior elites who lived in walled compounds and were buried in stone tombs with offerings. Herding of llamas and alpacas and high-altitude farming supported the economy. The culture is known for white kaolin pottery painted in red and black, often modelled as figures of chiefs, women and llamas, and for stone sculptures and lintels showing warriors with shields and trophy heads. Its contacts with the Moche on the coast were close.
recuay.e: Recuay declined around 600 to 700 CE, possibly under pressure from the expanding Wari Empire, whose influence reached Ancash. Its stone sculpture tradition remained a reference point for later highland cultures.

republic-of-austria.t: The Second Austrian Republic, restored in 1945 and rebuilt as a neutral, prosperous democracy in the heart of Europe.
republic-of-austria.o: As the Red Army took Vienna in April 1945, Karl Renner formed a provisional government and declared Austria's independence from Germany on 27 April 1945, restoring the 1920 constitution. Austria was divided into four Allied occupation zones, with Vienna under four-power control.
republic-of-austria.r: Governments were long formed by grand coalitions of the conservative People's Party and the Social Democrats, with social partnership between employers and unions. The State Treaty of 15 May 1955 ended the occupation, and Austria declared permanent neutrality. Vienna became a seat of United Nations agencies. The Waldheim affair of 1986 prompted a reckoning with Austrians' role under Nazism.
republic-of-austria.e: Austria joined the European Union in 1995 and adopted the euro in 1999. It remains a federal parliamentary republic of nine states, with Vienna as capital.

restored-hanthawaddy-kingdom.t: A Mon revival kingdom in Lower Burma that captured Ava in 1752, ending the Toungoo dynasty, but fell to Alaungpaya five years later.
restored-hanthawaddy-kingdom.o: In 1740 the Mon of Lower Burma, together with Karen and Burmese allies, rebelled against the weakened Restored Toungoo Kingdom. They chose Smim Htaw, a former monk, as king at Pegu, reviving the name of the old Hanthawaddy Kingdom.
restored-hanthawaddy-kingdom.r: Smim Htaw was replaced in 1747 by Binnya Dala, who with French assistance from Pondicherry built up an army and in 1752 captured Ava, deporting the last Toungoo king. The kingdom's base remained the Mon delta ports, where French and British traders competed for influence.
restored-hanthawaddy-kingdom.e: Alaungpaya, a village headman of Moksobo, raised an army in Upper Burma, retook Ava in 1753 and swept south, capturing Syriam and finally Pegu in 1757. The capital was sacked and many Mon fled to Siam. Lower Burma became part of the Konbaung dynasty.

republic-of-san-marco.t: The revolutionary Venetian republic of 1848–1849 led by Daniele Manin, which held out against an Austrian siege for seventeen months.
republic-of-san-marco.o: On 22 March 1848, as revolution spread across Europe, the Venetians rose against the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia, freed the lawyer Daniele Manin from prison and took the Arsenal. Manin proclaimed the Republic of San Marco, reviving the name of the old Republic of Venice.
republic-of-san-marco.r: Manin led the government, with the writer Niccolò Tommaseo among its ministers. The republic briefly voted in July 1848 to join the Kingdom of Sardinia, but after Piedmont's defeat at Custoza it returned to independence. Venetians raised loans, printed paper money and organised a national guard and defence of the lagoon, which became a symbol of Italian resistance.
republic-of-san-marco.e: Austrian forces besieged Venice from 1849, bombarding the city while cholera and hunger spread. The republic surrendered in August 1849, and Manin went into exile in Paris. Venetia joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1866.

ryukyu-kingdom.t: The island kingdom of Okinawa that thrived as a trading hub between China, Japan and Southeast Asia for four centuries before Japanese annexation.
ryukyu-kingdom.o: Sho Hashi of Chuzan completed the unification of Okinawa in 1429 by conquering Nanzan, and ruled from Shuri castle as a tributary king of Ming China. In 1470 a coup brought Sho En to power, founding the Second Sho dynasty that reigned until the end.
ryukyu-kingdom.r: King Sho Shin centralised power by bringing local aji lords to live at Shuri and organised priestesses under a royal high priestess. Ryukyu prospered as an entrepot, carrying Chinese silk and ceramics, Japanese swords and Southeast Asian spices and sappanwood. After the Satsuma Domain invaded in 1609, Ryukyu secretly paid tribute to Satsuma while remaining a Chinese tributary, and a distinctive court culture of dance, lacquer and textiles developed.
ryukyu-kingdom.e: Meiji Japan made the kingdom the Ryukyu Domain in 1872, and King Sho Tai lost his throne when it was annexed as Okinawa Prefecture in 1879.

rajpur-state-kathiawar.t: A minor chiefship of the Kathiawar peninsula, one of its many small hereditary estates.
rajpur-state-kathiawar.o: Rajpur was a small estate in Kathiawar held by a local chiefly family from around 1700. Its founding is not well documented.
rajpur-state-kathiawar.r: The ruler held a handful of villages and, after 1807, came under British supervision in the Kathiawar Agency. Little else is recorded in standard works.
rajpur-state-kathiawar.e: Rajpur merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960.

reichskommissariat-norwegen.t: German civilian occupation regime in Norway in 1940-1945, headed by Josef Terboven, with Vidkun Quisling's collaborationist government.
reichskommissariat-norwegen.o: Germany invaded Norway on 9 April 1940. Vidkun Quisling, leader of the fascist Nasjonal Samling, proclaimed himself head of government the same day, but the Germans soon pushed him aside. King Haakon VII and the government refused to surrender and went into exile in London, and in April 1940 Hitler appointed Josef Terboven as Reich Commissioner.
reichskommissariat-norwegen.r: Terboven held real power from Oslo, banning all parties except Nasjonal Samling. In 1942 Quisling became Minister-President of a collaborationist government, which tried to Nazify schools and the church but met mass resistance from teachers and clergy. Norway's resistance sabotaged the heavy water plant at Vemork, and in 1942 Norwegian Jews were deported to Auschwitz.
reichskommissariat-norwegen.e: German forces in Norway surrendered on 8 May 1945, and Terboven killed himself. Quisling was tried and executed in October 1945, and his name became a byword for traitor. The legal government returned and King Haakon VII came home to the Kingdom of Norway in June 1945.

republic-of-amalfi.t: Maritime republic on the Sorrento peninsula whose merchants traded with Constantinople, Egypt and Jerusalem in the 10th and 11th centuries.
republic-of-amalfi.o: Amalfi was a small fortified town on the steep coast of the Sorrento peninsula, part of the Byzantine Duchy of Naples. In 839, after the Lombard prince Sicard of Benevento had attacked it and taken its people away, the Amalfitans broke from Naples and elected their own leaders, first prefects and later judges.
republic-of-amalfi.r: From 958 Amalfi was ruled by dukes, among them Manso I, who also controlled Salerno. With little farmland, it lived from trade: its merchants had colonies in Constantinople, Antioch and Cairo and founded a hospital in Jerusalem from which the Knights Hospitaller later emerged. It minted gold tari, and the maritime code known as the Tabula Amalphitana was used across the Mediterranean.
republic-of-amalfi.e: Robert Guiscard took Amalfi in 1073. It revolted and was absorbed by Roger II's Kingdom of Sicily in 1131. Pisa sacked it in 1135 and 1137, and a storm in 1343 destroyed much of the lower town. Its cathedral and the Amalfi Coast are now famous.

republic-of-indian-stream.t: A tiny self-governing republic on the disputed border between New Hampshire and Lower Canada, home to about 300 settlers.
republic-of-indian-stream.o: The Treaty of Paris of 1783 set the border at the 'northwesternmost head of the Connecticut River', which could be read as several different streams. Settlers in the disputed valley found themselves taxed and called for service by both the United States and British Lower Canada. In 1832 they adopted a constitution and declared their own republic.
republic-of-indian-stream.r: Indian Stream was governed by an assembly of all adult male citizens, an elected council and its own courts, and it promised to last only until the boundary was settled. Its inhabitants were farmers and lumbermen. Divisions grew between residents loyal to New Hampshire and those leaning to Canada, and an arrest by a New Hampshire sheriff's deputy sparked clashes in 1835.
republic-of-indian-stream.e: New Hampshire sent militia in 1835 and annexed the territory in 1836. The Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842 confirmed it as American. The area is now the town of Pittsburg, New Hampshire.

republic-of-mulhouse.t: A Protestant city-republic in Alsace allied to the Swiss, which grew rich on printed cotton and chose to join France in 1798.
republic-of-mulhouse.o: Mulhouse was an imperial town in Upper Alsace that gradually freed itself from local lords and, by the mid-14th century, governed itself through a council and mayor under the emperor. In 1354 it joined the Décapole, the league of ten Alsatian imperial cities.
republic-of-mulhouse.r: Threatened by the Habsburgs, Mulhouse allied with Basel and the Swiss cantons, becoming an associate of the Swiss Confederation in 1515 and leaving the Décapole. It adopted the Reformed faith in the 1520s. From 1746 its merchants founded calico-printing works, making printed cotton, the indiennes, the basis of a major textile industry.
republic-of-mulhouse.e: Surrounded by French territory and strangled by customs barriers after the Revolution, the citizens voted in January 1798 to join the French First Republic. Mulhouse became a leading French industrial city.

republic-of-hawaii.t: The oligarchic republic proclaimed by the overthrow's leaders in 1894, which held Hawaii until it was annexed by the United States in 1898.
republic-of-hawaii.o: When President Grover Cleveland refused to annex Hawaii, the Provisional Government of Hawaii called a constitutional convention. The new constitution was proclaimed on 4 July 1894, creating a republic with Sanford B. Dole as president.
republic-of-hawaii.r: The constitution restricted voting through property, income and literacy tests and loyalty oaths, excluding most Native Hawaiians and all Asian immigrants. Power stayed with the American-descended business elite tied to sugar. In January 1895 royalists led by Robert Wilcox attempted a counter-revolution, which failed; Liliʻuokalani was arrested, forced to abdicate and imprisoned in ʻIolani Palace. Japanese and Chinese labour remained central to the plantations.
republic-of-hawaii.e: The Spanish-American War made Hawaii strategically valuable, and after a treaty failed in the Senate despite petitions by many Native Hawaiians, Congress annexed the islands by the Newlands Resolution in July 1898. Sovereignty was transferred on 12 August 1898, and the islands became the Territory of Hawaii.

republic-of-new-granada.t: The centralist republic formed from Gran Colombia's core around Bogotá, during which Colombia's Liberal and Conservative parties were born.
republic-of-new-granada.o: After Venezuela and Ecuador left Gran Colombia in 1830, the remaining provinces, including Panama, formed the Republic of New Granada under a constitution of 1832. Francisco de Paula Santander returned from exile and served as president from 1832 to 1837.
republic-of-new-granada.r: The republic faced regional revolts, notably the War of the Supremes from 1839 to 1842. Colombia's Liberal and Conservative parties emerged in 1848 and 1849. The liberal president José Hilario López carried out major reforms, abolishing slavery in 1851 and expelling the Jesuits. The Panama Railway, completed in 1855 during the California gold rush, made the isthmus a world trade route. The constitution of 1853 introduced universal male suffrage.
republic-of-new-granada.e: Pressure for federalism grew, and Panama became a self-governing state in 1855. The constitution of 1858 turned the republic into the Granadine Confederation. Its Liberal and Conservative parties dominated Colombian politics into the 21st century.

reichskommissariat-ostland.t: Nazi German occupation regime of the Baltic states and western Belarus from 1941 to 1945, scene of some of the largest massacres of the Holocaust.
reichskommissariat-ostland.o: After the invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941, Germany placed the occupied Baltic states and western Belarus under a civil administration, Reichskommissariat Ostland, created in July 1941 under Alfred Rosenberg's Ministry for the Occupied Eastern Territories. Hinrich Lohse became Reich Commissioner, with his seat in Riga.
reichskommissariat-ostland.r: Ostland was divided into general commissariats for Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and White Ruthenia, each with local auxiliary administrations. The occupiers exploited labour and food and planned eventual German colonisation. The Holocaust was carried out on a vast scale: Jews were murdered at Rumbula near Riga, Ponary near Vilnius, the Ninth Fort in Kaunas and Maly Trostenets near Minsk.
reichskommissariat-ostland.e: Soviet offensives in 1944 retook most of the territory, and Lohse fled. German forces trapped in the Courland Pocket held out until May 1945. The region returned to Soviet rule as the Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republics and Soviet Belarus.

riau-lingga-sultanate.t: Malay sultanate of the Riau islands, a centre of Malay literature under its Bugis viceroys until the Dutch deposed its last sultan.
riau-lingga-sultanate.o: The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 split the old Johor-Riau realm. The mainland and Singapore fell in the British sphere, while the Riau and Lingga islands stayed with the Dutch under a separate line of sultans based at Daik on Lingga, continuing the Malacca royal lineage.
riau-lingga-sultanate.r: Real power lay with the Yang Dipertuan Muda, Bugis viceroys based on Penyengat island. Gambier and pepper planted by Chinese settlers on Bintan funded the court. Penyengat became a cradle of Malay letters, where Raja Ali Haji wrote the Gurindam Dua Belas and an early Malay grammar, laying foundations for standard Malay.
riau-lingga-sultanate.e: Growing friction with the Dutch led them to depose Sultan Abdul Rahman Muazzam Shah in 1911; he fled to Singapore and the sultanate was formally abolished in 1913, its lands absorbed into the Dutch East Indies. Riau Malay later became the basis of Indonesian.

ranasan-state.t: A minor chiefship of the Mahi Kantha country in northern Gujarat, known mainly from colonial lists of tributary estates.
ranasan-state.o: Ranasan was one of the many petty holdings of the Mahi Kantha region, held by a local Rajput or Koli family from around 1600. Its founding is not well documented.
ranasan-state.r: Its Thakor ruled a few villages, paid tribute through the Gaekwads of Baroda and was supervised by the British Mahi Kantha Agency. Standard references record little about its rulers.
ranasan-state.e: Ranasan was merged into Bombay Province in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960.

republic-of-mountainous-armenia.t: An anti-Bolshevik Armenian state in Zangezur, led by Garegin Nzhdeh in 1921, whose resistance helped keep the region within Armenia.
republic-of-mountainous-armenia.o: After the Armenian SSR replaced the First Republic of Armenia in December 1920, the southern mountain district of Zangezur, defended by the commander Garegin Nzhdeh, refused to accept Soviet rule. Following the failed February 1921 uprising in Yerevan, the anti-Bolshevik forces retreated there and in April 1921 proclaimed the Republic of Mountainous Armenia, with its seat at Goris.
republic-of-mountainous-armenia.r: The republic was a wartime state led by Nzhdeh as commander and later prime minister, with Simon Vratsian and other former leaders of the First Republic. It relied on local militias and the mountainous terrain of Syunik and controlled a population swollen with refugees. It sought union with the rest of Armenia once free of Bolshevik rule.
republic-of-mountainous-armenia.e: In July 1921, after the Soviets reportedly promised to keep Zangezur in Soviet Armenia, the Red Army took the region and Nzhdeh withdrew to Iran. The area remained part of the Armenian SSR.

rampur-state.t: The Rohilla Nawabi state of Rampur in Rohilkhand, the only Rohilla principality to survive and home of the Raza Library.
rampur-state.o: After the British-backed Nawab of Awadh defeated the Rohillas in 1774, the Rohilla chief Faizullah Khan, son of Ali Muhammad Khan, was allowed to keep Rampur and surrounding lands by the Treaty of Lal Dhang. He founded the city and a library that became the Raza Library.
rampur-state.r: Rampur stayed loyal to the British in 1857 and was rewarded with land. Nawabs such as Kalb Ali Khan and Hamid Ali Khan patronised Urdu poetry, Hindustani music and scholarship, making Rampur a refuge for artists from Delhi and Lucknow. The state had a 15-gun salute and a roughly equal Hindu and Muslim population.
rampur-state.e: Raza Ali Khan acceded to India, and Rampur was merged into Uttar Pradesh in 1949. The Raza Library, with its Persian manuscripts and Mughal paintings, is now a national institution.

republic-of-tucuman.t: A short-lived provincial republic in northwestern Argentina created by the caudillo Bernabé Aráoz during the anarchy of 1820.
republic-of-tucuman.o: After central government in the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata collapsed in 1820, the governor of Tucumán, Bernabé Aráoz, proclaimed the Republic of Tucumán. It claimed the provinces of Tucumán, Catamarca and Santiago del Estero, and adopted a constitution that year.
republic-of-tucuman.r: Aráoz governed as supreme president, seeking to keep the northern provinces together under Tucumán's leadership. Santiago del Estero, under Juan Felipe Ibarra, rejected his authority and declared its own autonomy, and the two sides went to war. Catamarca also broke away. The republic faced constant conflict with Salta, governed by Martín Miguel de Güemes.
republic-of-tucuman.e: Aráoz was overthrown in 1821, and the republic dissolved into the separate provinces of Tucumán, Catamarca and Santiago del Estero, which later joined the Argentine Confederation. Aráoz was executed in 1824.

republic-of-san-marino.t: Tiny republic on Monte Titano that claims to be the oldest surviving sovereign state and republic in the world, traditionally founded in 301.
republic-of-san-marino.o: Tradition holds that Saint Marinus, a Christian stonemason from the island of Rab in Dalmatia, founded a monastic community on Monte Titano on 3 September 301 to escape persecution under Diocletian. A self-governing community around the monastery and fortress is documented from the early Middle Ages, with an assembly of household heads, the Arengo.
republic-of-san-marino.r: San Marino has been governed since at least the 13th century by two Captains Regent elected every six months, with a Great and General Council as legislature. Its statutes of 1600 served as a written constitution. It kept its independence through its mountain position, alliances with the Montefeltro and recognition by the Papacy in 1631. Catholicism and Italian are dominant; the economy today rests on tourism, banking and stamps.
republic-of-san-marino.e: San Marino survived the occupation by Cardinal Alberoni in 1739–40, declined Napoleon's offer of more territory in 1797, sheltered Garibaldi in 1849 and was left independent at Italian unification. It joined the Council of Europe in 1988 and the United Nations in 1992.

rewa-state.t: The kingdom of the Baghel Rajputs, which gave its name to Baghelkhand, sent the singer Tansen to Akbar's court and gave the world its first known white tigers.
rewa-state.o: The Baghel Rajputs, a branch of the Solanki clan of Gujarat, moved into the region in the 13th century; tradition credits Vyaghra Deva with the founding. Their early stronghold was the hill fort of Bandhogarh (Bandhavgarh).
rewa-state.r: Raja Ramchandra was patron of the musician Tansen, who left his court for Akbar's in the 1560s. Bandhogarh was taken by the Mughals in 1597, and the capital moved to Rewa. The state was large and rural, with forests rich in game. In 1812 Rewa entered treaty relations with the British, and its rulers later sent troops to help against the rebels of 1857.
rewa-state.e: In 1948 Rewa became the leading member and capital of Vindhya Pradesh, which merged into Madhya Pradesh in 1956. In 1951 Maharaja Martand Singh captured the white tiger Mohan, ancestor of many captive white tigers.

rogaland.t: West Norwegian kingdom whose seat at Avaldsnes guarded the Karmsund strait, the 'north way' that gave Norway its name.
rogaland.o: Rogaland, around modern Stavanger, was home to a powerful Iron Age elite. At Avaldsnes on Karmøy, great mounds and a ship burial of the late 8th century mark a seat of kings who controlled shipping through the narrow Karmsund strait along the coast.
rogaland.r: Control of the sea route allowed the rulers to tax or plunder traffic passing north and south. The district had good farmland on Jæren and close links across the North Sea. Its kings, known only from the sagas, were rivals of the kings of Vestfold.
rogaland.e: The decisive Battle of Hafrsfjord, traditionally dated around 872, was fought in Rogaland, where Harald Fairhair defeated the western kings. He made Avaldsnes one of his royal residences, and Rogaland became part of the Kingdom of Norway.

rohilla-state.t: An Afghan state in the plains of Rohilkhand, north-east of Delhi, built by Rohilla soldiers in the decline of the Mughal Empire.
rohilla-state.o: Afghan soldiers, known as Rohillas, settled in the Katehr region east of the Ganges from the late 17th century. Ali Muhammad Khan, adopted son of a Rohilla chief, built a power base there from the 1720s, making Aonla his capital, and was recognised by the Mughal court as nawab.
rohilla-state.r: After Ali Muhammad's death in 1748, Hafiz Rahmat Khan ruled as regent for his sons and led a confederacy of Rohilla chiefs from Bareilly. The Rohillas supported Ahmad Shah Durrani at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761. They promoted Afghan settlement, built towns and mosques, and patronised Persian and Pashto learning.
rohilla-state.e: In 1774 the Nawab of the Awadh State, with East India Company troops, defeated and killed Hafiz Rahmat Khan in the Rohilla War. Most of Rohilkhand was annexed to Awadh, while the Rohilla chief Faizullah Khan kept the small state of Rampur.

republic-of-aras.t: A short-lived Muslim republic in Nakhchivan and the Araxes valley, set up in 1918 to resist incorporation into Armenia.
republic-of-aras.o: After the Ottoman withdrawal from the South Caucasus at the end of the First World War, the mainly Muslim population of Nakhchivan, Sharur and Ordubad, backed by former Ottoman officers, proclaimed the Republic of Aras in November 1918 to block the claims of the First Republic of Armenia to these districts.
republic-of-aras.r: The republic was led by Jafar Qulu Khan Nakhchivanski, of the family of the former khans of Nakhichevan, and had a small administration and militias drawn from the local Muslim population. It sought union with the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic or Ottoman protection and contested control of villages with Armenian forces amid widespread intercommunal violence and refugee movements.
republic-of-aras.e: In 1919 British forces and then Armenian troops took control of Nakhchivan, ending the republic. After further fighting, Nakhchivan became an autonomous republic within Soviet Azerbaijan in the 1920s, an exclave status it keeps today.

royal-prussia.t: The western part of Prussia that rebelled against the Teutonic Knights and lived for three centuries under the Polish Crown, keeping its own diet and privileges.
royal-prussia.o: In 1454 the towns and nobles of the Prussian Confederation rose against the State of the Teutonic Order and placed themselves under King Casimir IV of Poland. After the Thirteen Years' War, the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466 gave Poland Pomerelia, Chelmno Land, Malbork, Elblag and the Prince-Bishopric of Warmia, which together formed Royal Prussia.
royal-prussia.r: Royal Prussia kept wide autonomy, with its own diet, council and laws, and its great cities of Gdansk, Torun and Elblag were largely German-speaking and Lutheran after the Reformation. Gdansk shipped Polish grain to Amsterdam and became the Commonwealth's richest city. Nicolaus Copernicus was born in Torun in 1473. After the Union of Lublin in 1569 the province was drawn more closely into the Crown.
royal-prussia.e: The First Partition of Poland in 1772 gave most of Royal Prussia to the Kingdom of Prussia, which made it the province of West Prussia, and Gdansk and Torun followed in 1793. Gdansk later became the Free City of Danzig (1807-1814).

republic-of-winburg.t: One of the first Voortrekker states north of the Orange River, a loose Boer community between the Vet and Vaal rivers.
republic-of-winburg.o: Voortrekkers under Andries Hendrik Potgieter obtained land between the Vet and Vaal rivers from the Taung chief Makwana in 1836. After the defeat of Mzilikazi's Ndebele in 1837, a settlement was laid out whose name, Winburg, is said to recall that victory.
republic-of-winburg.r: Government was a simple Volksraad of elected burghers with a commandant leading the commando. The farmers raised cattle and sheep and dealt with Sotho and Tswana neighbours by treaty and raid. From 1843 Winburg was loosely joined with the settlements north of the Vaal as Potchefstroom-Winburg.
republic-of-winburg.e: Britain declared the Orange River Sovereignty in 1848 and defeated Andries Pretorius at Boomplaats. Winburg came under British rule and was later part of the Orange Free State.

rhodes.t: Island republic created in 408 BCE that became the leading Hellenistic naval and commercial power of the eastern Mediterranean, home of the Colossus.
rhodes.o: The three old Dorian cities of the island, Ialysos, Kamiros and Lindos, joined in 408-407 BCE to found a single new city of Rhodes at the island's northern tip. Laid out on a regular grid with fine harbours, it quickly drew population and trade, while the old towns survived as districts of the unified state.
rhodes.r: Rhodes was governed by an assembly, council and annual prytaneis, with a moderate democracy that favoured its wealthy shipowners. It lived by trade in grain and wine, policed the sea against pirates, and its maritime law influenced later Roman law. Withstanding the siege of Demetrius Poliorcetes in 305-304 BCE, it built the Colossus. Its schools of rhetoric and philosophy attracted Romans.
rhodes.e: Siding with Rome against Philip V and Antiochus III won Rhodes lands in Caria and Lycia, but Rome punished its wavering by making Delos a free port in 167 BCE. Cassius sacked it in 43 BCE. Claudius withdrew its freedom in 44 CE, and it was later absorbed into the province of Asia.

roman-republic-1798-1799.t: A French-sponsored republic proclaimed in Rome in 1798 after Pope Pius VI was deposed and sent into exile.
roman-republic-1798-1799.o: After the French general Duphot was killed in a riot in Rome in December 1797, French troops under General Berthier occupied the city. On 15 February 1798 a republic was proclaimed in the Forum, ending the temporal power of the Papal States. Pope Pius VI was deported and died in exile at Valence in 1799.
roman-republic-1798-1799.r: The republic adopted a constitution modelled on the French Directory but using ancient Roman titles, with consuls, a senate and a tribunate. It absorbed the Anconine Republic and the Tiberina Republic. French commissioners controlled it, heavy levies and confiscations of art and church property caused hardship, and peasant revolts broke out.
roman-republic-1798-1799.e: In November 1798 the Kingdom of Naples briefly occupied Rome. As the French retreated from Italy in 1799, Neapolitan troops ended the republic in September, and the papacy was restored under Pius VII.

republic-of-anguilla.t: Self-declared republic of a small Caribbean island that rebelled against rule from Saint Kitts and, unusually, asked to stay British.
republic-of-anguilla.o: Anguillians had long resented being governed from Basseterre as part of Saint Christopher-Nevis-Anguilla. When the colony became an Associated State in 1967, islanders expelled the Saint Kitts police on 30 May 1967, and a referendum in July voted for separation. Ronald Webster emerged as the leader of the movement.
republic-of-anguilla.r: An island council under Webster ran affairs, with little money and a few thousand people living from fishing, salt and remittances. Negotiations with Britain produced an interim arrangement, but when it broke down Anguilla declared itself a republic in February 1969 and expelled a British envoy. Its aim was not independence for its own sake but freedom from Saint Kitts, preferably under direct British rule.
republic-of-anguilla.e: On 19 March 1969 British paratroopers and London police landed unopposed in Operation Sheepskin, an episode widely mocked in the press. A British commissioner took over, the Anguilla Act of 1971 confirmed direct rule, and Anguilla was formally separated in 1980. It is now a British Overseas Territory.

rapa-nui.t: The Polynesian society of Easter Island, the most remote inhabited island in the Pacific, famous for its giant moai statues and the undeciphered rongorongo script.
rapa-nui.o: Polynesian voyagers reached Rapa Nui around 1200, probably from eastern Polynesia via Mangareva or the Marquesas. Island tradition names the founding chief as Hotu Matuʻa, who landed at Anakena Bay and divided the land among his sons, ancestors of the island's clans. Over the next centuries the population grew to several thousand.
rapa-nui.r: Kin groups (mata) each held a wedge of coast and built stone platforms (ahu) carrying moai carved from the Rano Raraku crater, nearly 900 in all. A paramount ariki of the Miru clan held sacred rank. Later the Tangata manu or birdman cult at Orongo chose a yearly leader through a race to collect the first sooty tern egg. People farmed sweet potato in stone-mulched gardens and rock shelters on a largely treeless island.
rapa-nui.e: Jacob Roggeveen arrived on Easter Day 1722. Peruvian slave raids in 1862 and the smallpox that followed cut the population to around 110 by 1877. In 1888 Chile annexed the island through an agreement between Policarpo Toro and the ariki Atamu Tekena. Rapa Nui remains part of Chile.

republic-of-biak-na-bato.t: Short-lived revolutionary republic proclaimed by Emilio Aguinaldo in the hills of Bulacan, with the first Filipino constitution.
republic-of-biak-na-bato.o: After Spanish offensives drove the revolutionaries from Cavite in 1897, Emilio Aguinaldo retreated to the caves of Biak-na-Bato in San Miguel, Bulacan. There, on 1 November 1897, his followers adopted a provisional constitution drafted by Isabelo Artacho and Felix Ferrer, modelled on a Cuban revolutionary charter.
republic-of-biak-na-bato.r: The constitution created a Supreme Council with Aguinaldo as president, declared separation from Spain and guaranteed basic rights such as freedom of religion. In practice the republic controlled little beyond its mountain base and the guerrilla bands loyal to it, and it lacked money and arms.
republic-of-biak-na-bato.e: Exhausted, both sides accepted the Pact of Biak-na-Bato, mediated by Pedro Paterno in December 1897. Aguinaldo and other leaders went into exile in Hong Kong in return for payment, ending the republic. Aguinaldo returned in 1898 to found the Revolutionary Government of the Philippines.

republic-of-yemen.t: The unified Yemeni state created in 1990, troubled by civil wars and since 2014 divided by a devastating conflict.
republic-of-yemen.o: On 22 May 1990 the Yemen Arab Republic and South Yemen united as the Republic of Yemen, with Ali Abdullah Saleh as president, Ali Salim al-Beidh as vice-president and Sanaa as capital. Unification was rushed, and the two armies and administrations were never fully merged.
republic-of-yemen.r: In 1994 southern leaders tried to secede; northern forces won a short civil war and took Aden. Saleh ruled through patronage among tribes, the army and his party, while oil revenues declined. In the north the Houthi movement fought six wars with the government from 2004. Yemen remained the poorest country in the Arab world.
republic-of-yemen.e: After the 2011 uprising Saleh handed power to Abd Rabbuh Mansur Hadi. The Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, and a Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015. The war caused a severe humanitarian crisis; since 2022 a Presidential Leadership Council has led the recognised government.

republic-of-egypt.t: Modern republican Egypt, founded after the 1952 revolution, a leading Arab state under Nasser, Sadat, Mubarak and their successors.
republic-of-egypt.o: After the Free Officers overthrew King Farouk in 1952, they abolished the Kingdom of Egypt on 18 June 1953, proclaiming a republic with Muhammad Naguib as president. Gamal Abdel Nasser sidelined Naguib in 1954 and became president in 1956.
republic-of-egypt.r: Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal in 1956, surviving the Anglo-French-Israeli invasion, built the Aswan High Dam and pursued Arab socialism and pan-Arabism, merging with Syria as the United Arab Republic from 1958 to 1961. After defeat in 1967, Anwar Sadat fought the 1973 war and made peace with Israel in 1979. Hosni Mubarak ruled from 1981 for three decades.
republic-of-egypt.e: Mubarak fell in the 2011 uprising. The elected president Mohamed Morsi was removed by the army in 2013, and Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has ruled since 2014. The Arab Republic of Egypt remains the most populous Arab state.

roxolani.t: A Sarmatian people of the steppe between the Don and the Danube, famous for heavy cavalry and repeated raids on Roman Moesia.
roxolani.o: The Roxolani were one of the main Sarmatian tribes, first recorded between the Don and the Dnieper in the 2nd century BCE. Under their leader Tasius they fought on the Scythian side against Diophantes, general of Mithridates VI, around 107 BCE. Over the following century they moved west towards the lower Danube.
roxolani.r: Like other Sarmatians they were mounted pastoralists ruled by kings and nobles. Roman writers describe their lancers in scale armour, terrifying in a charge but helpless when unhorsed. Their relations with Rome swung between raids across the Danube and treaties paid for with subsidies.
roxolani.e: In 69 CE a large Roxolani raid into Moesia was destroyed in winter, and Hadrian later restored payments to their king Rasparaganus. Gothic expansion in the 3rd century and the Hunnic invasion of the 370s broke them up, and their remnants merged with Goths, Alans and Huns.

robogdii.t: People of the north coast of Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, near a headland he called Robogdium, probably in County Antrim.
robogdii.o: The Robogdii are known only from Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, which places them on the north coast of Ireland. A nearby headland, Robogdium Promontorium, is usually identified with Fair Head or a neighbouring point in north Antrim, facing Kintyre across the North Channel.
robogdii.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, settlements or customs. Their coast lay only a short sea crossing from Scotland, a route that in later centuries carried the Dál Riata between Antrim and Argyll, and similar close contact across the channel was probably already important in their time.
robogdii.e: The Robogdii are not mentioned again, and no Irish population name has been securely matched with theirs. North Antrim later formed part of the lands of Dál Riata and the Dal nAraidi.

republic-of-cuba.t: Revolutionary Cuba since 1959, the only communist state in the Americas, ruled by Fidel and Raúl Castro and their successors for over six decades.
republic-of-cuba.o: Fidel Castro's 26th of July Movement overthrew Fulgencio Batista, who fled on 1 January 1959. Castro became prime minister and launched land reform and nationalisation of American and Cuban businesses. The United States imposed an embargo, and Castro declared the revolution socialist in April 1961, during the failed Bay of Pigs invasion.
republic-of-cuba.r: Cuba allied with the Soviet Union, and the stationing of Soviet missiles caused the crisis of October 1962. The Communist Party, founded in 1965, rules as the sole party under the 1976 and 2019 constitutions. The state provided free health care and education while suppressing dissent, and over a million Cubans emigrated, many in the Mariel boatlift of 1980. Cuban troops fought in Angola and Ethiopia. Sugar sold to the Soviet bloc was the economic mainstay.
republic-of-cuba.e: Soviet collapse brought the Special Period of severe shortages in the 1990s. Raúl Castro succeeded Fidel in 2008, and Miguel Díaz-Canel became president in 2018. Mass protests in 2021, blackouts and record emigration mark the republic's current crisis.

republic-of-nicaragua.t: The independent Nicaraguan state since 1838, shaped by foreign intervention, the Somoza dynasty and the Sandinista revolution.
republic-of-nicaragua.o: Nicaragua was the first state to leave the Federal Republic of Central America, on 30 April 1838. The rivalry between liberal León and conservative Granada continued, and in 1852 the small town of Managua, between the two, was chosen as a compromise capital.
republic-of-nicaragua.r: Nicaragua's possible canal route drew foreign powers. The American filibuster William Walker, invited by León's liberals, made himself president in 1856 before a Central American coalition expelled him. Conservative governments then ruled until the liberal José Santos Zelaya, who took the Mosquito Reserve in 1894. United States Marines occupied the country from 1912 to 1933, resisted by Augusto Sandino. The Somoza family ruled from 1936 to 1979.
republic-of-nicaragua.e: The Sandinista revolution overthrew Anastasio Somoza Debayle in 1979, followed by the Contra war. Violeta Chamorro's election in 1990 brought peace, but Daniel Ortega returned to power in 2007 and has since ruled in an increasingly authoritarian manner.

rajahnate-of-butuan.t: A gold-working trading state in northeastern Mindanao, which sent embassies to Song China from 1001 and built the famous balangay boats.
rajahnate-of-butuan.o: Butuan grew at the mouth of the Agusan River, where excavations have found plank boats called balangay, some dated to the 4th century and later. In 1001 it sent its first mission to the Song court, and Chinese records name rulers who sought the same status as Champa.
rajahnate-of-butuan.r: Butuan's wealth came from gold, worked into fine jewellery and regalia found in large hoards, and from trade with China, Champa and the Malay world. In 1007 its ruler Kiling asked for equal rank with Champa, and in 1011 Sri Bata Shaja sent another embassy. The Golden Tara of Agusan suggests Hindu-Buddhist influence.
rajahnate-of-butuan.e: Butuan's prominence faded by the 14th century as trade shifted to Cebu and Sulu. Rajah Siagu met Ferdinand Magellan's expedition in 1521. Butuan came gradually under Spanish rule, and its archaeology is now central to Philippine national history.

republic-of-panama.t: Isthmian republic created in 1903 with US backing to build the Panama Canal, which it finally took full control of in 1999.
republic-of-panama.o: Panama had been part of Colombia since 1821. When the Colombian senate rejected the Hay-Herrán Treaty for a canal, Panamanian leaders, encouraged by Philippe Bunau-Varilla and protected by US warships, declared independence on 3 November 1903. Weeks later the Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty granted the United States the Panama Canal Zone.
republic-of-panama.r: Manuel Amador Guerrero became the first president, and the canal, opened in 1914, dominated the economy and politics. The United States intervened repeatedly in early decades. Arnulfo Arias was elected and overthrown three times. In 1968 the National Guard seized power, and Omar Torrijos negotiated the Torrijos-Carter Treaties of 1977, which provided for the canal's transfer. Ship registration, banking and the Colón Free Zone diversified the economy.
republic-of-panama.e: After Manuel Noriega's rule, the United States invaded in December 1989 and removed him. Democracy was restored, and Panama took full control of the canal on 31 December 1999. An expanded canal with larger locks opened in 2016.

rawwadid-emirate.t: An Arab-Kurdish dynasty that ruled Tabriz and Azerbaijan in the late 10th and 11th centuries until the Seljuk Turks absorbed it.
rawwadid-emirate.o: The Rawwadids descended from an Arab family of the Azd tribe settled near Tabriz in the 8th century, which became Kurdified over time. In the 950s Muhammad ibn Husayn al-Rawwadi made himself master of Tabriz, and around 981 his successors took over the remaining lands of the Sallarid Emirate.
rawwadid-emirate.r: The emirs ruled north-western Iran from Tabriz, which grew into a major city, and fought the Armenian kingdoms and Georgians. Abu'l-Hayja Wahsudan, who ruled from about 1019, welcomed the poet Qatran Tabrizi, whose verses record the destructive earthquake of 1042 at Tabriz.
rawwadid-emirate.e: Wahsudan submitted to the Seljuk Turks under Tughril Beg in 1054, and the dynasty became Seljuk vassals. Alp Arslan removed the last emir in 1071, and Azerbaijan passed directly under Seljuk Empire rule.

republic-of-pechina.t: A self-governing community of Andalusi sailors near Almería that traded across the Mediterranean and founded Oran in 902.
republic-of-pechina.o: Around 884 a community of Andalusi seafarers, the bahriyyun, settled at Bajjana (Pechina) in the lower Andarax valley near Almería, with the permission of the emir and alongside local Arab families. They formed a self-governing body during the decline of central authority in al-Andalus.
republic-of-pechina.r: Pechina was run by a council of sailors rather than a single ruler, recognising the emir only nominally. It lived from maritime trade with North Africa, and its sailors founded trading posts on the African coast, including Oran in 902. Almería served as its harbour and watchtower, and the town grew wealthy as a port for the Mediterranean.
republic-of-pechina.e: Abd al-Rahman III brought Pechina under direct control around 922. Its harbour, Almería, then eclipsed it, becoming the main naval base of the Caliphate of Córdoba, and Pechina declined into a village.

republic-of-acre.t: A short-lived state proclaimed by Brazilian rubber tappers in Bolivian territory, whose struggle ended with Brazil buying Acre in 1903.
republic-of-acre.o: During the Amazon rubber boom, thousands of Brazilian rubber tappers settled in Acre, which belonged to Bolivia by treaty. When Bolivia set up a customs post at Puerto Alonso in 1899, the Spanish adventurer Luis Gálvez Rodríguez de Arias, backed by local interests, proclaimed the Independent State of Acre on 14 July 1899.
republic-of-acre.r: Gálvez declared himself president and set up ministries and decrees in Puerto Alonso, intending eventual union with Brazil. Brazil, which still recognised Bolivian sovereignty, sent a force that removed him in 1900. Conflict revived in 1902 when Bolivia leased the region to an Anglo-American company, the Bolivian Syndicate, and the Brazilian José Plácido de Castro led an armed uprising of rubber tappers.
republic-of-acre.e: Plácido de Castro took Puerto Alonso in 1903, and Brazil occupied the territory. By the Treaty of Petrópolis in 1903 the Republic of Bolivia ceded Acre to Brazil for £2 million and the promise of the Madeira-Mamoré railway.

roman-republic-1849.t: The republic proclaimed in Rome in 1849 and led by Mazzini, whose defence by Garibaldi against French troops became a legend of Italian unification.
roman-republic-1849.o: After the murder of Pope Pius IX's minister Pellegrino Rossi in November 1848, the pope fled to Gaeta in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. An elected Constituent Assembly met in Rome and on 9 February 1849 abolished the temporal power of the Papal States and proclaimed a republic.
roman-republic-1849.r: A triumvirate of Giuseppe Mazzini, Aurelio Saffi and Carlo Armellini governed. The republic abolished the death penalty, introduced religious freedom and drafted a democratic constitution, promulgated on 3 July 1849. Giuseppe Garibaldi led volunteers in defence of the city, notably on the Janiculum hill.
roman-republic-1849.e: Louis-Napoleon's France sent an army under General Oudinot, which besieged Rome from June and entered the city in early July 1849. Garibaldi retreated with his volunteers, and papal rule was restored under French protection.

restored-toungoo-kingdom.t: The Burmese kingdom rebuilt from Ava after the collapse of Bayinnaung's empire, with a compact, centralised state that lasted until 1752.
restored-toungoo-kingdom.o: After the First Toungoo Empire disintegrated in 1599, Nyaungyan Min, a son of Bayinnaung, rebuilt royal power from Ava in Upper Burma. His son Anaukpetlun retook Lower Burma, destroying the Portuguese Syriam of Filipe de Brito in 1613 and reconquering Lan Na in 1615.
restored-toungoo-kingdom.r: Thalun, king from 1629, moved the capital back to Ava in 1635, ordered a revenue inquest and organised royal service groups, the ahmudan, to supply soldiers and labour. The state was smaller and more centralised than Bayinnaung's empire, ruling Upper and Lower Burma, the Shan states and Lan Na. Buddhist learning and court literature flourished.
restored-toungoo-kingdom.e: In the 18th century Manipuri raids devastated Upper Burma, and in 1740 the Mon rose and founded the Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom. Its forces captured Ava in 1752, ending the dynasty, but Alaungpaya then rallied resistance, founding the Konbaung dynasty.

rwanda.t: A small, densely populated republic of the Great Lakes, which suffered the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi and has since been rebuilt under the RPF.
rwanda.o: After the Hutu revolution of 1959 to 1961 abolished the Kingdom of Rwanda, the country became independent from Belgian Ruanda-Urundi on 1 July 1962 as a republic led by Gregoire Kayibanda and his Parmehutu party. Hundreds of thousands of Tutsi fled abroad as violence against them recurred.
rwanda.r: Kayibanda's First Republic was overthrown in 1973 by Juvenal Habyarimana, who ruled a one-party state. In 1990 the Rwandan Patriotic Front, formed by Tutsi exiles in Uganda, invaded. After Habyarimana's plane was shot down in April 1994, Hutu extremists organised a genocide that killed some 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, in about 100 days, until the RPF took power in July.
rwanda.e: Under the RPF and Paul Kagame, president since 2000, Rwanda has rebuilt its economy and institutions, held community gacaca courts and switched to English as a main language, while critics point to restrictions on political freedom. It remains a republic with Kigali as capital.

republic-of-north-ingria.t: Breakaway state of the Ingrian Finns near Petrograd in 1919-1920, backed by Finland and returned to Soviet Russia by the Treaty of Tartu.
republic-of-north-ingria.o: The Ingrian Finns, Lutheran Finnish-speakers living around Petrograd, resisted Bolshevik requisitions and conscription. In 1919, with help from Finland, inhabitants of the northern Ingrian parishes near the Finnish border rose in revolt and declared the Republic of North Ingria, based in the village of Kirjasalo.
republic-of-north-ingria.r: The small republic had its own government, flag, stamps and an armed force of a few hundred men, and sought union with Finland. It controlled only a narrow strip of territory and depended on Finnish supplies and volunteers.
republic-of-north-ingria.e: In the Treaty of Tartu between Finland and Soviet Russia in October 1920, Finland agreed to return North Ingria, while Russia promised the Ingrians cultural autonomy. The republic was dissolved in December 1920, and many inhabitants fled to Finland. The promised autonomy was later revoked, and Ingrian Finns suffered Stalinist deportations.

republic-of-honduras.t: The independent Honduran state since 1838, the original 'banana republic', shaped by American fruit companies, military rule and Cold War politics.
republic-of-honduras.o: Honduras declared its separation from the Federal Republic of Central America on 26 October 1838. Its early decades were marked by intervention from Guatemala and Nicaragua and by attempts to revive the union. Comayagua remained capital until Marco Aurelio Soto moved the government to Tegucigalpa in 1880.
republic-of-honduras.r: Soto's liberal reforms opened the country to foreign mining and investment. From the 1900s the United Fruit, Standard Fruit and Cuyamel companies built banana plantations and railways on the north coast and wielded great political influence, inspiring the term 'banana republic'. Tiburcio Carías Andino ruled as dictator from 1933 to 1949. Frequent coups and military governments followed, and in 1969 Honduras fought the brief Football War with El Salvador.
republic-of-honduras.e: Civilian rule returned in 1982, while the country served as a base for the Contras. Hurricane Mitch devastated it in 1998. A coup removed President Manuel Zelaya in 2009, and Honduras remains a presidential republic struggling with poverty and violence.

restoration-spain.t: The restored Bourbon monarchy of Alfonso XII and Alfonso XIII, a stable but rigged parliamentary system that lost Spain's last colonies in 1898.
restoration-spain.o: In December 1874 General Arsenio Martínez Campos proclaimed Alfonso XII, son of Isabella II, at Sagunto, ending the Sexenio Democrático. The conservative statesman Antonio Cánovas del Castillo designed the new order and its Constitution of 1876.
restoration-spain.r: Under the turno pacífico, Cánovas's Conservatives and Sagasta's Liberals alternated in power through elections managed by local bosses, the caciques. The system kept order but excluded workers and regionalists. Defeat by the United States in 1898 cost Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines, and the Tragic Week of 1909 and the disaster of Annual in Morocco in 1921 shook the regime.
restoration-spain.e: Alfonso XIII backed Miguel Primo de Rivera's dictatorship from 1923 to 1930. After republican victories in the municipal elections of April 1931, the king left Spain, and the Second Spanish Republic was proclaimed.

republic-of-formosa.t: A short-lived republic proclaimed on Taiwan in 1895 to resist the island's cession to Japan, among the first republics declared in East Asia.
republic-of-formosa.o: The Treaty of Shimonoseki of April 1895 forced the Qing Empire to cede Taiwan to Japan after the First Sino-Japanese War. Local gentry and officials, hoping for foreign intervention, proclaimed the Republic of Formosa on 25 May 1895 with the Qing governor Tang Jingsong as president and a tiger flag.
republic-of-formosa.r: The republic was essentially a resistance government. It had a president, a parliament of gentry and its own stamps and banknotes, but it professed loyalty to the Qing and relied on Chinese garrison troops, local militias and the Black Flag Army of Liu Yongfu in the south.
republic-of-formosa.e: Japanese troops landed at the end of May; Tang Jingsong fled to the mainland and Taipei fell in early June. Liu Yongfu continued resistance from Tainan as leader, but the city fell in October 1895 and he escaped. Taiwan under Japanese rule followed.

ranpur-state.t: A small Odisha princely state near Khurda, where a popular uprising in 1939 led to the killing of the British Political Agent.
ranpur-state.o: Ranpur's ruling family claimed very ancient descent, and tradition dates the state to around 1400. Its early history is not reliably documented.
ranpur-state.r: Ranpur was a hilly, wooded state south-west of Cuttack, tributary first to the kings of Khurda and later, from 1803, to the British as one of the Orissa Tributary Mahals. In January 1939, during agitation by the Praja Mandal against the Raja's exactions, a crowd killed the Political Agent, Major R. L. Bazalgette; the rising was put down and leaders were hanged.
ranpur-state.e: Ranpur merged into Orissa on 1 January 1948 and is now in Nayagarh district.

republic-of-maldives.t: The Indian Ocean island republic of the Maldives, transformed by tourism and threatened by rising sea levels.
republic-of-maldives.o: After independence from British protection in 1965, a referendum in 1968 abolished the Sultanate of the Maldives and established a presidential republic. Ibrahim Nasir, the former prime minister, became the first president on 11 November 1968, governing the atolls from Male.
republic-of-maldives.r: Nasir developed tourism from 1972 and fishing modernisation. Maumoon Abdul Gayoom ruled from 1978 to 2008, surviving a coup attempt in 1988 that was defeated with Indian help, while restricting opposition. Islam is the state religion. The 2004 tsunami devastated many islands, and the low-lying country has become a voice for climate action.
republic-of-maldives.e: A new constitution in 2008 introduced multiparty elections, won by Mohamed Nasheed. His resignation under pressure in 2012 began a period of political turmoil, and the republic continues with competitive elections.

republic-of-bergamo.t: A republic proclaimed when Bergamo rose against Venetian rule with French backing in March 1797, before joining the Cisalpine Republic.
republic-of-bergamo.o: Bergamo had been a mainland city of the Republic of Venice since 1428. In March 1797, with French troops in the city, local Jacobins proclaimed Bergamo's independence from Venice and set up a provisional government.
republic-of-bergamo.r: The Bergamasque Republic was a provisional regime of local patriots under French protection. It abolished Venetian institutions, planted liberty trees and sought union with the new republics of Lombardy. Its revolt helped trigger risings in Brescia and Crema, which weakened Venice in the last weeks before its fall.
republic-of-bergamo.e: Venice fell in May 1797, and later that year Bergamo was united to the Cisalpine Republic, created by Napoleon.

rharhabe-xhosa-kingdom.t: The western Xhosa kingdom between the Kei and Fish rivers, which bore the brunt of the frontier wars with the Cape Colony.
rharhabe-xhosa-kingdom.o: Rharhabe, a son of Phalo, quarrelled with his brother Gcaleka and led followers west of the Kei, founding a separate kingdom when the Xhosa Kingdom split around 1775. His successors ruled the Xhosa closest to the advancing Cape frontier.
rharhabe-xhosa-kingdom.r: The kingdom was weakened by rivalry between the regent Ndlambe and Rharhabe's grandson Ngqika, who sought British support; Ndlambe's forces defeated Ngqika at the Battle of Amalinde in 1818. Under Ngqika's sons Maqoma and Sandile, the Rharhabe fought repeated frontier wars, losing land as the Cape pushed its border from the Fish to the Keiskamma and beyond.
rharhabe-xhosa-kingdom.e: After the War of the Axe, Britain annexed the territory between the Keiskamma and Kei as British Kaffraria in 1847, ending Rharhabe independence. Sandile was killed in 1878 during the last frontier war.

republic-of-utrecht.t: A tiny Boer republic on the Buffalo River, created on land obtained from the Zulu king Mpande.
republic-of-utrecht.o: In 1854 Boer farmers obtained a strip of land along the Buffalo River on the Zulu border from King Mpande and founded the village of Utrecht, organising themselves as a small independent republic.
republic-of-utrecht.r: Little is known beyond its simple Volksraad government and a population of a few hundred farming families, who depended on good relations with the Zulu Kingdom.
republic-of-utrecht.e: Utrecht joined the Republic of Lydenburg in 1858, and with it entered the South African Republic in 1860. The district's border with Zululand remained disputed, a grievance behind the Anglo-Zulu War of 1879.

riograndense-republic.t: A breakaway republic in southern Brazil born of the Ragamuffin War, which fought the empire for nearly a decade and gave Garibaldi his first battles.
riograndense-republic.o: In September 1835 ranchers of Rio Grande do Sul, angry at imperial taxes that favoured imported jerked beef, rose against the Empire of Brazil under Bento Gonçalves in the Ragamuffin War, or Farroupilha. After victory at Seival, Antônio de Sousa Neto proclaimed the Riograndense Republic on 11 September 1836.
riograndense-republic.r: Bento Gonçalves served as president, and the republic's capital moved between Piratini, Caçapava and Alegrete as fighting shifted. It was run by a ranching elite and recruited gauchos and enslaved black soldiers, the Lanceiros Negros, promising them freedom. The Italian revolutionary Giuseppe Garibaldi fought for it, leading an expedition that created the Juliana Republic in 1839.
riograndense-republic.e: The imperial commander Luís Alves de Lima e Silva, later Duke of Caxias, combined military pressure with negotiation, and the Treaty of Ponche Verde on 1 March 1845 ended the war with an amnesty. The republic's flag inspired the flag of Rio Grande do Sul.

republic-of-the-rio-grande.t: Federalist breakaway republic in northeastern Mexico, proclaimed at Laredo in January 1840 and defeated within the year.
republic-of-the-rio-grande.o: Opposition to the Centralist Republic of Mexico ran deep in the northern frontier states of Tamaulipas, Nuevo León and Coahuila. In January 1840 federalist leaders meeting near Laredo declared an independent republic, naming Jesús de Cárdenas president and Antonio Canales commander of its army, with Antonio Zapata as a leading officer.
republic-of-the-rio-grande.r: The republic existed mainly as a military campaign. Its leaders hoped to restore the federal Constitution of 1824, and some sought help from the Republic of Texas, recruiting Texan volunteers. Its government moved between Laredo, Guerrero and other border towns, and it never controlled the main cities of the region or collected regular revenues.
republic-of-the-rio-grande.e: Centralist forces under Mariano Arista defeated the rebels; Zapata was captured and executed in March 1840. Canales surrendered in November 1840 and later served the Mexican government. The flag of the republic is still displayed in Laredo, Texas, as one of the city's historic flags.

republic-of-genoa-1814.t: A brief restoration of the old Genoese republic under British protection in 1814, before the Congress of Vienna gave Genoa to Piedmont.
republic-of-genoa-1814.o: In April 1814 British forces under Lord William Bentinck landed and took Genoa from the French. Bentinck, hoping to rally Italians against Napoleon, proclaimed the restoration of the Republic of Genoa under the old constitution of 1797, with a provisional government led by Girolamo Serra.
republic-of-genoa-1814.r: The provisional government tried to revive the institutions of the old aristocratic republic and lobbied the allied powers for recognition. It controlled Genoa and the Ligurian coast but had no army of its own and relied on British protection.
republic-of-genoa-1814.e: The great powers had already decided to strengthen Piedmont as a barrier against France. The Congress of Vienna gave Genoa to the Kingdom of Sardinia, which took possession in January 1815, despite Genoese protests.

russian-america.t: Russia's only overseas colony, a chain of fur-trading posts in Alaska run by the Russian-American Company until the territory was sold to the United States.
russian-america.o: After Vitus Bering's voyage of 1741, Siberian traders hunted sea otters in the Aleutian Islands, and Grigory Shelikhov founded a permanent settlement on Kodiak Island in 1784. In 1799 Emperor Paul I granted a monopoly charter to the Russian-American Company, which was to govern the territory on the state's behalf.
russian-america.r: The Company's chief managers ruled from Kodiak and, from 1808, from New Archangel (Sitka), built by Alexander Baranov after the Tlingit destroyed an earlier fort in 1802. Aleut and Alutiiq hunters were forced to hunt sea otters, whose pelts were sold to China. The colony depended on imported food and briefly ran Fort Ross in California. Orthodox missionaries, including Innocent Veniaminov, converted many Native people.
russian-america.e: With sea otters depleted and Russia fearing it could not defend Alaska against Britain after the Crimean War, the territory was sold to the United States in 1867 for $7.2 million. The Russian Orthodox Church remains a lasting legacy in Alaska.

republic-of-pernambuco.t: A short-lived republic proclaimed in Recife in 1817, the first serious attempt to break part of Brazil away from the Portuguese crown.
republic-of-pernambuco.o: Pernambuco's planters and merchants resented the heavy taxes imposed to support the royal court in Rio de Janeiro, and Masonic lodges spread liberal and republican ideas. On 6 March 1817 officers resisting arrest killed their commander in Recife, and a provisional republican government took power.
republic-of-pernambuco.r: The provisional government, including the merchant Domingos José Martins and the priest João Ribeiro, abolished some taxes, proclaimed freedom of conscience and the press, and drafted an organic law. It sent an envoy, Antônio Gonçalves da Cruz, to seek recognition from the United States. The revolt spread to Paraíba and Rio Grande do Norte, but slavery was left untouched to keep planter support.
republic-of-pernambuco.e: Royal forces of the Kingdom of Brazil blockaded Recife by sea and advanced overland from Bahia. The republic fell in May 1817, after about 75 days. Several leaders, including Martins, were executed, and others, such as Frei Caneca, imprisoned, later joining the Confederation of the Equator.

republic-of-south-vietnam.t: The provisional revolutionary government set up by the communist-led National Liberation Front in 1969, which formally ruled the south after Saigon's fall.
republic-of-south-vietnam.o: In June 1969 the National Liberation Front and allied groups formed the Provisional Revolutionary Government of the Republic of South Vietnam to give the southern insurgency a governmental form for negotiations. It was led by the architect Huynh Tan Phat, with Nguyen Huu Tho as head of its advisory council.
republic-of-south-vietnam.r: The PRG operated from jungle bases near the Cambodian border and later in liberated zones, rather than a fixed capital. It was a party to the Paris peace talks, where Nguyen Thi Binh served as foreign minister and signed the 1973 accords. It was recognised by many communist and non-aligned states, though it was controlled by the Workers' Party in Hanoi.
republic-of-south-vietnam.e: After the fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975 the PRG became the nominal government of the south. Hanoi moved quickly to reunification, and on 2 July 1976 it merged with the Democratic Republic of Vietnam to form the Socialist Republic of Vietnam.

royal-audiencia-of-charcas.t: The Spanish high court and province of Upper Peru, home to the silver mountain of Potosí, from which the Republic of Bolivia emerged.
royal-audiencia-of-charcas.o: The silver deposits of Cerro Rico at Potosí were discovered in 1545, making the highlands south of Lake Titicaca immensely valuable. In 1559 the crown created a Royal Audiencia at La Plata, also called Chuquisaca and now Sucre, to govern the region of Charcas, or Upper Peru, within the Viceroyalty of Peru.
royal-audiencia-of-charcas.r: The Audiencia was both a high court and a governing body under a president. Potosí, worked by indigenous labour drafted through the mita, became one of the largest cities in the world by 1600, and its silver was minted into coins traded across the globe. La Plata held an archbishopric and the University of San Francisco Xavier, founded in 1624, which educated many future revolutionaries. Aymara and Quechua communities paid tribute and labour.
royal-audiencia-of-charcas.e: In 1776 Charcas was transferred to the new Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata. Revolts in Chuquisaca and La Paz in 1809 began the struggle for independence. After Sucre's victories, the Republic of Bolivia was proclaimed in 1825.

reddi-kingdom.t: A Telugu kingdom of coastal Andhra founded after the fall of the Kakatiyas, known for its forts and its literary court.
reddi-kingdom.o: Prolaya Vema Reddi, a former Kakatiya follower, joined the revolt of the Musunuri Nayaks against the Delhi Sultanate and around 1325 established his own rule in coastal Andhra. He made Addanki and then Kondavidu his capital, and the dynasty extended along the coast from the Krishna to the Godavari.
reddi-kingdom.r: The Reddi kings ruled through a network of hill forts such as Kondavidu and Kondapalli and controlled the port of Motupalli, encouraging trade. Their court supported Telugu and Sanskrit literature: the great poet Srinatha served Pedakomati Vema, and Errana completed the Telugu Mahabharata. The kings granted land generously to Brahmins and temples.
reddi-kingdom.e: Caught between the Vijayanagara Empire, the Bahmani Sultanate and the Gajapatis of Odisha, the Reddis lost territory steadily. Kondavidu fell to Vijayanagara around 1424, and the Rajahmundry branch was absorbed by the Gajapati Kingdom by 1448.

republic-of-zakopane.t: A local Polish government in the Tatra resort of Zakopane, headed by the novelist Stefan Zeromski in the first days of independence.
republic-of-zakopane.o: In late October 1918, as Austria-Hungary disintegrated, the citizens of Zakopane and the Podhale highlands took over local power from Austrian officials. A National Organisation was formed, and on 13 November the writer Stefan Zeromski, who was living in the town, became chairman of its council.
republic-of-zakopane.r: The so-called republic was a temporary administration rather than a separate state: it declared loyalty to a reborn Poland, took control of the town's offices and police, and organised volunteers to guard the border with Slovakia. It also had to deal with food shortages in the mountain region.
republic-of-zakopane.e: Within weeks the new Polish government in Warsaw and Krakow extended its authority to Podhale, and by the end of 1918 Zakopane was simply part of the Second Polish Republic.

rashtrakuta-dynasty.t: The Deccan empire that carved the Kailasa temple at Ellora and was ranked by Arab travellers among the four great kingdoms of the world.
rashtrakuta-dynasty.o: Dantidurga, a feudatory of the Chalukyas of Badami, overthrew his overlord Kirtivarman II in 753 and founded the Rashtrakuta empire in the northern Deccan. His uncle Krishna I completed the conquest of the Chalukya lands and commissioned the Kailasa temple at Ellora, carved from a single mass of rock.
rashtrakuta-dynasty.r: Dhruva and Govinda III led armies to the Ganges plain, defeating the Gurjara-Pratihara and the Pala Empire. Amoghavarsha I, ruling from 814 to 878, founded the capital Manyakheta, was a patron of Jainism and is credited with the Kavirajamarga, the earliest surviving work on Kannada poetics. The Arab merchant Sulaiman described him as one of the four great kings of the world. Krishna III defeated the Cholas at Takkolam in 949.
rashtrakuta-dynasty.e: In 972 the Paramara king Siyaka sacked Manyakheta. The next year Tailapa II, a feudatory, overthrew Karka II and founded the Western Chalukya Empire; Rashtrakuta claimants held out until 982.

republic-of-negros.t: Republic of sugar planters on Negros island that broke from Spain in 1898 and soon sought American protection.
republic-of-negros.o: On 5 November 1898 revolutionaries on Negros, led by Aniceto Lacson and Juan Araneta, rose against the Spanish garrison and secured the island within days. They established a cantonal republic centred on Bacolod, first linked to the Federal State of the Visayas.
republic-of-negros.r: Its leaders were wealthy sugar planters who wanted order and access to markets more than full independence. Lacson served as president and Araneta as war secretary. Unlike most revolutionary governments, it welcomed American forces in 1899 and became a protectorate under United States supervision, adopting its own constitution.
republic-of-negros.e: The United States Military Government of the Philippine Islands gradually absorbed its functions, and the republic was dissolved in April 1901 when Negros became a province under the Insular Government of the Philippine Islands. The rising is still commemorated on 5 November.

republic-of-pisa.t: A Tuscan maritime republic that dominated the western Mediterranean in the 12th century and left the Piazza dei Miracoli with its famous leaning tower.
republic-of-pisa.o: Pisan fleets attacked Muslim bases in Sardinia, Sicily and North Africa in the 11th century, and booty from a raid on Palermo in 1063 paid for the cathedral. Consuls governing the city are attested by 1085. Archbishop Daibert led a Pisan fleet in the First Crusade and became the first Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem.
republic-of-pisa.r: Pisa built trading quarters in Acre, Tyre, Constantinople and Alexandria, ruled much of Sardinia and Corsica, and conquered the Balearic Islands briefly in 1113–1115. Loyal to the emperors, it was a Ghibelline stronghold. Its merchants brought back Arabic learning: Leonardo Fibonacci's Liber Abaci of 1202 introduced Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe. The cathedral square, with baptistery and bell tower begun in 1173, shows its wealth.
republic-of-pisa.e: Genoa destroyed the Pisan fleet at Meloria in 1284, and the Kingdom of Aragon took Sardinia in 1324. Weakened by faction and the silting of its port, Pisa was sold to the Republic of Florence in 1405 and surrendered after a siege in 1406.

romania.t: Present-day Romania, a democracy since the revolution of 1989 and a member of NATO and the European Union.
romania.o: The revolution of December 1989 overthrew Nicolae Ceaușescu and ended the Socialist Republic of Romania. The National Salvation Front, led by Ion Iliescu, took power and won the elections of May 1990, though violent interventions by miners in Bucharest in 1990 cast doubt on its commitment to democracy. A new constitution was adopted in 1991.
romania.r: Romania is a semi-presidential republic with a directly elected president and a bicameral parliament. Power first passed peacefully to the opposition in 1996 under Emil Constantinescu. Privatisation and reform were slow in the 1990s, but growth accelerated in the 2000s, driven by industry, services and IT. Millions of Romanians emigrated to work in Western Europe.
romania.e: Romania joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007. Anti-corruption campaigns and mass protests in 2017 shaped politics, and the annulment of the 2024 presidential election over alleged foreign interference caused a political crisis before a rerun in 2025.

republic-of-china.t: Asia's first republic, founded on the mainland in 1912, which after 1949 continued on Taiwan and became a prosperous democracy.
republic-of-china.o: The Wuchang Uprising of October 1911 spread across the southern provinces, and on 1 January 1912 the Republic of China was proclaimed at Nanjing with Sun Yat-sen as provisional president. The last Qing emperor abdicated in February, and Yuan Shikai became president, ruling from Beijing.
republic-of-china.r: After Yuan's death the Beiyang government in Beijing lost control to regional warlords. Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government reunified much of China in 1928 and led resistance to Japan from 1937 to 1945, but lost the civil war to the Communists. In 1949 the government moved to Taipei, ruling Taiwan under martial law while presiding over rapid industrial growth.
republic-of-china.e: The People's Republic of China took China's United Nations seat in 1971. Martial law ended in 1987, President Lee Teng-hui oversaw democratic reforms and the first direct presidential election in 1996, and power passed peacefully to the opposition in 2000. The Republic today governs Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu.

reval.t: Hanseatic port of medieval Tallinn, a self-governing merchant city under Danish and then Order rule whose old town survives almost intact.
reval.o: Reval grew around the Danish castle on Toompea, built after the Battle of Lindanise in 1219. In 1248 King Eric IV of Denmark granted the town Lübeck law, giving it self-government, and it soon joined the Hanseatic network linking Novgorod with Lübeck and the west.
reval.r: A council of German merchants ran the lower town, while the castle hill was the seat of the ruler and the nobility. The Great Guild, the Brotherhood of the Blackheads and craft guilds organised trade and society. Reval prospered on the transit trade with Novgorod, building its Gothic town hall, completed in 1404, and the tall spire of St Olaf's Church.
reval.e: Reval passed from the Duchy of Estonia (1219-1346) to the Livonian Order in 1346 and adopted Lutheranism in the 1520s. Threatened by Russia during the Livonian War, the city submitted to Eric XIV of Sweden in 1561, becoming the capital of the Duchy of Estonia (1561-1721).

republic-of-siena-at-montalcino.t: The last stand of the Sienese republic, kept alive in the hill town of Montalcino with French support for four years after Siena fell.
republic-of-siena-at-montalcino.o: When Siena surrendered to imperial and Florentine forces in April 1555, several hundred citizens who refused to submit withdrew to the fortified town of Montalcino, south of the city, and continued the government of the Republic of Siena there under French protection.
republic-of-siena-at-montalcino.r: The exiles kept the republic's magistracies and seal, minted coins and governed Montalcino and a few nearby towns. They depended on French troops and on Piero Strozzi, the Florentine exile who commanded for France in Tuscany. The republic's territory was small, its resources were slight and it lived under the constant threat of the Duchy of Florence.
republic-of-siena-at-montalcino.e: The Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis between France and Spain in 1559 withdrew French support, and Montalcino surrendered to Cosimo I de' Medici, joining the future Grand Duchy of Tuscany. The town's people are still nicknamed the last Sienese.

roman-numidia.t: Rome's frontier province in eastern Algeria, home of the Third Augustan Legion, the city of Timgad and the Donatist church.
roman-numidia.o: Numidia came under Rome after the defeat of Juba I in 46 BCE and was long administered as part of Africa Proconsularis, although the commander of the Third Augustan Legion effectively governed it. Around 198 Septimius Severus made it a separate province, governed by the legate from the fortress at Lambaesis.
roman-numidia.r: The legion guarded the Aurès mountains and the desert frontier, and veterans settled in new towns such as Thamugadi (Timgad), founded by Trajan in 100. Cirta was the leading city, renamed Constantina by Constantine. The high plains produced grain and olive oil. Numidia was the stronghold of the Donatist church and the birthplace of Augustine at Thagaste. Diocletian briefly split it into Numidia Cirtensis and Numidia Militiana.
roman-numidia.e: After 435 the Vandals took control of parts of Numidia, and their capture of Carthage in 439 ended Roman rule. Byzantine forces later reoccupied much of it, while Berber kingdoms such as the Kingdom of the Aures held the mountains.

republic-of-tamrash.t: Self-governing community of Muslim Pomak villages in the Rhodope mountains that refused Russian and Bulgarian rule after the war of 1877 to 1878.
republic-of-tamrash.o: During the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 to 1878, Muslim Bulgarian-speaking Pomaks in the western Rhodopes resisted the advancing Russian army. After the war, about twenty villages around Tamrash refused to submit to the Russian administration or to Eastern Rumelia, and organised their own defence and government in the mountains.
republic-of-tamrash.r: Known mainly from diplomatic reports, the community was governed by local Muslim notables and village councils, under the nominal suzerainty of the Ottoman sultan. It survived because of its remote terrain and because the Great Powers left its status unresolved.
republic-of-tamrash.e: When Bulgaria absorbed Eastern Rumelia in 1885, the Bulgarian-Ottoman agreement of 1886 transferred the Pomak villages and the Kardzhali district back to direct Ottoman rule. They became part of Bulgaria after the Balkan Wars of 1912 to 1913.
