republic-of-central-albania.t: Rival Albanian government set up by Essad Pasha Toptani in Durrës in 1913, a symptom of the struggle for power in the newly independent country.
republic-of-central-albania.o: Essad Pasha Toptani, an Ottoman general from a leading landowning family of central Albania, commanded the defence of Shkodër in the First Balkan War, then surrendered it to Montenegro in April 1913 in exchange for safe passage. Opposing Ismail Qemali's Provisional Government of Albania, he set up his own government in Durrës in October 1913.
republic-of-central-albania.r: Essad ruled central Albania, from Durrës to around Tirana and Elbasan, through a senate of local notables and the support of Muslim landowners and his own armed retainers. He cultivated ties with Serbia and Italy. The state was essentially his personal domain and was never recognised by the Great Powers.
republic-of-central-albania.e: Essad accepted the authority of Wilhelm of Wied in early 1914, becoming minister of the interior and war in the Principality of Albania, but was expelled for intrigue in May 1914. He returned later in 1914 to rule central Albania until 1916, and was assassinated in Paris in 1920.

republic-of-ossola.t: The best-known partisan republic of wartime Italy, which governed the Alpine valleys around Domodossola for about forty days in 1944.
republic-of-ossola.o: In September 1944 Italian partisan formations drove German and Fascist garrisons out of the Val d'Ossola, near the Swiss border, and entered Domodossola on 10 September. A provisional government junta was formed, presided over by the socialist Ettore Tibaldi.
republic-of-ossola.r: The junta brought together members of the different anti-Fascist parties. In a few weeks it reorganised local government, schools, justice and food supply, and planned democratic reforms, while the Swiss border allowed contacts with the Allies. Its experience of self-government later influenced debates on the Italian constitution.
republic-of-ossola.e: In October 1944 German and Fascist troops of the Italian Social Republic launched an offensive and reoccupied the valley. Thousands of civilians and partisans fled into Switzerland.

republic-of-poljica.t: Self-governing peasant and minor-noble community between Split and Omiš that kept its own law and elected rulers for nearly four centuries.
republic-of-poljica.o: Poljica, a hilly district between the Cetina river and the coast near Split, had long enjoyed local autonomy under Croatian and Hungarian kings. Its customary law was written down in the Poljica Statute, traditionally dated to 1440, which fixed the rights of its villages and noble families. As the Ottomans advanced, Poljica placed itself under Venetian protection.
republic-of-poljica.r: Each year an assembly at Gata elected a grand knez from the local nobility, assisted by village knezes, judges and a chancellor. Land was held by kin groups, and the statute regulated inheritance, feuds and grazing. The statute was written in Croatian in Bosnian Cyrillic script. Poljica paid tribute to the Ottomans while serving Venice as a frontier buffer.
republic-of-poljica.e: After Venice fell in 1797, Poljica came under Austria and then, in 1806, France. When Poljica men joined a Russian-backed rising, Marshal Marmont abolished the republic in 1807 and merged it into French Dalmatia, later the Illyrian Provinces. The statute remains a key source for Croatian law.

republic-of-cyrene.t: Cyrene after its kings, a quarrelsome Greek republic famous for silphium, horses and the Cyrenaic school of philosophy.
republic-of-cyrene.o: Around 440 BCE the last Battiad king, Arcesilaus IV, was overthrown and the Kingdom of Cyrene became a republic. The city remained the leading power of Cyrenaica, a group of Greek cities later called the Pentapolis, together with Barca, Euesperides, Taucheira and its own port, Apollonia.
republic-of-cyrene.r: Government swung between democracy and oligarchy, with bloody civil strife in the early 4th century BCE. Cyrene remained rich from silphium, grain and horses, and it treated with Carthage over its western border at the Altars of the Philaeni. It was an intellectual centre: Aristippus founded the Cyrenaic school of philosophy, and the mathematician Theodorus taught there. Cyrene submitted to Alexander the Great in 331 BCE.
republic-of-cyrene.e: In 324 to 322 BCE the Spartan adventurer Thibron attacked the city, and its factions called in Ptolemy I, whose general Ophellas annexed Cyrene to the Ptolemaic Empire in 322 BCE. It later became the centre of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Cyrene.

ruanda-urundi.t: The Belgian mandate over the kingdoms of Rwanda and Burundi, whose colonial policies sharpened the Hutu and Tutsi divide.
ruanda-urundi.o: Belgian troops from the Congo occupied the north-western part of German East Africa in 1916. After the war the League of Nations assigned the territory to Belgium as a mandate, confirmed in 1924, and in 1946 it became a United Nations trust territory. Its administrative centre was Usumbura, now Bujumbura.
ruanda-urundi.r: Belgium ruled indirectly through the mwami of the Kingdom of Rwanda and the Kingdom of Burundi and their chiefs, favouring a Tutsi elite and replacing Hutu chiefs. Identity cards introduced in the 1930s fixed ethnic labels. The Catholic Church ran schools and missions, and coffee became the main cash crop, often grown under compulsion. The territory was administered jointly with the Belgian Congo from 1925.
ruanda-urundi.e: From 1959 the Hutu revolution in Rwanda overthrew the monarchy, while Burundi stayed a kingdom. The UN failed to keep the two together, and on 1 July 1962 they became independent as the republic of Rwanda and the Kingdom of Burundi.

republic-of-central-lithuania.t: A Polish-controlled state around Vilnius, created by a staged mutiny in 1920 and annexed by Poland in 1922.
republic-of-central-lithuania.o: In October 1920, days after an armistice gave Vilnius to Lithuania, the Polish general Lucjan Zeligowski led troops in a staged mutiny, approved secretly by Pilsudski, and captured the city. He proclaimed the Republic of Central Lithuania, claiming to act for the local Polish-speaking population.
republic-of-central-lithuania.r: Zeligowski ruled as supreme commander through a provisional governing commission, and the state had its own stamps, army and courts. Its population was mixed: Poles, Jews, Lithuanians and Belarusians. League of Nations attempts to arrange a plebiscite failed, and elections in January 1922 were boycotted by most Lithuanians, Jews and Belarusians.
republic-of-central-lithuania.e: The resulting assembly voted in February 1922 to join Poland, and the territory became part of the Second Polish Republic. Lithuania refused to recognise this and broke off relations until 1938, regaining Vilnius from the Soviet Union in 1939.

real-audiencia-of-panama.t: The royal court and government of the Isthmus of Panama, the vital crossing through which Peruvian silver passed on its way to Spain.
real-audiencia-of-panama.o: The Audiencia of Panama was established in 1538 to govern Castilla de Oro and the surrounding provinces of Tierra Firme. It was briefly abolished in 1543 and restored in the 1560s, and from 1542 it fell within the sphere of the Viceroyalty of Peru.
real-audiencia-of-panama.r: Panama's role was transit: silver from Potosí was shipped to Panama City, carried across the isthmus by mule and river, and traded at the great fairs of Nombre de Dios and later Portobelo for European goods. The trade attracted attacks: Henry Morgan sacked Panama City in 1671, and it was rebuilt on a new site in 1673. Edward Vernon captured Portobelo in 1739.
real-audiencia-of-panama.e: As Spain shifted to sailing around Cape Horn, the isthmus declined. The audiencia was abolished in 1751, and Panama was placed under the Viceroyalty of New Granada. It later joined Gran Colombia.

republic-of-upingtonia.t: A short-lived republic of Dorsland trekkers at Grootfontein in northern Namibia, swallowed by German South West Africa.
republic-of-upingtonia.o: Boer Dorsland trekkers who had crossed the Kalahari settled around Grootfontein, on land bought in 1885 from the Ndonga king Kambonde by the trader William Worthington Jordan. They proclaimed a republic, naming it Upingtonia after the Cape prime minister Thomas Upington.
republic-of-upingtonia.r: The settlement consisted of a few dozen families farming in a fertile but isolated area. Its title to the land was disputed by the Herero Paramountcy, which claimed the region, and the settlers lacked the means to defend themselves.
republic-of-upingtonia.e: Jordan was murdered in 1886, and the settlers, under pressure from the Herero and with no outside support, renamed the state Lijdensrust and dissolved it in 1887. Many moved on to Angola, and the area passed to German South West Africa.

republic-of-uzice.t: Liberated territory in western Serbia held by Tito's Partisans in autumn 1941, the first large free zone in occupied Europe.
republic-of-uzice.o: In the uprising of summer 1941 against the German occupation of Serbia, Communist-led Partisans and Chetnik units liberated much of western Serbia. The Partisans took Užice on 24 September 1941, and Josip Broz Tito set up his headquarters there, making the town the centre of a liberated territory covering several districts.
republic-of-uzice.r: Local people's liberation committees took over administration, schools and supplies, while the town's arms factory produced rifles and ammunition in an underground vault, and the Communist newspaper Borba was printed there. Relations with Draža Mihailović's Chetniks broke down into open fighting in early November 1941.
republic-of-uzice.e: A German offensive in late November 1941 retook Užice, and the Partisans withdrew into the Sandžak and eastern Bosnia, where they formed the First Proletarian Brigade. Under the later Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Užice was renamed Titovo Užice.

republic-of-lucca.t: A silk-weaving Tuscan city-republic that kept its independence behind its great walls for over six centuries, until Napoleon.
republic-of-lucca.o: Lucca had been the capital of the march of Tuscany, and a commune of consuls emerged in the late 11th century. In 1160 Duke Welf VI granted the city wide rights, confirming its self-government over the surrounding district.
republic-of-lucca.r: Lucca prospered from silk weaving and banking, and venerated the Volto Santo crucifix. Castruccio Castracani made himself lord from 1316 to 1328 and won a large state, but after his death the city was sold among foreign lords until Emperor Charles IV restored its freedom in 1369. Paolo Guinigi ruled as lord from 1400 to 1430. Afterwards an oligarchy of merchant families governed, building the massive walls of the 16th and 17th centuries.
republic-of-lucca.e: The French occupied Lucca in 1799, and in 1805 Napoleon replaced the republic with the Principality of Lucca and Piombino for his sister Elisa.

republic-of-afghanistan-1973-1978.t: The republic founded by Mohammad Daoud Khan after he overthrew his cousin King Zahir Shah, ended five years later by a communist coup.
republic-of-afghanistan-1973-1978.o: On 17 July 1973 the former prime minister Mohammad Daoud Khan, cousin and brother-in-law of King Zahir Shah, seized power in a bloodless coup with the support of army officers, including members of the communist Parcham faction. He abolished the Kingdom of Afghanistan and declared a republic with himself as president.
republic-of-afghanistan-1973-1978.r: Daoud ruled in an authoritarian style, pursuing the Pashtunistan dispute with Pakistan and economic development with Soviet and Western aid. He suppressed Islamist opponents, many of whom fled to Pakistan, and gradually pushed the communists out of government. A new constitution in 1977 created a one-party state, and he sought closer ties with Iran and the Gulf states, angering Moscow.
republic-of-afghanistan-1973-1978.e: After the murder of the communist leader Mir Akbar Khyber led to mass protests, Daoud arrested communist leaders. On 27 April 1978 army officers loyal to the People's Democratic Party killed Daoud and his family in the Saur Revolution, establishing the Democratic Republic of Afghanistan.

radhanpur-state.t: A Babi Pathan Nawabi state in northern Gujarat, founded by a Mughal officer on the edge of the Rann of Kutch.
radhanpur-state.o: Kamal-ud-din Khan Babi, known as Jawan Mard Khan, was a Mughal officer in Gujarat from the Babi family that also ruled Junagadh State. After the Marathas took Ahmedabad in 1753 he secured Radhanpur and nearby districts as his own principality.
radhanpur-state.r: The Nawabs ruled a dry territory on the trade route towards Kutch and Sindh. Under British protection Radhanpur was an 11-gun salute state, first under the Palanpur Agency and later the Western India States Agency, with a largely Hindu farming population.
radhanpur-state.e: After accession to India Radhanpur was merged into Bombay State in 1948 and has been part of Gujarat since 1960; it is now in Patan district.

rabih-az-zubayrs-state.t: The conquest state of the Sudanese warlord Rabih, which overran Bornu before French forces destroyed it at Kousseri in 1900.
rabih-az-zubayrs-state.o: Rabih az-Zubayr had served the slave-trading magnate al-Zubayr Rahma Mansur in the Bahr al-Ghazal. When Egyptian forces crushed al-Zubayr's son Sulayman in 1879, Rabih led an army of several hundred riflemen west into the borderlands of Dar al Kuti and the Chari basin, where he built a new power.
rabih-az-zubayrs-state.r: Rabih ruled as a military chief, with a disciplined army of slave soldiers armed with rifles, raiding widely for captives. He made Muhammad al-Sanusi of Dar al Kuti his vassal, attacked the Kingdom of Baguirmi and in 1893 conquered the ancient Kanem-Bornu Empire, ruling from a new capital at Dikwa.
rabih-az-zubayrs-state.e: French columns converged on the Chari, and on 22 April 1900 Rabih was killed at Kousseri, where the French commander Lamy also died. His son Fadlallah was killed in 1901, and the lands were divided among France, Britain and Germany.

ran-wei.t: The brief empire of Ran Min, a Chinese general who seized the Later Zhao capital in 350 and ordered the massacre of the Jie and other northern peoples.
ran-wei.o: Ran Min was a Chinese general adopted into the family of the Later Zhao emperor Shi Hu. In the civil war after Shi Hu's death he seized Ye, and in 350 he proclaimed himself emperor of a new Wei dynasty.
ran-wei.r: Ran Min ordered the killing of the Jie and other non-Chinese in Ye; sources claim some 200,000 died. The massacre made his regime a rallying point for Chinese hostility to the northern conquerors but left it surrounded by enemies. Ran Wei held little more than the Ye region and was constantly at war with Later Zhao remnants.
ran-wei.e: In 352 the Former Yan general Murong Ke defeated and captured Ran Min at Liantai; he was executed, and Ye fell later that year. In modern times Ran Min has been both condemned for genocide and praised by nationalists.

rehoboth-basters.t: The self-governing community of the Rehoboth Basters in central Namibia, which kept its own captaincy and laws for more than a century.
rehoboth-basters.o: The Basters, descendants of Cape Dutch settlers and Khoekhoe women, left the northern Cape in 1868 and under Kaptein Hermanus van Wyk settled at Rehoboth, south of Windhoek, in 1870, acquiring land from the Swartbooi Nama.
rehoboth-basters.r: In 1872 they adopted written Paternal Laws, the Vaderlike Wette, establishing an elected kaptein, a Volksraad and courts. They farmed cattle and sheep, spoke Afrikaans and were Lutheran Christians. A protection treaty with Germany in 1885 preserved their autonomy, and they fought on the German side against the Nama in 1904, but clashed with German troops at Sam Khubis in 1915.
rehoboth-basters.e: Under South African rule the Basters kept partial self-government, becoming a self-governing homeland in 1979. Their autonomy ended with Namibian independence in 1990, though the Kaptein's council continued to press its claims.

rif-republic.t: Abd el-Krim's Berber republic in northern Morocco, which crushed a Spanish army at Annual and inspired anticolonial movements worldwide.
rif-republic.o: Muhammad ibn Abd el-Krim al-Khattabi, a Rifian judge and journalist, united the tribes of the Rif against the Spanish protectorate in Morocco. In July 1921 his forces destroyed a Spanish army at Annual, killing thousands. He proclaimed a republic with its capital at Ajdir, formally constituted in 1923.
rif-republic.r: The republic had ministries, a national assembly of tribal representatives, taxes and a disciplined army that used captured artillery and trench warfare. Abd el-Krim banned feuds and enforced Islamic law, aiming at a modern state. In 1925 his offensive against the French protectorate in Morocco brought France into the war.
rif-republic.e: A combined Franco-Spanish force of hundreds of thousands, with a landing at Alhucemas in 1925 and Spanish use of chemical weapons, overwhelmed the Rif. Abd el-Krim surrendered in May 1926 and was exiled to Réunion.

republic-of-chile.t: The South American republic along the Pacific that became independent in 1818 and is known for long periods of constitutional stability, broken by the 1973 coup.
republic-of-chile.o: After the collapse of the Patria Vieja, the Army of the Andes under José de San Martín and Bernardo O'Higgins defeated the royalists at Chacabuco in 1817. O'Higgins, as Supreme Director, signed the declaration of independence dated 1 January 1818 and proclaimed on 12 February, and victory at Maipú in April secured it.
republic-of-chile.r: After a decade of instability, the Constitution of 1833, shaped by Diego Portales, created a strong presidential state. Chile defeated the Peru-Bolivian Confederation in 1839 and won the War of the Pacific from 1879 to 1883, gaining nitrate-rich Tarapacá and Antofagasta. It conquered Araucanía by 1883. Copper later replaced nitrates. Salvador Allende's socialist government was overthrown on 11 September 1973 by Augusto Pinochet, whose dictatorship lasted until 1990.
republic-of-chile.e: Chile returned to democracy after the 1988 plebiscite and has since become one of Latin America's most prosperous economies. Proposals to replace Pinochet's 1980 constitution were rejected in referendums in 2022 and 2023.

republic-of-bologna.t: The city-republic of Europe's oldest university and its forest of towers, which held a captive king for 23 years and later flourished under the Bentivoglio.
republic-of-bologna.o: In 1116 Emperor Henry V granted privileges to the citizens of Bologna, the starting point of the commune. Its law school, traditionally dated to 1088 and associated with the jurist Irnerius, drew students from all over Europe and made the city famous.
republic-of-bologna.r: Bologna was ruled by consuls, then a podestà and popular councils. Noble families built hundreds of defensive towers, including the Asinelli and Garisenda. Guelph Bologna captured King Enzo, son of Frederick II, at Fossalta in 1249 and held him until his death in 1272; the Liber Paradisus of 1256 freed the serfs of its countryside. Nominally under the Papal States, the city was dominated by the Pepoli and then the Bentivoglio families.
republic-of-bologna.e: Pope Julius II marched on Bologna in 1506 and drove out Giovanni II Bentivoglio. The city then passed under direct papal rule, which lasted until 1796, when it briefly became the Bolognese Republic.

rhodanic-republic.t: Napoleonic client republic in the Valais, kept separate from Switzerland to secure the Simplon pass.
rhodanic-republic.o: Napoleon wanted control of the Simplon pass between France and Italy. In 1802 he separated the Valais from the Helvetic Republic and made it a nominally independent Republic of the Rhône (République rhodanienne), under the joint protection of France, the Italian Republic and the Helvetic Republic.
rhodanic-republic.r: The republic was governed by a small administration in Sion under a constitution imposed by France, with a diet and a council of state. Its main obligation was to maintain the new Simplon road, completed by French engineers in 1805, and to allow free passage to French troops. The population was Catholic and largely rural.
rhodanic-republic.e: In November 1810 Napoleon annexed the Valais to France as the department of Simplon. After his fall it became a canton of the Swiss Confederation in 1815.

republic-of-genoa.t: A maritime republic whose fleets and bankers dominated Mediterranean and Black Sea trade and later financed the Spanish Empire, lasting nearly seven centuries.
republic-of-genoa.o: Genoese citizens formed a sworn association, the compagna communis, around 1099, as fleets returned rich from the First Crusade under leaders such as Guglielmo Embriaco. The commune won trading privileges in the crusader states and fought Pisa and Muslim powers for the western Mediterranean.
republic-of-genoa.r: Genoa built colonies at Pera beside Constantinople, Caffa in the Crimea and Chios, and destroyed Pisa's fleet at Meloria in 1284. Factions of great families, the Doria, Spinola, Fieschi and Grimaldi, competed for power; from 1339 doges such as Simone Boccanegra headed the state. The Bank of Saint George, founded in 1407, managed public debt and colonies. Columbus was a Genoese.
republic-of-genoa.e: After losing the War of Chioggia to Venice in 1381, Genoa often fell under French or Milanese rule. Andrea Doria's constitution of 1528 created an aristocratic republic allied to Habsburg Spain, which Genoese bankers financed. Genoa sold Corsica to France in 1768 and became the Ligurian Republic in 1797.

raj-of-sarawak.t: Kingdom in northern Borneo ruled for a century by an English family, the White Rajahs of the Brooke dynasty.
raj-of-sarawak.o: The English adventurer James Brooke helped the Brunei Sultanate put down a revolt of Malays and Bidayuh near Kuching in 1839 to 1841. As a reward the sultan made him Rajah of Sarawak in 1841. Brooke and his successors then took further river basins from Brunei until Sarawak far exceeded the sultanate in size.
raj-of-sarawak.r: The Brookes ruled personally, with a small European staff and Malay chiefs, and governed through longhouse headmen among Iban and other Dayak peoples. They suppressed piracy and headhunting, often with Iban levies, and limited European plantation companies. Chinese settlers grew pepper and mined gold. Charles Brooke ruled for nearly fifty years, and Sarawak became a British protectorate in 1888.
raj-of-sarawak.e: After Japanese occupation from 1941 to 1945, Charles Vyner Brooke ceded Sarawak to Britain in 1946 despite strong local opposition, creating the Crown Colony of Sarawak. It joined Malaysia in 1963.

republic-of-ecuador.t: The Andean republic on the equator, formed when Quito, Guayaquil and Cuenca left Gran Colombia in 1830, which includes the Galápagos Islands.
republic-of-ecuador.o: In May 1830 an assembly in Quito declared the southern district of Gran Colombia an independent state, naming it Ecuador after the equator. The Venezuelan general Juan José Flores became the first president. Ecuador annexed the Galápagos Islands in 1832.
republic-of-ecuador.r: Politics were shaped by rivalry between conservative Quito and liberal Guayaquil. Gabriel García Moreno built a strongly Catholic state until his assassination in 1875, while Eloy Alfaro's Liberal Revolution of 1895 separated church and state and completed the Guayaquil-Quito railway in 1908. Exports of cacao and then bananas drove the economy. After war with Peru in 1941, Ecuador lost much of its Amazon claim under the Rio Protocol of 1942. Oil exports began in 1972.
republic-of-ecuador.e: Democracy returned in 1979. After a banking crisis, Ecuador adopted the US dollar in 2000. Rafael Correa's government from 2007 to 2017 introduced a 2008 constitution recognising the rights of nature. Rising drug-related violence has marked recent years.

republic-of-siena.t: Florence's great Tuscan rival, a banking and wool republic whose Palazzo Pubblico frescoes picture the ideals of good government.
republic-of-siena.o: Siena's citizens took power from their bishop in the early 12th century, and consuls are recorded by 1125. Lying on the Via Francigena pilgrim road, the commune prospered from banking and trade and expanded its territory across southern Tuscany.
republic-of-siena.r: Siena was generally Ghibelline and crushed Florence at Montaperti in 1260 under leaders such as Provenzan Salvani. From 1287 to 1355 the merchant government of the Nine built the Palazzo Pubblico, where Ambrogio Lorenzetti painted his Allegory of Good and Bad Government in 1338–1339. Duccio and Simone Martini made the city a centre of painting. The Black Death of 1348 halted its growth; the Monte dei Paschi bank dates from 1472.
republic-of-siena.e: After a period of rule by Pandolfo Petrucci, Siena rebelled against a Spanish garrison in 1552. Imperial and Florentine troops besieged it until it surrendered in April 1555. Exiles continued as the Republic of Siena at Montalcino, and Siena was granted to the Duchy of Florence in 1557.

republic-of-katagalugan.t: Last revolutionary republic of the Philippine-American War, led by Macario Sakay in the mountains of southern Luzon.
republic-of-katagalugan.o: After the United States declared the Philippine-American War over in 1902, the former Katipunan member Macario Sakay refused to accept defeat. In 1902 he revived the name of Andres Bonifacio's Tagalog Republic and proclaimed the Republic of Katagalugan, with himself as president, in the hills of Rizal and neighbouring provinces.
republic-of-katagalugan.r: The republic had a constitution, a cabinet and a flag, and it organised guerrilla bands that raided towns in Rizal, Cavite, Laguna and Batangas. American authorities labelled its fighters bandits under the Brigandage Act of 1902 and used reconcentration of villagers to cut them off from support.
republic-of-katagalugan.e: In July 1906 Sakay surrendered after the labour leader Dominador Gomez promised amnesty, but he was arrested, tried for banditry and hanged in 1907. He is now honoured as a Filipino patriot.

republic-of-sale.t: A corsair republic of Morisco exiles at the mouth of the Bou Regreg, whose ships raided from the Atlantic coasts to Iceland.
republic-of-sale.o: Moriscos expelled from Spain between 1609 and 1614, among them the Hornacheros from Extremadura, settled in the kasbah of Rabat opposite Salé. In 1627 they declared independence from the Saadi Sultanate, forming a self-governing corsair state.
republic-of-sale.r: The republic was ruled by a council, the divan, and an elected governor. Its corsairs, including the Dutch renegade Jan Janszoon, known as Murat Reis, raided European shipping and coasts, and in 1627 raiders reached Iceland. Captives were ransomed or sold, and European powers signed treaties and bombarded the port in turn. Feuds divided the Hornacheros and later Andalusi settlers.
republic-of-sale.e: From 1641 the Dila'iyya dominated Salé, and in 1668 the Alaouite ruler Moulay al-Rashid took the twin towns. Corsairing continued under the Alaouite Sultanate into the 19th century.

republic-of-haiti-1806-1849.t: The southern Haitian republic of Pétion and Boyer, which reunited Haiti, ruled all of Hispaniola for two decades and paid France a crushing indemnity.
republic-of-haiti-1806-1849.o: After the assassination of Jacques I in 1806, Alexandre Pétion and the southern elite drafted a republican constitution that limited presidential power, prompting Henri Christophe to found a rival state in the north. Pétion was elected president of the republic, based at Port-au-Prince, in 1807, and the two halves fought an inconclusive civil war.
republic-of-haiti-1806-1849.r: Pétion broke up state plantations and distributed land to soldiers and smallholders, creating a peasant economy based on coffee and food crops. He sheltered and armed Simón Bolívar in 1815 to 1816. His successor Jean-Pierre Boyer reunited the north in 1820 and occupied the east in 1822. In 1825 he accepted France's demand for an indemnity of 150 million francs in return for recognition, a debt that burdened Haiti for generations.
republic-of-haiti-1806-1849.e: Boyer was overthrown in 1843, and the Dominican Republic broke away in 1844. A string of short presidencies followed until the senate chose Faustin Soulouque in 1847; he proclaimed himself emperor in 1849, creating the Second Empire of Haiti.

rani.t: A Slavic people on the island of Rügen whose temple of Svantevit at Arkona was the last great pagan sanctuary on the Baltic until the Danes destroyed it.
rani.o: The Rani were West Slavic settlers of the island of Rügen and nearby coast from around the 8th or 9th century. Their island position and the prestige of their sanctuary gave them influence over neighbouring Slavic peoples, and they are mentioned in German and Danish chronicles from the 10th century.
rani.r: The Rani were ruled by princes, but Saxo Grammaticus and Helmold of Bosau describe the high priest of Arkona as the real power. The temple of the four-faced god Svantevit stood on a cliff at Cape Arkona, receiving tribute from other Slavs and keeping a sacred white horse for divination. The Rani raided Danish coasts and traded across the Baltic.
rani.e: In 1168 King Valdemar I of Denmark and Bishop Absalon captured Arkona and destroyed the idol of Svantevit. Prince Jaromar I accepted Christianity and Danish overlordship, founding the Principality of Rügen, which lasted until its absorption into the Duchy of Pomerania in 1325.

republic-of-cospaia.t: A tiny Umbrian republic born of a surveying error in 1440 that lived for nearly four centuries largely on tax-free tobacco.
republic-of-cospaia.o: In 1440 Pope Eugene IV sold Borgo Sansepolcro to the Republic of Florence. The new border was set along a stream, but two streams had the same name, and a strip of land about two kilometres long between them was left out of both states. Its few hundred inhabitants declared themselves independent.
republic-of-cospaia.r: Cospaia had no army, no prisons and no written constitution; a council of elders and heads of families settled affairs in the church. Its motto, Perpetua et firma libertas, was carved over the church door. From the 16th century the villagers grew tobacco, which escaped the monopolies and taxes of the Papal States and the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, and the hamlet became a centre for smuggling.
republic-of-cospaia.e: In 1826 the Papal States and Tuscany agreed to divide the territory. The inhabitants accepted in return for a silver coin each and the right to keep growing tobacco.

regional-defence-council-of-aragon.t: An anarchist-led regional government in eastern Aragon during the Spanish Civil War, known for its sweeping rural collectives.
regional-defence-council-of-aragon.o: In the summer of 1936 anarchist militia columns from Catalonia advanced into eastern Aragon, where collectives sprang up in hundreds of villages. In October 1936 the CNT created the Regional Defence Council of Aragon, first at Fraga and then at Caspe, under Joaquín Ascaso.
regional-defence-council-of-aragon.r: The council organised the collectivisation of land and trade, in some villages abolishing money, and coordinated supplies for the Aragon front. It was later broadened to include other Republican parties and was recognised by Largo Caballero's government in December 1936, though Communists and Republicans criticised it.
regional-defence-council-of-aragon.e: After the May Days of 1937 weakened the anarchists, the Negrín government dissolved the council in August 1937. Enrique Líster's troops arrested its leaders and broke up many collectives. Aragon was overrun by Franco in 1938.

republic-of-iceland.t: Independent Icelandic republic proclaimed at Þingvellir in 1944, a small NATO member famous for its fisheries disputes and parliamentary tradition.
republic-of-iceland.o: After a referendum in which Icelanders voted overwhelmingly to end the union with Denmark, the Kingdom of Iceland became a republic on 17 June 1944, the birthday of the independence leader Jón Sigurðsson, in a ceremony at Þingvellir. Sveinn Björnsson became its first president.
republic-of-iceland.r: Iceland is a parliamentary republic governed through the Althing. It has no army but joined NATO as a founding member in 1949, and a US base operated at Keflavík until 2006. Fishing dominated the economy, and Iceland extended its fishing limits in the Cod Wars with Britain between 1958 and 1976. In 1980 Vigdís Finnbogadóttir became the world's first democratically elected female president.
republic-of-iceland.e: Iceland grew prosperous, diversifying into aluminium smelting with geothermal and hydro power, and tourism. Its banking system collapsed in 2008, but the economy recovered. It remains outside the EU but belongs to the European Economic Area and the Schengen Area.

rhodesia.t: The unrecognised white-minority state declared by Ian Smith in 1965, which fought a long guerrilla war before giving way to Zimbabwe.
rhodesia.o: After the end of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, Britain insisted on progress towards majority rule before independence. Rather than accept this, Ian Smith's Rhodesian Front government of Southern Rhodesia issued a Unilateral Declaration of Independence on 11 November 1965, keeping Salisbury as the capital.
rhodesia.r: No state recognised Rhodesia, and the United Nations imposed sanctions, though trade continued through South Africa and Portuguese Mozambique. A republic was declared in 1970 with Clifford Dupont as president. From the late 1960s and especially after 1972, ZANU and ZAPU guerrillas fought the Bush War, known to nationalists as the second Chimurenga; tens of thousands died and white emigration grew.
rhodesia.e: Under military and economic pressure, Smith signed an Internal Settlement in March 1978 with moderate African leaders including Abel Muzorewa, and the state was renamed Zimbabwe Rhodesia in June 1979.

republic-of-alba.t: A republic proclaimed for a few days in the Piedmontese town of Alba in 1796, the first Jacobin republic on Italian soil.
republic-of-alba.o: As Napoleon's army drove back the Piedmontese troops of the Kingdom of Sardinia in April 1796, local Jacobins led by Ignazio Bonafous and the exiled publicist Giovanni Antonio Ranza entered Alba and proclaimed a republic, hoping for French support for a revolution in Piedmont.
republic-of-alba.r: The republic planted a liberty tree and issued proclamations calling on the Piedmontese to rise, but it had no real institutions and relied on the presence of French troops. Its leaders hoped to spread the revolution to other towns of southern Piedmont.
republic-of-alba.e: Napoleon preferred to make peace with the king. The Armistice of Cherasco, signed on 28 April 1796, returned Alba to the Kingdom of Sardinia, and the republic disappeared after only a few days.

rus-khaganate.t: A shadowy 9th-century polity of Scandinavian Rus' whose ruler took the title khagan, predecessor of the state of Kievan Rus'.
rus-khaganate.o: In 839 envoys of a people called the Rhos, whose ruler was styled chacanus, reached the court of Louis the Pious with a Byzantine embassy and turned out to be Swedes. Historians use the term Rus' Khaganate for this polity of Scandinavian traders and warriors in north-western Russia, but its location, perhaps Ladoga or the Novgorod region, is debated.
rus-khaganate.r: Arab geographers such as Ibn Rusta describe the Rus' as living on a marshy island under a khagan, collecting slaves and furs from the Slavs and selling them for silver. The title was borrowed from the Khazars and claimed equal rank with their ruler. The Rus' attack on Constantinople in 860 may have been launched from this state.
rus-khaganate.e: Its fate is unclear. The chronicle tradition of Rurik's arrival around 862 and Oleg's capture of Kiev in 882 describes the creation of Kievan Rus', into which the earlier khaganate was presumably absorbed. Later Kievan rulers such as Vladimir I were still occasionally called khagan.

republic-of-haiti.t: Haiti as a republic since 1859, shaped by an unpayable debt, US occupation, the Duvalier dictatorship and repeated disasters and crises.
republic-of-haiti.o: General Fabre Geffrard overthrew Emperor Faustin I in December 1858 and restored the republic in 1859. Geffrard signed a concordat with the Vatican in 1860, which brought French clergy to run churches and schools, and invited African American immigrants.
republic-of-haiti.r: Frequent revolts, often by peasant armies called cacos, toppled most 19th-century presidents. The indemnity to France and later loans drained revenue. The United States occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934, building roads but imposing forced labour and crushing resistance led by Charlemagne Péralte. François Duvalier, elected in 1957, ruled with the Tonton Macoute militia; his son Jean-Claude succeeded him in 1971. Coffee and peasant farming sustained the economy as forests vanished.
republic-of-haiti.e: Jean-Claude Duvalier fled in 1986. Jean-Bertrand Aristide was elected in 1990, overthrown in 1991 and removed again in 2004. An earthquake in 2010 killed over 200,000 people. After President Jovenel Moïse was assassinated in 2021, gangs took control of much of Port-au-Prince, and a transitional council has governed since 2024.

republic-of-ragusa.t: Aristocratic merchant republic of Dubrovnik, which grew rich on Balkan and Mediterranean trade and kept its freedom for four and a half centuries.
republic-of-ragusa.o: Ragusa (Dubrovnik) had been a Byzantine and then Venetian-ruled commune. In 1358, under the Treaty of Zadar, Venice gave up Dalmatia to Louis I of Hungary, and Ragusa became a self-governing republic under loose Hungarian protection.
republic-of-ragusa.r: Power lay with the noble Great Council; a rector served a one-month term to prevent anyone gaining personal power. Ragusan merchants carried silver, lead and goods from the Kingdom of Bosnia and Serbian mines, and their fleet traded across the Mediterranean. The republic paid tribute to the Ottomans from 1458 and stayed neutral, banned the slave trade in 1416 and set up early quarantine. Writers such as Marin Držić and Ivan Gundulić made it a centre of Croatian literature.
republic-of-ragusa.e: A great earthquake in 1667 devastated the city, but the republic recovered. French troops occupied it in 1806, and Marshal Marmont abolished it in 1808; it passed to Austria in 1815 and is now part of Croatia.

republic-of-cuba-in-arms.t: The insurgent republic proclaimed by Cuban rebels in their wars of independence against Spain, with its own constitutions, presidents and assembly.
republic-of-cuba-in-arms.o: On 10 October 1868 the planter Carlos Manuel de Céspedes freed his enslaved workers and proclaimed independence at La Demajagua, starting the Ten Years' War. In April 1869 an assembly at Guáimaro adopted a constitution creating the Republic of Cuba in Arms, with Céspedes as president.
republic-of-cuba-in-arms.r: The republic had no fixed capital; its government moved through the eastern countryside held by rebel armies. A legislative House of Representatives often clashed with the president and deposed Céspedes in 1873. Generals Máximo Gómez and Antonio Maceo led the fighting. After the Pact of Zanjón of 1878 the republic lapsed. José Martí's Cuban Revolutionary Party relaunched the war in 1895, and new constitutions at Jimaguayú in 1895 and La Yaya in 1897 revived it.
republic-of-cuba-in-arms.e: The United States intervened in 1898 and defeated Spain, but excluded the Cuban republic from the peace talks. Its assembly dissolved itself in 1899, and Cuba passed under the United States Military Government in Cuba.

rajauri-state.t: A hill state on the road from the Punjab to Kashmir, known as Rajapuri in Kashmiri chronicles and ruled in later centuries by Muslim Jarral Rajas.
rajauri-state.o: Rajapuri appears in Kalhana's Rajatarangini as a hill kingdom bordering Kashmir. Tradition holds that the Jarral dynasty, Rajputs who became Muslim, took power around 1194.
rajauri-state.r: Rajauri controlled a stage on the Mughal road over the Pir Panjal to Kashmir, which the emperors used on their journeys to the valley; Mughal gardens and inns survive along it. In the early 19th century Raja Agar Khan dealt with and fought against the Sikh Empire during Ranjit Singh's Kashmir campaigns.
rajauri-state.e: Rajauri fell under Sikh control and then to Gulab Singh of Jammu, and in 1846 it became part of Jammu and Kashmir (princely state). It is now a district of Jammu and Kashmir.

realm-of-jovan-nenad.t: Brief Serbian realm in the southern Hungarian plain, created by the self-proclaimed tsar Jovan Nenad in the chaos after the battle of Mohács.
realm-of-jovan-nenad.o: After the Ottoman victory at Mohács in 1526, a Serbian adventurer known as Jovan Nenad, the Black Man, gathered an army of Serbian refugees and peasants in Bačka and Banat that may have numbered 15,000. He drove off Ottoman raiders, took control of the region and proclaimed himself tsar, setting up his court at Subotica.
realm-of-jovan-nenad.r: His realm was a military regime resting on his army, which lived from the land and from requisitions on Hungarian nobles. In the contest for the Hungarian throne Jovan Nenad first backed John Zápolya, then switched to Ferdinand of Habsburg. His claim to a Serbian imperial title and his origins remain obscure, and contemporary accounts are partisan.
realm-of-jovan-nenad.e: Zápolya's forces defeated Jovan Nenad in the summer of 1527, and he was killed soon afterwards near Szeged. His army dispersed and the region fell to the Ottomans within a few years. Serbian tradition remembers him as a forerunner of later Serbian autonomy in Vojvodina.

recherla-nayakas.t: Telugu warrior rulers of Rachakonda and Devarakonda who replaced the Musunuris in Telangana and allied with the Bahmanis.
recherla-nayakas.o: The Recherla family were Velama Nayaka commanders who had served the Kakatiya dynasty. In the 1360s, allied with the Bahmani Sultanate, Anapota Nayaka defeated and killed Kapaya Nayaka of the Musunuri Nayaks around 1368 and established rule over Telangana from the hill forts of Rachakonda and Devarakonda.
recherla-nayakas.r: The Recherlas, also called Padmanayakas, ruled through a network of hill forts and warrior families. Their courts supported Telugu and Sanskrit writing; Sarvajna Singabhupala wrote the Rasarnava Sudhakara, a treatise on poetics. They generally sided with the Bahmanis against the Vijayanagara Empire and the Reddi Kingdom.
recherla-nayakas.e: Over the 15th century the Bahmani Sultanate turned against its former allies and gradually annexed their forts; Rachakonda and Devarakonda were absorbed by about 1475. Velama families later served as zamindars under the Golconda Sultanate and the British.

republic-of-cuba-1902-1959.t: Independent Cuba under US tutelage, a sugar republic of dictators and reformers that ended when Fidel Castro's revolution drove out Batista.
republic-of-cuba-1902-1959.o: After the United States Military Government in Cuba ended, the Republic of Cuba was inaugurated on 20 May 1902 with Tomás Estrada Palma as president. Its constitution included the Platt Amendment, which allowed US intervention, and Washington soon used it, occupying the island again from 1906 to 1909.
republic-of-cuba-1902-1959.r: Sugar, largely owned by American firms, dominated the economy, and Havana became a magnet for tourists and gamblers. Gerardo Machado's dictatorship from 1925 ended in revolution in 1933, after which the army sergeant Fulgencio Batista became the power behind governments. The Platt Amendment was repealed in 1934, and a progressive constitution was adopted in 1940. Batista served as elected president from 1940 to 1944, and corruption marked the governments of Grau and Prío that followed.
republic-of-cuba-1902-1959.e: Batista seized power in a coup in 1952. Fidel Castro attacked the Moncada barracks in 1953 and returned on the Granma in 1956 to wage guerrilla war in the Sierra Maestra. Batista fled on 1 January 1959, and the revolutionary Republic of Cuba began.

ramdurg-state.t: A small Maratha Brahmin state in the southern Maratha country, ruled by a branch of the family of Nargund.
ramdurg-state.o: Ramdurg and Nargund were held by the Bhave family, Brahmin officials of the Peshwas. Around 1799 the holding was divided, and Ramdurg became a separate state under a branch of the family.
ramdurg-state.r: Under British rule Ramdurg was a minor state of the Southern Maratha Country, later the Deccan States Agency. Its population was mainly Kannada-speaking farmers. In 1939 peasant agitation for responsible government ended in violence and police firing.
ramdurg-state.e: After accession to India Ramdurg was merged into Bombay State in 1948, and since 1956 its lands have been in Belagavi district of Karnataka.

republic-of-liege.t: The short-lived revolutionary government of Liège, which drove out its prince-bishop in 1789 in a 'happy revolution' inspired by events in Paris.
republic-of-liege.o: Resentment against the authoritarian prince-bishop Constantin-François de Hoensbroeck had grown among Liège's burghers and Enlightenment-minded elites. On 18 August 1789, weeks after the fall of the Bastille, citizens seized the town hall and installed new mayors; the prince-bishop fled, and the Prince-Bishopric of Liège came under patriot control.
republic-of-liege.r: The patriots, led by Jacques-Joseph Fabry and Jean-Rémy de Chestret, governed through a revived city council and the estates, proclaimed the rights of citizens and sought support from Prussia, whose troops briefly occupied the city. The revolution was largely bloodless and called the 'happy revolution', though divisions grew between moderates and radicals.
republic-of-liege.e: After Prussia withdrew, Austrian troops of the Holy Roman Empire restored the prince-bishop in January 1791. His return was brief: French armies arrived in 1792 and again in 1794, and Liège was annexed to France in 1795.

ringerike.t: Inland petty kingdom north-west of Oslo whose last king, Sigurd Syr, was stepfather of Saint Olaf and father of Harald Hardrada.
ringerike.o: Ringerike lay around Lake Tyrifjorden in the inland Upplands of eastern Norway. The sagas name a king Sigurd Hart as ruler here in the 9th century and make his daughter the mother of Harald Fairhair. Like its neighbours, it was a farming district ruled by local kings who might accept a more powerful overlord.
ringerike.r: The area was fertile and well settled, and its kings held large estates. Ringerike lent its name to an art style of the early 11th century, seen on carved stones quarried in the district, with tendrils and animal motifs. Local kings kept their titles under the overlordship of Harald Fairhair's successors.
ringerike.e: Its best-known king, Sigurd Syr, married Åsta, mother of Olaf Haraldsson, and supported Olaf's bid for the Norwegian throne in 1015. Sigurd died around 1018, and Olaf soon put an end to the Uppland petty kings, so Ringerike became part of the Kingdom of Norway. Sigurd's son was Harald Hardrada.

ritsuryo-japan.t: The classical Japanese imperial state of the Nara and Heian periods, governed by Chinese-style law codes and home to the courtly culture of The Tale of Genji.
ritsuryo-japan.o: The Taiho code of 701 gave Japan a full system of penal and administrative law modelled on Tang China, completing reforms begun under Yamato. In 710 the court moved to the planned capital of Heijo-kyo at Nara, and the first histories, the Kojiki of 712 and the Nihon shoki of 720, presented the emperors as descendants of the sun goddess.
ritsuryo-japan.r: A Council of State, eight ministries and provincial governors administered land allotted to cultivators in return for taxes and labour. Emperor Shomu built Todai-ji with its Great Buddha, dedicated in 752. Kammu moved the capital to Heian-kyo in 794. From the 9th century Fujiwara regents ruled in the emperor's name, and court women wrote masterpieces in the new kana script.
ritsuryo-japan.e: Private estates eroded the tax base and provincial warriors grew powerful. The Genpei War of 1180 to 1185 brought Minamoto no Yoritomo to power and the Kamakura shogunate, though the imperial court survived in Kyoto.

rai-dynasty.t: A dynasty of Sindh known from the Chach Nama, which ruled the lower Indus from Aror before the Brahman dynasty took power.
rai-dynasty.o: The Rai dynasty is known almost entirely from the Chach Nama, a Persian history of the Arab conquest of Sindh written in the 13th century from earlier Arabic sources. It describes a line of five kings ruling Sindh from Aror, near modern Sukkur, from around the end of the 5th century.
rai-dynasty.r: The Chach Nama portrays a large kingdom stretching from Kashmir's borders to the sea and from Makran to the edge of Rajasthan, divided into provinces under governors. Buddhism was widespread in Sindh in this period, as Xuanzang confirms, and the dynasty was reportedly Buddhist or tolerant of Buddhism. One king is said to have died fighting an army from Sasanian Persia.
rai-dynasty.e: According to the Chach Nama, after the death of the last king, Rai Sahasi II, his Brahmin chamberlain Chach married the widowed queen and seized the throne around 632, founding the Brahman dynasty of Sindh.

revolutionary-government-of-the-philippi.t: Government set up by Emilio Aguinaldo in 1898 that declared Philippine independence from Spain and prepared the Malolos Republic.
revolutionary-government-of-the-philippi.o: After the United States destroyed the Spanish fleet at Manila Bay on 1 May 1898, Emilio Aguinaldo returned from exile in Hong Kong and on 24 May proclaimed a dictatorial government at Cavite. He declared independence at Kawit on 12 June 1898, and on the advice of Apolinario Mabini converted his regime into a Revolutionary Government on 23 June.
revolutionary-government-of-the-philippi.r: Aguinaldo ruled as president with a cabinet of secretaries, while provincial and municipal governments were organised in liberated areas. Revolutionary armies took most of Luzon from Spanish garrisons. A congress met at Barasoain church in Malolos in September 1898 and drafted the Malolos Constitution, drawing on Spanish and Latin American models.
revolutionary-government-of-the-philippi.e: The United States refused to recognise the government, and the Treaty of Paris of December 1898 transferred the islands from Spain to America. The Revolutionary Government gave way to the First Philippine Republic on 23 January 1899.

roman-egypt.t: Egypt as the richest province of the Roman and Byzantine empires, the granary of Rome and a cradle of Christian monasticism.
roman-egypt.o: After the deaths of Antony and Cleopatra VII in 30 BCE, Octavian annexed the Ptolemaic Empire's heartland. Egypt was governed by an equestrian prefect answerable to the emperor alone, and senators were forbidden to enter without permission, so valuable was its grain.
roman-egypt.r: Egypt's harvest fed Rome and later Constantinople. Alexandria remained a great centre of Greek learning, home to Ptolemy, Plotinus and the Catechetical School. Papyri from Oxyrhynchus document daily life in detail. Christianity spread quickly: Anthony and Pachomius founded desert monasticism and Athanasius shaped orthodoxy. After the Council of Chalcedon in 451, most Egyptians followed the Coptic Church against the imperial church, and Coptic writing developed from Egyptian.
roman-egypt.e: The Persians occupied Egypt as Sasanian Egypt from 619 to 629, and Heraclius recovered it. In 639 to 641 Amr ibn al-As invaded for the Rashidun Caliphate, and Alexandria surrendered by treaty, ending nearly seven centuries of Roman rule.

roman-cyrenaica.t: The Roman and Byzantine province of eastern Libya, a Greek-speaking land of five cities on the Jebel Akhdar.
roman-cyrenaica.o: Cyrenaica was bequeathed to Rome by Ptolemy Apion of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Cyrene in 96 BCE and organised as a province in 74 BCE. After Quintus Metellus conquered Crete in 67 BCE, the two were joined as the province of Crete and Cyrenaica, administered by a proconsul.
roman-cyrenaica.r: The Greek cities of the Pentapolis, Cyrene, Apollonia, Ptolemais, Taucheira and Berenice, kept Greek language and institutions. The region exported grain and wine, though silphium died out under Roman rule. A large Jewish community rose in the revolt of 115 to 117 CE, devastating Cyrene. Diocletian split the region into Libya Superior and Libya Inferior. Bishop Synesius of Ptolemais described raids by the Austuriani around 400.
roman-cyrenaica.e: From 395 the province belonged to the Byzantine Empire, but its cities declined. In 642 to 643 Arab forces under Amr ibn al-As took Barca and the Pentapolis for the Rashidun Caliphate, and the region became an Islamic province known as Barqa.

republic-of-lower-california.t: Paper republic proclaimed by the American filibuster William Walker after his raid on Baja California in 1853, which collapsed within months.
republic-of-lower-california.o: William Walker, a Tennessee-born adventurer, sailed from San Francisco with about 45 men and landed at La Paz in November 1853. He arrested the governor and declared Baja California an independent republic with himself as president, then moved north to Ensenada.
republic-of-lower-california.r: The republic existed mainly on paper. In January 1854 Walker also proclaimed the Republic of Sonora, claiming the mainland state, and introduced the laws of Louisiana, including slavery. His men had little food or money, many deserted, and Mexican forces and local ranchers harassed them. He controlled only a few settlements on the Pacific coast.
republic-of-lower-california.e: Walker's attempt to march into Sonora failed, and in May 1854 he and his remaining men surrendered to US forces at the border. He was tried in San Francisco for violating neutrality laws and acquitted. He later seized power in Nicaragua and was executed in Honduras in 1860.

rairakhol-state.t: A small, forested princely state in western Odisha, one of the Garhjat states ruled by local Rajas until 1948.
rairakhol-state.o: The ruling family was connected with the Chauhan rulers of Sambalpur State, and tradition dates the state to around 1500. Its early history is poorly recorded.
rairakhol-state.r: Rairakhol was a hilly, thinly populated state of forest and small farms. It was part of the Sambalpur group of chiefships under the Marathas and came under British supervision in the 19th century, joining the Orissa Tributary States in 1905.
rairakhol-state.e: Rairakhol merged into Orissa on 1 January 1948 and is now in Sambalpur district.

republic-of-brescia.t: A republic proclaimed in Brescia in March 1797 when the city overthrew Venetian rule, one of the blows that hastened the end of Venice.
republic-of-brescia.o: Brescia had been a Venetian mainland city since 1426. On 18 March 1797, a few days after Bergamo, local patriots backed by French troops and Bergamasque volunteers seized power, expelled the Venetian governor and proclaimed the Brescian Republic.
republic-of-brescia.r: The provisional government abolished Venetian institutions, planted liberty trees and raised a national guard. It sent forces to spread the revolt to the Brescian valleys and Lake Garda towns, where peasants loyal to Venice and the Church resisted. It depended on French protection, and its leaders sought union with the Lombard republics.
republic-of-brescia.e: After the fall of the Republic of Venice in May 1797, Brescia was incorporated into the Cisalpine Republic in late 1797.

republic-of-lithuania-1918-1940.t: Interwar independent Lithuania, ruled from Kaunas because of the loss of Vilnius, and later under the authoritarian presidency of Antanas Smetona.
republic-of-lithuania-1918-1940.o: On 16 February 1918 the Council of Lithuania in Vilnius, chaired by Jonas Basanavicius with Antanas Smetona as a leading member, declared independence. After a brief attempt at the Kingdom of Lithuania (1918), it fought Soviet, Bermontian and Polish forces. When Poland seized Vilnius in 1920, Kaunas became the temporary capital.
republic-of-lithuania-1918-1940.r: The constitution of 1922 created a parliamentary republic under presidents Aleksandras Stulginskis and Kazys Grinius. Land reform broke up great estates, and dairy and flax exports grew. Lithuania took Klaipeda in 1923. In December 1926 a military coup restored Smetona as president, and he ruled in an authoritarian, nationalist style until 1940.
republic-of-lithuania-1918-1940.e: In 1939 Lithuania lost Klaipeda to Nazi Germany and regained Vilnius from the USSR. In June 1940 the Soviet Union occupied the country, and a staged parliament proclaimed the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic. Smetona fled abroad.

republic-of-paraguay.t: A landlocked South American republic shaped by long dictatorships and one of history's most devastating wars, and among the most bilingual nations in the world.
republic-of-paraguay.o: In 1811 Paraguay defeated an army from Buenos Aires under Manuel Belgrano and in May overthrew the Spanish governor of the Governorate of Paraguay, becoming independent. José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia ruled as perpetual dictator from 1814 to 1840, closing the country to outside contact and confiscating church lands.
republic-of-paraguay.r: Carlos Antonio López opened Paraguay and built railways and an ironworks. His son Francisco Solano López led it into the War of the Triple Alliance against Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay from 1864 to 1870, in which Paraguay lost much of its population and territory. In the Chaco War of 1932 to 1935 it defeated the Republic of Bolivia. Alfredo Stroessner ruled from 1954 to 1989.
republic-of-paraguay.e: After Stroessner's overthrow in 1989, Paraguay adopted a democratic constitution in 1992. The Itaipú dam, shared with Brazil, made it a major exporter of electricity, alongside soya and beef. Guaraní and Spanish are both official languages.

republic-of-india.t: The world's most populous country and largest democracy, a federal republic since its constitution came into force in 1950.
republic-of-india.o: The Dominion of India became a republic on 26 January 1950, when the constitution drafted by the Constituent Assembly under B. R. Ambedkar came into force. Rajendra Prasad became the first president, while Jawaharlal Nehru continued as prime minister, governing a federation of states and union territories from New Delhi.
republic-of-india.r: India is a parliamentary democracy with universal suffrage, an independent judiciary and a federal structure; states were reorganised on linguistic lines from 1956. Nehru pursued planned development and non-alignment. Indira Gandhi's Emergency of 1975 to 1977 suspended civil liberties. Wars were fought with China in 1962 and Pakistan in 1965 and 1971, nuclear tests followed in 1974 and 1998, and economic liberalisation began in 1991.
republic-of-india.e: The republic continues today with regular elections and coalition and single-party governments. It annexed Goa from Portuguese India in 1961 and Sikkim joined in 1975. India's population overtook China's around 2023.

republic-of-west-florida.t: A 74-day republic declared by American settlers in Spanish West Florida in 1810, swiftly annexed by the United States.
republic-of-west-florida.o: The strip of Gulf Coast between the Mississippi and Perdido rivers remained Spanish after the Louisiana Purchase, though the United States claimed it. Many settlers in the Baton Rouge district were Americans. On 23 September 1810 rebels stormed the Spanish fort at Baton Rouge, and three days later a convention declared independence.
republic-of-west-florida.r: The republic adopted a constitution modelled on American practice, elected Fulwar Skipwith as governor and set its capital at St. Francisville. It flew a blue flag with a single white star, later known as the Bonnie Blue Flag. Its leaders hoped for admission to the United States on favourable terms, and it raised a small militia that tried to march on Mobile.
republic-of-west-florida.e: President James Madison proclaimed the territory part of the United States in October 1810, and American troops took over in December. Most of it became the Florida Parishes of Louisiana; the area east of the Pearl River later went to Mississippi and Alabama.

republic-of-somaliland.t: A self-declared republic in northern Somalia, stable and democratic by regional standards, which has sought international recognition since 1991.
republic-of-somaliland.o: After the fall of Siad Barre, the Somali National Movement, which had fought his regime in the north, declared the restoration of Somaliland's independence at Burao on 18 May 1991, within the borders of former British Somaliland. A conference of clan elders at Borama in 1993 chose Muhammad Haji Ibrahim Egal as president.
republic-of-somaliland.r: Somaliland built a hybrid system combining an elected president and parliament with a House of Elders, the Guurti, rooted in clan institutions. After clan conflicts in the mid-1990s it has stayed largely peaceful, holding contested but competitive elections. Its economy depends on livestock exports, remittances and the port of Berbera, developed with DP World investment.
republic-of-somaliland.e: No UN member state has formally recognised Somaliland, and Somalia regards it as part of its territory. It maintains its own currency, army and passports, and power has changed hands through elections, as in 2024. Its capital is Hargeisa.

republic-of-franceville.t: A short-lived self-governing commune at Port Vila in the New Hebrides, often said to be the first polity with universal suffrage regardless of sex or race.
republic-of-franceville.o: In 1887 Britain and France agreed that neither would annex the New Hebrides, leaving the islands without any government over the settlers. In 1889 residents of the Port Vila area, mostly French settlers linked to the Société Française des Nouvelles-Hébrides, declared an independent municipality called Franceville.
republic-of-franceville.r: Its charter gave the vote to all adult residents, men and women, without regard to race, though only white men could hold office. It had a small elected council and an elected president, and it relied on the goodwill of planters and traders in a population of a few hundred Europeans and many more ni-Vanuatu. Little is recorded of its day-to-day administration.
republic-of-franceville.e: Britain and France, unwilling to accept an independent settler state, refused to recognise it, and the commune collapsed in 1890. The islands later came under joint rule as the New Hebrides Condominium, and the site is now Port Vila, capital of Vanuatu.

republic-of-crema.t: A brief Jacobin republic proclaimed in Crema in March 1797, when the town broke from Venice in the last weeks of the Serenissima.
republic-of-crema.o: Crema, a Lombard town between Milan and Cremona, had belonged to the Republic of Venice since 1449. On 28 March 1797, following the revolts of Bergamo and Brescia and with French troops present, local patriots deposed the Venetian governor and proclaimed the Cremasque Republic.
republic-of-crema.r: The republic was a provisional government of local notables and Jacobins under French protection. It abolished Venetian institutions and noble privileges, set up committees on the French model and looked to union with the new Lombard republics. Little is known of its brief administration.
republic-of-crema.e: After the fall of Venice in May 1797, Crema was absorbed into the Cisalpine Republic later that year, ending its separate existence.

republic-of-german-austria.t: The short-lived first Austrian republic of 1918-19, created from the German-speaking lands of the Habsburg monarchy and seeking union with Germany.
republic-of-german-austria.o: As Austria-Hungary dissolved, the German-speaking members of the Imperial Council formed a provisional national assembly on 21 October 1918. On 12 November 1918, the day after Emperor Charles I withdrew from government, it proclaimed the Republic of German-Austria, declaring it part of the German Republic.
republic-of-german-austria.r: Karl Renner of the Social Democrats led the government as state chancellor. The republic claimed the Sudetenland, South Tyrol and other German-speaking areas, but could not enforce these claims. It faced hunger, inflation, returning soldiers and a communist putsch attempt, and abolished the nobility and banished the Habsburgs in April 1919.
republic-of-german-austria.e: The Treaty of Saint-Germain in September 1919 forbade union with Germany and set Austria's borders. On 21 October 1919 the state was renamed the Republic of Austria, the First Austrian Republic.

republic-of-sassari.t: A self-governing Sardinian city-republic that rose from the ruins of the Judicate of Logudoro and wrote its laws partly in Sardinian.
republic-of-sassari.o: After the death of Adelasia ended the Judicate of Logudoro in 1259, the growing town of Sassari took control of its own affairs and part of the surrounding territory. From 1272 it governed itself as a commune under Pisan influence, before allying with the Republic of Genoa in 1294.
republic-of-sassari.r: The free commune was led by a podestà sent from Genoa and local councils. Its statutes of 1316, the Statuti Sassaresi, survive in Latin and Sardinian versions and regulated trade, farming and justice. Sassari lived from grain, livestock and trade through Porto Torres.
republic-of-sassari.e: In 1323 Sassari submitted to the Infante Alfonso of the Kingdom of Aragon at the start of the Aragonese conquest, becoming part of the new Kingdom of Sardinia. It revolted several times in the following years.

roman-kingdom.t: Rome under its seven kings, traditionally 753–509 BCE, when a Latin settlement on the Tiber became a city with temples, a forum and institutions that outlived the monarchy.
roman-kingdom.o: Rome grew from Iron Age villages on the Palatine and nearby hills by the Tiber crossing. Tradition dated its founding by Romulus to 753 BCE; archaeology shows settlement from the 10th century BCE and the drainage and paving of the Forum around 650–600 BCE, when the villages became a single city.
roman-kingdom.r: The king (rex) ruled with the advice of a Senate of clan elders, and the people were organised in thirty curiae. Tradition credits Numa Pompilius with Rome's religious institutions and Servius Tullius with the census and a new army based on wealth classes. The last three kings had Etruscan links; under them Rome built the Cloaca Maxima and the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol, and became the leading city of Latium.
roman-kingdom.e: Tradition says that after Sextus Tarquinius raped Lucretia, Lucius Junius Brutus led the nobles in expelling Tarquinius Superbus in 509 BCE. The kingship was replaced by two annually elected consuls, founding the Roman Republic. The title rex survived only in a priesthood, and Romans long hated the very word.

rattanakosin-kingdom.t: Siam under the Chakri dynasty from the founding of Bangkok in 1782 to the 1932 revolution, the only Southeast Asian state to escape colonisation.
rattanakosin-kingdom.o: In 1782 Chao Phraya Chakri, Taksin's leading general, deposed the Thonburi Kingdom's king and became Rama I. He moved the capital across the Chao Phraya to Bangkok, on Rattanakosin island, where he built the Grand Palace and installed the Emerald Buddha at Wat Phra Kaew.
rattanakosin-kingdom.r: Early Chakri kings rebuilt Siamese power, reasserting control over Lan Na, the Lao kingdoms and Cambodia. Rama III expanded Chinese trade. Mongkut signed the Bowring Treaty with Britain in 1855, opening the economy. Chulalongkorn abolished slavery, created ministries and provincial administration, and built railways, while ceding Laos and Cambodian provinces to France and Malay states to Britain to keep independence.
rattanakosin-kingdom.e: Growing discontent among the educated elite led to the bloodless revolution of 24 June 1932 by the Khana Ratsadon, which ended absolute monarchy under Prajadhipok. Siam continued as a constitutional monarchy, renamed Thailand in 1939.

ryukyu-domain.t: The transitional status imposed on the Ryukyu Kingdom by Meiji Japan from 1872 until its annexation as Okinawa Prefecture in 1879.
ryukyu-domain.o: After the abolition of domains in mainland Japan in 1871, the Meiji government moved to assert sole control over Ryukyu, which had long been a tributary of both Qing China and the Satsuma Domain. In 1872 King Sho Tai was named lord of the new Ryukyu Domain.
ryukyu-domain.r: The royal government at Shuri continued to run local affairs, but foreign relations passed to Tokyo. Japan used the killing of shipwrecked Ryukyuan sailors in Taiwan in 1871 to launch its Taiwan expedition of 1874, presenting Ryukyuans as Japanese subjects. In 1875 Tokyo ordered Ryukyu to stop sending tribute to China, which the court resisted.
ryukyu-domain.e: In 1879 the official Matsuda Michiyuki arrived with police and troops, abolished the domain and created Okinawa Prefecture; Sho Tai was moved to Tokyo. The Qing protested, but the annexation stood.

republic-of-ararat.t: A Kurdish self-proclaimed republic around Mount Ararat, crushed by Turkey in 1930.
republic-of-ararat.o: After the failure of the Sheikh Said rebellion of 1925, Kurdish nationalists founded the Xoybun league in 1927. That year, in October, it proclaimed a Kurdish republic in the region of Mount Ararat, near the borders with Iran and the Soviet Union, with Ihsan Nuri Pasha as military commander and the tribal leader Ibrahim Heski as civil governor.
republic-of-ararat.r: The republic was a rebel administration based in the mountain villages, with its centre at Kurd Ava, relying on tribal fighters and support from Kurdish exiles. Its control was limited to the Ararat massif and surrounding valleys.
republic-of-ararat.e: Turkey launched major campaigns in 1930, accompanied by mass killings in the Zilan valley. Using Iranian territory with Tehran's consent, Turkish forces encircled the rebels, who were defeated by autumn 1930. Turkey and Iran adjusted their border in 1932, giving Turkey the slopes of Little Ararat.

rinpungpa.t: A family of ministers from Tsang who overshadowed the Phagmodrupa kings and dominated western and central Tibet for over a century.
rinpungpa.o: The Rinpung family served the Phagmodrupa dynasty as governors in the Tsang region of west-central Tibet. In 1435, after a succession crisis at the Phagmodru court, Norbu Zangpo of Rinpung seized the fortress of Samdrubtse (Shigatse), and the family became the real power in Tsang while still nominally serving the Phagmodru kings.
rinpungpa.r: The Rinpungpa governed through fortress-districts and alliances with local nobles. They were patrons of the Karma Kagyu school and its Karmapa lamas, and under Donyö Dorje, at the height of their power around 1500, they took control of the Lhasa region and banned Gelug monks from Lhasa's great prayer festival between 1498 and 1517.
rinpungpa.e: Their power declined after 1512 through internal quarrels. Zhingshak Tseten Dorje, a former Rinpungpa official at Samdrubtse, rebelled in the 1550s and in 1565 founded the Tsangpa dynasty, which took over Rinpung's position.

republic-of-estonia.t: The Estonian nation-state, declared in 1918, occupied by the Soviet Union from 1940 and restored in 1991 as a digital-minded EU and NATO member.
republic-of-estonia.o: The Salvation Committee declared the Republic of Estonia on 24 February 1918, building on the Autonomous Governorate of Estonia. After German occupation, Estonia fought the War of Independence against Soviet Russia and the Baltic German Landeswehr, and the Treaty of Tartu in February 1920 secured its independence.
republic-of-estonia.r: The interwar republic carried out a radical land reform breaking the Baltic German estates, and granted cultural autonomy to minorities. Konstantin Päts ruled by decree from 1934. The Soviet Union occupied Estonia in 1940, creating the Estonian Soviet Socialist Republic, followed by German occupation and renewed Soviet rule, with mass deportations.
republic-of-estonia.e: The Singing Revolution of the late 1980s led to the restoration of independence on 20 August 1991, based on legal continuity with the pre-war republic. Estonia joined the EU and NATO in 2004 and the eurozone in 2011, and became known for its e-government and technology sector.

roman-republic.t: The Roman state from the expulsion of the kings to Augustus, which grew from a city in Latium to master of the Mediterranean before collapsing in civil war.
roman-republic.o: Tradition dates the Republic to 509 BCE, when Roman aristocrats expelled Tarquinius Superbus and replaced the king with two consuls elected each year. The early Republic was a small city-state in Latium, at war with its neighbours and divided internally between patricians and plebeians.
roman-republic.r: Power was shared between annual magistrates, the Senate of former officials and the citizen assemblies, with tribunes protecting plebeians. The Twelve Tables of 451–450 BCE codified law. Rome conquered Italy by 270 BCE through alliances and colonies, defeated Carthage in the Punic Wars, and took Macedon, Greece, Spain and Africa. Conquest brought slaves, wealth and an army of professional soldiers loyal to their generals, while Greek culture transformed Roman literature and art.
roman-republic.e: From the Gracchi in 133 BCE, political violence grew: Marius, Sulla, Pompey and Julius Caesar fought civil wars, and Caesar became dictator for life before his murder in 44 BCE. After Octavian defeated Antony at Actium in 31 BCE he received the name Augustus in 27 BCE, beginning the Roman Empire.

republic-of-saint-titus.t: Rebel republic proclaimed by Venetian colonists in Crete in 1363, which briefly united Latin and Greek Cretans against Venice.
republic-of-saint-titus.o: In 1363 Venice demanded a new tax from the feudal settlers of Venetian Crete to pay for repairs to the harbour of Candia. The colonists, already resentful at being excluded from power in Venice, rebelled under leaders including Marco Gradenigo and Tito Venier, imprisoned the Venetian duke and proclaimed independence under Saint Titus, patron of Crete.
republic-of-saint-titus.r: The rebels formed a government in Candia led by a governor and councillors. To win Greek support they made concessions to the Orthodox church and drew in Greek nobles such as the Kallergis family. Their republic lacked outside allies: the pope and other powers backed Venice.
republic-of-saint-titus.e: Venice sent a mercenary army under Luchino dal Verme, which retook Candia in May 1364. Leaders were executed and Saint Mark's banner restored, though Greek rebels led by the Kallergis brothers fought on until 1367.

roman-britain.t: The Roman province of Britannia, ruled from 43 until about 410, which brought towns, roads, villas, Latin and Christianity to most of what is now England and Wales.
roman-britain.o: Julius Caesar raided Britain in 55 and 54 BCE, but conquest began only in 43, when Claudius sent Aulus Plautius with four legions. Camulodunum fell, and over the next forty years the army pushed west and north, overcoming the revolt of Boudica in 60 or 61 and reaching the far north under Agricola, who defeated the Caledonians at Mons Graupius in 83 or 84.
roman-britain.r: Britain was governed by a senatorial legate commanding up to three legions, based at Caerleon, Chester and York. Hadrian's Wall, begun in 122, and briefly the Antonine Wall marked the northern frontier. Severus divided the province in two, and later four provinces formed a diocese. Towns such as Londinium, the main city, grew with fora and baths; villas, wool, grain, lead and tin sustained the economy. Christianity spread from the 3rd century.
roman-britain.e: From the late 3rd century Saxon, Pictish and Irish raids increased, and usurpers such as Carausius and Constantine III drew troops away. By about 410, when Honorius reportedly told the cities to look to their own defence, Roman rule had ended. Successor kingdoms such as the Kingdom of Powys and the Kingdom of Dumnonia arose from its remains.

raigarh-state.t: A Gond-ruled state of eastern Chhattisgarh whose music-loving ruler made it a centre of Kathak dance.
raigarh-state.o: Raigarh was ruled by a Raj Gond dynasty whose traditions say they came from Chanda (Chandrapur). The register dates the state to around 1625. It was later a dependency of the Bhonsles of Nagpur before passing under British paramountcy.
raigarh-state.r: The Rajas ruled a territory of rice fields and forests along the Mand river. Raja Chakradhar Singh, who reigned from 1924, gathered leading musicians and dancers at his court and wrote treatises on dance, giving rise to the Raigarh gharana of Kathak.
raigarh-state.e: Raigarh merged into the Central Provinces and Berar in 1948, later Madhya Pradesh. Since 2000 it has been in Chhattisgarh, where the annual Chakradhar Samaroh festival of music recalls its court.

rajkot-state.t: A Jadeja Rajput state of Kathiawar whose capital hosted the British agency for the peninsula and where Gandhi spent his boyhood.
rajkot-state.o: Rajkot was founded in 1620 by Vibhaji Ajoji, a grandson of Jam Sataji of Nawanagar, who received the area as his share. The town was later briefly held by Mughal officers, but the Jadeja line recovered it.
rajkot-state.r: The Thakore Sahibs ruled a small territory, but Rajkot became important as the seat of the British agency for Kathiawar and of Rajkumar College for princes. Karamchand Gandhi, father of Mohandas Gandhi, served as its diwan. Lakhajirajsinhji II introduced a representative assembly, while the 1939 Rajkot satyagraha challenged his successor.
rajkot-state.e: Rajkot merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948 and served as that state's capital until 1956. It became part of Bombay State and then Gujarat in 1960, and is now one of Gujarat's largest cities.
